pages.title: Steve CAD
pages.description: Build, inspect, edit and export on this machine.
pages.html:
Start with a part

Use File → New part, then sketch and add features, or ask Steve to build one. The model, its feature history and its Python source describe the same design. Start with your first part or browse the modeling tools.

Work with an assembly

A design combines components, shared parameters and links to other saved documents. Use the assembly tools to place components, add joints and inspect fit. Linked documents use a specific saved revision, so changing a part doesn't silently change every assembly.

Inspect before exporting

Select faces and edges in the view. Use Measure, Section analysis, the Inspector and the feature history to check the result. Create engineering drawings when you need dimensions and manufacturing notes. Export STEP for CAD exchange, STL or 3MF for printing, and PDF, SVG or DXF for drawings.

Keep your work

Ctrl+S saves a local document revision. Save with message… adds a note to the revision. Version history lets you inspect and restore earlier work. Keep exported source and imported geometry together when moving a project between machines.

This desktop workspace

CAD computation and saved documents stay on this machine. Chat uses your connected subscription; configured remote MCP services communicate with their own servers. Manage these in Settings. The modeling reference follows the Studio CAD runtime shipped with this build. This manual is available offline.

pages.title: Your first part
pages.description: A plate with a hole, made with the human tools.
pages.html:
Create the plate

  1. Choose File → New part and give the part a useful name.
  2. Click Sketch and choose the XY plane.
  3. Draw a closed rectangle. Use dimensions to set its width and depth.
  4. Finish the sketch. Select it and click Extrude.
  5. Set the distance to 6 mm, then click OK.

Add a hole

  1. Select the plate's top face and click Hole.
  2. Set the hole diameter and its position on the face.
  3. Leave Depth empty for a through hole, or enter a depth for a blind hole, then click OK. See Hole for the available fields.

Inspect and change it

Use Fit all to frame the model. Select the plate or a face to inspect its dimensions and properties. Select the feature in the history and choose Edit to change its inputs; Cancel discards an uncommitted preview. Read selection and feature history for the detailed controls.

Save and export

Press Ctrl+S. To describe a milestone, use File → Save with message…. Choose Export STEP and select a destination on your machine. Use Download source as well if you need to keep editing the feature-based model elsewhere.

pages.title: Save & version history
pages.description: Inspect an earlier model or restore it without deleting later revisions.
pages.html:
Save a revision

Ctrl+S saves the name, source files and links. Save with message… also records a short description. Geometry is attached only when it was built successfully from that revision's source. Saving unbuilt edits does not attach an older model as if it were the new one.

View an earlier revision

Open Versions with Ctrl+Shift+H. Select a revision, then choose Source to read its code or View to show its saved model. The viewport banner identifies the revision being previewed. The Inspector reports that model's dimensions, material and mass. Back to current returns to your current model. View is unavailable when a revision has no matching saved geometry.

Restore

Save or discard current edits before restoring. Select an earlier revision and choose Restore or Make current. Steve saves it as a new revision. Later revisions remain in history, so you can restore them again.

Local scope

The desktop currently keeps a linear revision history. Branching and merging are not implemented locally. Document revision history is separate from the feature timeline and the source editor's undo history.

pages.title: Work with Steve
pages.description: Use the assistant alongside the CAD viewport.
pages.html:
Connect your account

Open Settings → STEVE and sign in with ChatGPT. The sign-in flow opens in your browser. After connecting, choose a model and an effort level in the assistant.

Ask for a CAD change

Describe the geometry, units, constraints and intended result. Keep the relevant document open. Steve can use the local CAD tools to read, build, inspect, edit and export it. Ask for explicit inspection of dimensions or clearances when they matter, and review the resulting model. Ctrl+Enter sends a message; Enter inserts a new line. Use Stop to cancel a running response.

Show Steve an image

Paste with Ctrl+V in the message field, drop an image, or use Attach images. Use Attach the current view to capture the CAD viewport. You can attach up to four images, with or without a written message. Click a sent image to open it full size. Images are stored encrypted locally and sent to the selected model with your conversation.

Diagnose a failed request

Open Settings → STEVE → Diagnostics for the failure's reference ID, original error details and stack locations. Recent records persist encrypted on this device. Copy diagnostics copies the records for review and sharing. Failures from builds without logging cannot be recovered.

Instructions, skills and memory

Settings → Instructions controls the system prompt. Skills configures trusted instruction libraries. Memory lets you review and edit the local notes available to Steve. These guide future requests; they do not change an existing CAD document by themselves.

Tools and services

Enable file/script tools and configure MCP servers in Settings → Tools & MCP. A remote service may ask you to authenticate with that service. Connecting to the hosted Studio MCP is optional and separate from your ChatGPT subscription and local CAD runtime.

pages.title: Settings
pages.description: Configure the local workspace and assistant.
pages.html:
Navigation and display

Open Settings with Ctrl+, or the gear in the top bar. Navigation controls view interaction. Display controls the appearance of the workspace. Code editor controls editor behavior.

Performance

Performance sets the shared CPU budget for local CAD work. The default is 80%. Warm workers reduce startup latency; each job runs in its own process and retires afterward. Independent jobs and supported native geometry operations can run in parallel. A single build may still have serial phases, so the CPU budget is a ceiling rather than a promised utilization level. Use Stop build to cancel.

Tools & MCP

Configure local stdio or remote HTTP MCP servers in Tools & MCP. Use the server's sign-in control when authentication is required. A remote server's account is separate from your ChatGPT account. Enable only the services and local capabilities you intend Steve to use.

Instructions, skills and memory

Use Instructions for the system prompt and script settings, Skills for instruction libraries, and Memory for Steve's local notes. Account connection lives in STEVE.

pages.title: Commands & shortcuts
pages.description: Find a tool by name and keep your hands on the keyboard.
pages.html:
Find any command

Press Ctrl+K to open the command palette. Search by a tool's name, such as Fillet, Section analysis, Save with message, or Export drawing. Unavailable commands explain what they need. Press ? to see the current keyboard shortcut reference inside the workspace.

Action Shortcut
Save Ctrl+S
Open documents Ctrl+O
Version history Ctrl+Shift+H
Settings Ctrl+,
Help F1
Assistant Ctrl+I
Send a chat message Ctrl+Enter
Extrude E
Fillet Shift+F
New sketch Shift+S

Single-letter modeling shortcuts do not run while typing in a text field. Sketching has its own tool shortcuts.

pages.title: Design parts
pages.description: Model single parts in STEVE's Design workspace, with sketches, features, parameters, materials and the code behind them.
pages.html:
The Design workspace is where you model. A part is built from sketches and features, in order, and every step is a line of CadQuery code that you can read and edit.

Model

  • Parts, sketches and constraints: what a part is, how to draw a sketch, and how dimensions and constraints pin it down.
  • Modelling features: every command on the Solid ribbon of the ribbon: extrude, revolve, sweep, loft, hole, primitives, fillet, chamfer, shell, draft, move, decal, patterns, mirror and construction planes.
  • Select faces, edges and bodies: clicking in the 3D view, the selection filter, and how picks become references in the code.
  • Edit features and the history: the timeline, editing a feature, renaming, suppressing, rolling back, deleting, and parameters.
  • The code view: the Source tab, and how your edits there and the tools' edits stay in step.

Finish and check

  • Materials and appearance: assign an engineering material, a finish or a colour to the part or to some bodies.
  • Measure and section: distances, angles, radii and areas, and a cut through the model.
  • Sheet metal: base flanges, flanges, bends, the flat pattern and its DXF.
  • Surfaces and surface analysis: the Surface ribbon, and zebra stripes, curvature, draft and continuity checks for curved parts.

Bring parts in and out

  • Import parts: STEP files, McMaster-Carr parts and standard parts.
  • Export: STEP, STL, 3MF, images and the source.

New to STEVE? Make your first part first. Parts made of several components, placed and jointed together, are designs: see Assemblies.

pages.title: Parts, sketches and constraints
pages.description: What a part is, how to draw a sketch on a plane or a face, and how dimensions and constraints pin it down.
pages.html:
Parts

A part is a document with one file, model.py. It is built step by step: sketches, then features that make and change solid bodies (extrude, fillet, hole and so on). A part can hold several bodies, for example after an extrude with New body; they are listed under Bodies in the Browser and exported together.

To start one, choose File → New part (Alt+N). An empty part shows "An empty part" in the canvas, with New sketch, Ask STEVE and Use a sample.

Sketches

A sketch is a flat drawing on a plane: lines, rectangles, circles, arcs and other curves, with dimensions and constraints. The closed regions of a sketch are its profiles, which features such as Extrude and Revolve turn into solids. A region inside another stays a hole.

In the code a sketch is one with model.sketch(...) block:

with model.sketch("sketch_1", on="XY", name="Sketch 1") as s:
    s.center_rect("r1", (0, 0), 80, 50)
    s.horizontal_distance("r1.bottom.start", "r1.bottom.end", 80)
    s.vertical_distance("r1.right.start", "r1.right.end", 50)
    s.coincident("origin", "r1.center")

Start a sketch

  1. Click Sketch on the ribbon (Shift+S). The Dock shows New sketch, "Choose where to draw".
  2. Choose where it goes:
    • click XY, XZ or YZ under Origin plane in the Dock, or click an origin plane in the view; or
    • click a flat face of the model.

The view turns to look straight at the plane, and the ribbon shows the Sketch tab.

If you select a flat face before you click Sketch, the sketch goes straight onto that face. You can also right-click a construction plane in the Browser and choose New sketch on this plane. Sketches need a flat face; a curved face is refused with "Sketches need a flat face. Pick a planar face or a plane."

While you sketch, the left mouse button draws and selects. Orbit with the right button, pan with the middle button, and zoom with the wheel.

Draw

Pick a tool on the ribbon's Draw group, or press its key:

Tool Key How to draw it
Line L Click to start, keep clicking to chain lines. Esc ends the chain.
Rectangle (two corners) R Click a corner, then the opposite one.
Center rectangle Click the centre, then a corner.
Circle (center, radius) C Click the centre, then a point on the circle.
Circle through 3 points Click three points on the circle.
Arc (3 points) A Click the start, the end, then a point the arc passes through. Started at the end of a line or arc, it can continue tangent to it.
Center arc Click the centre, the start, then the end (counter-clockwise).
Polygon Click the centre, then a corner. Sides (3 to 64) and Fit (Inscribed or Circumscribed) are in the Dock.
Slot Click the two centres, then the width.
Ellipse Click the centre, the end of the major axis, then a point for the minor radius.
Spline S Click control points. OK (Enter) or a double-click finishes it; click the first point again to close it.
Point Click to place a point, for example a hole centre.
Project P Click model edges, faces (their outline), vertices or another sketch's curves to bring them into this sketch. They stay linked to their source and update with it.

The rectangle, circle and arc tools each have a menu on the ribbon with their variants; in the Dock, Mode switches between them.

Type sizes while you draw. After the first click, type a length and press Enter. For a rectangle, type the width, press Tab, type the height, then Enter. For a line, Tab moves to the angle. The Size fields in the Dock show the same values. Typed sizes become dimensions in the sketch. A size can carry its unit, such as 1in, 1", 2ft, 3cm or 0.5 m; without one it's in the units the status bar shows.

Snaps. As you draw, STEVE infers coincident points, horizontal and vertical lines, parallel and perpendicular lines, tangency and alignment with other points, shows them, and adds them as constraints. Hold Alt to draw without them.

Construction geometry (Q, or the Construction switch in the Dock) is for reference only: it never forms a profile. Select existing geometry and press Q to toggle it.

Dimensions

Use Dimension (D): click a line, circle or arc, or two points or lines, move the dimension where you want it and click to place it, then type its value. It gives lengths, distances, radii, diameters and angles depending on what you picked.

  • A value can be a number or an expression of parameters, such as width / 2 + 3.
  • A length can carry a unit: mm, cm, m, in or ", ft or ', also inside an expression (width + 1in adds an inch to width). It's written into the sketch in millimetres (1in becomes 25.4, width + 1in becomes width + (1 * 25.4)). Angles are in degrees.
  • The sketch's first dimension scales the whole drawing to it, so a rough sketch keeps its proportions.
  • Every dimension is listed under Dimensions in the Dock. Click a value there to change it, and press Enter.
  • To nudge a plain number, press on it and drag sideways: in the Dock's dimension values, Size fields and polygon Sides, on the sizes shown while you draw, or by the unit beside a dimension you're editing in the view. Steps follow the number's own precision; hold Shift for steps ten times larger, Alt or Ctrl for ten times smaller. The value is applied when you let go, and Esc puts it back. A value written as an expression, such as width / 2, isn't changed by dragging; type it instead.
  • Sizes and dimensions follow the "mm"/"in" chip at the right of the status bar. With inches chosen, they show in inches and a plain number you type is taken in inches (2 is written to the code as 50.8). A unit typed after a number is that number's, such as 10mm or 1in. In an expression with a parameter, plain numbers are as the code reads them (width / 2 halves it), and the code is always in millimetres.

Constraints

Constraints fix relationships between curves and points. They are on the ribbon's Constrain group:

Constraint Key What it does
Coincident Joins two points, or puts a point on a curve.
Horizontal H Makes lines (or two points) horizontal.
Vertical V Makes lines (or two points) vertical.
Parallel Makes two lines parallel.
Perpendicular Makes two lines perpendicular.
Tangent T Makes two curves tangent.
Equal E Equal lengths, or equal radii.
Symmetric Mirrors two points about a line or point.
Midpoint Puts a point at a line's midpoint.
Concentric Shares a centre between circles or arcs.
Collinear Puts two lines on one line.
Fix F Locks points where they are.

The last five are under More on the ribbon.

There are two ways to add one:

  • Select first. Select the geometry (click, Shift+click to add), then click the constraint. It applies at once if the selection fits it.
  • Tool first. Click the constraint with nothing suitable selected. It becomes the active tool and the Dock lists the picks it needs, one at a time. Only geometry it accepts lights up under the pointer. It keeps adding constraints until you press OK, Esc or choose Select.

When you select geometry, the Dock also shows the constraints that apply to it. Constraints are listed under Constraints in the Dock; hover over one to highlight its geometry, or click the bin to delete it.

Is the sketch defined?

The Dock's header and footer show the solver's verdict:

  • Fully defined (the header says Defined): every curve is pinned down by dimensions and constraints.
  • "N degrees of freedom" (the header says "N DOF"): blue geometry can still move. Add dimensions or constraints to pin it, or leave it; an under-defined sketch still works.
  • "Over-defined: N conflicting constraints" (Conflict): remove or change a highlighted constraint. Select selects the ones in conflict.

The Browser shows the same under Sketches: "defined", or how many degrees of freedom are free.

You can drag a curve to move it, or a point to reshape it; constraints and dimensions hold what they define.

Edit, undo and finish

  • Delete (Delete or Backspace) removes the selected geometry or constraints.
  • Undo (Ctrl+Z) and Redo (Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y) work inside the sketch.
  • Finish sketch (Ctrl+Enter, Finish on the ribbon) writes the sketch into the code and rebuilds the model.
  • Cancel sketch (Cancel on the ribbon) leaves without changing the design.

Esc steps back one level at a time: it drops what you are drawing, then returns to Select, then clears the selection. It never leaves the sketch.

To edit a sketch later, double-click it in the Browser or the timeline, or right-click it and choose Edit sketch.

Common problems

  • "Sketch 1 has conflicting constraints" after finishing. The sketch keeps its last solved shape until you fix them. Edit the sketch and remove a constraint marked in the list.
  • "This sketch is written as custom code". The sketch block contains code the sketch editor can't edit (for example a loop). Edit it in Source, or ask STEVE to convert it into an editable sketch.
  • The build fails with "Sketch 'Sketch 1' has no closed profile". The sketch has no closed region of normal (non-construction) curves. Close the outline, or turn construction off for its curves (select them and press Q).

A length can carry a unit: `mm`, `cm`, `m`, `in` or `"`, `ft` or `'`, also inside an expression (`width + 1in` adds an inch to `width`). It's written into the sketch in millimetres (`1in` becomes `25.4`, `width + 1in` becomes `width + (1 * 25.4)`). Angles are in degrees. The sketch's first dimension scales the whole drawing to it, so a rough sketch keeps its proportions. Every dimension is listed under **Dimensions** in the Dock. Click a value there to change it, and press Enter. To nudge a plain number, press on it and drag sideways: in the Dock's dimension values, **Size** fields and polygon **Sides**, on the sizes shown while you draw, or by the unit beside a dimension you're editing in the view. Steps follow the number's own precision; hold Shift for steps ten times larger, Alt or Ctrl for ten times smaller. The value is applied when you let go, and Esc puts it back. A value written as an expression, such as `width / 2`, isn't changed by dragging; type it instead. Sizes and dimensions follow the "mm"/"in" chip at the right of the status bar. With inches chosen, they show in inches and a plain number you type is taken in inches (`2` is written to the code as `50.8`). A unit typed after a number is that number's, such as `10mm` or `1in`. In an expression with a parameter, plain numbers are as the code reads them (`width / 2` halves it), and the code is always in millimetres. Constraints Constraints fix relationships between curves and points. They are on the ribbon's **Constrain** group: Constraint Key What it does **Coincident**  Joins two points, or puts a point on a curve. **Horizontal** H Makes lines (or two points) horizontal. **Vertical** V Makes lines (or two points) vertical. **Parallel**  Makes two lines parallel. **Perpendicular**  Makes two lines perpendicular. **Tangent** T Makes two curves tangent. **Equal** E Equal lengths, or equal radii. **Symmetric**  Mirrors two points about a line or point. **Midpoint**  Puts a point at a line's midpoint. **Concentric**  Shares a centre between circles or arcs. **Collinear**  Puts two lines on one line. **Fix** F Locks points where they are. The last five are under **More** on the ribbon. There are two ways to add one: *Select first.* Select the geometry (click, Shift+click to add), then click the constraint. It applies at once if the selection fits it. *Tool first.* Click the constraint with nothing suitable selected. It becomes the active tool and the Dock lists the picks it needs, one at a time. Only geometry it accepts lights up under the pointer. It keeps adding constraints until you press **OK**, Esc or choose **Select**. When you select geometry, the Dock also shows the constraints that apply to it. Constraints are listed under **Constraints** in the Dock; hover over one to highlight its geometry, or click the bin to delete it. Is the sketch defined? The Dock's header and footer show the solver's verdict: **Fully defined** (the header says **Defined**): every curve is pinned down by dimensions and constraints. "N degrees of freedom" (the header says "N DOF"): blue geometry can still move. Add dimensions or constraints to pin it, or leave it; an under-defined sketch still works. "Over-defined: N conflicting constraints" (**Conflict**): remove or change a highlighted constraint. **Select** selects the ones in conflict. The Browser shows the same under **Sketches**: "defined", or how many degrees of freedom are free. ![A sketched triangle with its bottom line selected, a Horizontal constraint and a 50 mm dimension on it; the Dock lists the selection, the dimension and five constraints, and says 2 degrees of freedom.](../../../assets/design/sketch-constraints.png) You can drag a curve to move it, or a point to reshape it; constraints and dimensions hold what they define. Edit, undo and finish **Delete** (Delete or Backspace) removes the selected geometry or constraints. **Undo** (Ctrl+Z) and **Redo** (Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y) work inside the sketch. **Finish sketch** (Ctrl+Enter, **Finish** on the ribbon) writes the sketch into the code and rebuilds the model. **Cancel sketch** (**Cancel** on the ribbon) leaves without changing the design. Esc steps back one level at a time: it drops what you are drawing, then returns to **Select**, then clears the selection. It never leaves the sketch. To edit a sketch later, double-click it in the Browser or the timeline, or right-click it and choose **Edit sketch**. Common problems *"Sketch 1 has conflicting constraints" after finishing.* The sketch keeps its last solved shape until you fix them. Edit the sketch and remove a constraint marked in the list. *"This sketch is written as custom code".* The sketch block contains code the sketch editor can't edit (for example a loop). Edit it in **Source**, or ask STEVE to convert it into an editable sketch. *The build fails with "Sketch 'Sketch 1' has no closed profile".* The sketch has no closed region of normal (non-construction) curves. Close the outline, or turn construction off for its curves (select them and press Q).

pages.title: Modelling features
pages.description: Every modelling command on the Design workspace's Solid tab, with its fields, defaults and the code it writes.
pages.html:
Each command on the Solid ribbon opens its options in the Dock and writes one call into the part's code. This page lists them in ribbon order: Create, Modify, Pattern and Construct.

How every feature dialog works

  1. Select geometry first if you like: the dialog fills in what fits (a face for a hole, edges for a fillet, the last sketch for an extrude).
  2. Click the command. Its options open in the Dock, titled with the feature's name and the id it will get (extrude_1, fillet_2…).
  3. Fields that take geometry (faces, edges, a sketch line) show "Click, then pick in the view". The first one is waiting for picks when the dialog opens. Click faces or edges in the view to add them; click one again to remove it. The × on a chip removes it too.
  4. Number fields take a number or an expression of parameters, such as thickness * 2. A field marked • is required. Lengths are in millimetres and angles in degrees; a length can also be typed with its unit, such as 0.25in, 3cm or thickness + 1in, and is written in millimetres.
  5. The model previews as you type ("Previewing…", then "Preview ready"). The line under the fields is the exact code that will be written.
  6. OK (Enter) adds the feature; Cancel (Esc) discards it. Either way you are back at Select.

Features go in at the end of the history, or after the history marker if you have rolled it back (see Edit features and the history). Nothing is saved until you save the document.

Operation

Features that make solids have an Operation choice:

Choice Meaning
Auto (default) Cuts when the new shape goes into the solid; joins (or starts the model) when it goes out of it. The button shows what Auto stands for now, for example "Auto · Cut".
New body Makes a separate body.
Join Adds to the body.
Cut Removes from the body.
Intersect Keeps only the overlap.

Create

Extrude

Push a sketch profile into a solid, or cut it into one. Shortcut E. Code: model.extrude("extrude_1", "sketch_1", distance=10).

Field Default Notes
Profile the last sketch A sketch: all its closed regions; holes stay holes.
Extent Distance Distance, Symmetric (half each way) or Through all.
Distance 10 Negative goes the other way. Not shown for Through all. You can also drag the arrow in the view.
Operation Auto See above.

You can also right-click a sketch in the Browser and choose Extrude….

Revolve

Spin a profile around an axis. Code: model.revolve("revolve_1", "sketch_1", axis="Z").

Field Default Notes
Profile the last sketch
Axis Z X axis, Y axis, Z axis, or Pick an edge or sketch line: click a straight model edge, or a line of any sketch shown in the view (it's written as "sketch_1.l3"). While you pick, every sketch is drawn, even ones other features already use, and the chosen line is marked. A selected edge fills it in.
Angle 360 Degrees.
Operation Auto

Sweep

Sweep a closed profile along a path. Code: model.sweep("sweep_1", "sketch_1", "sketch_2").

Field Default Notes
Profile the last sketch
Path A sketch whose curves form the path (construction lines count).
Orientation Default How the profile turns along the path: Default, Keep twist (Frenet), Fixed direction or Guide curve.
Direction (0, 0, 1) With Fixed direction: a direction the profile keeps the same angles to all along, so it never twists. For a U-shaped path in one plane, use that plane's normal. On a path that turns toward the direction, the profile leans off square to the path. Code: binormal=(0, 1, 0).
Guide curve With Guide curve: a sketch whose curves run beside the path from its start to its end (drawn in either direction). At each point the profile turns to face where the guide crosses it, and when the guide starts on the profile's outline the profile also grows or shrinks so the guide stays on its side (a widening guide widens the sweep; not with More sections). Code: guide="sketch_3".
More sections none Closed profiles after the first, in order along the path; the section blends from one to the next. Code: sections=["sketch_4"], and optionally positions=[0, 1] to place each section (the first included) at a fraction of the path's length.
Corners Sharp Sharp, Round or Transformed.
Operation Auto

When a guide curve or sections can't be swept, the error says which one to fix (for example, a guide that doesn't run the length of the path). Faces are named from the first profile. With any of these options the path runs from its end at the profile, so sweep_1.start is the profile's end.

The sweep's faces meet as the profile's curves and the path's segments meet: tangent where those are tangent. Sweeps don't control or check curvature (G2) continuity, and Class-A surfacing is beyond these tools.

Its faces are named sweep_1.start, sweep_1.end and sweep_1.side(<profile curve>), and each side face also after the path segment it runs along: sweep_1.along(<path curve>), like sweep_1.along(w.side0) for a straight or sweep_1.along(bend1) for a bend (a path given as edges counts them in order: sweep_1.along(0), sweep_1.along(1), …). A drawing can dimension the path itself: refer to its sketch curves, like "path.w.side0" for a straight's length or two of them for the angle of the bend between, and the drawing shows each one it measures as a centre line.

Loft

A smooth solid through two or more profiles, in order. Code: model.loft("loft_1", ["sketch_1", "sketch_2"]).

Field Default Notes
Sections Click the sketches in order; each shows its number. A construction point can be the first or last section, closing the loft to a tip (a dome or a nose).
Straight sides off Ruled surfaces between sections.
Smoothing off Fairs the surface so it bulges less between unevenly spaced sections. Smooth lofts only.
Continuity Default (C2) C1 keeps tangents through each section; C2 keeps curvature too. Applies inside the loft only, between its own sections, not where it meets other faces. Smooth lofts only.
Max degree empty (8) 2 to 25: lower is stiffer, higher follows the sections more closely. Smooth lofts only.
Operation Auto

Sections with different numbers of edges (a rectangle and a circle) are matched up before lofting, so the sides don't twist. Continuity shapes the loft's own surface; its start and end faces meet neighbouring faces with no continuity guarantee. G2 (curvature) continuity between separate faces and Class-A surface quality are beyond STEVE's modelling tools. A smooth loft through unevenly spaced sections (a few close together, then a long gap) can bulge well past them. When it does, the loft still builds and shows a warning; turn on Smoothing or Straight sides, or space the sections more evenly.

Code: model.loft("dome", ["base", "apex"], smoothing=True) where apex is a construction point.

Hole

Simple, counterbored or countersunk holes normal to a flat face. Code: model.hole("hole_1", on="extrude_1.end", points=[(0, 0)], diameter=6.6).

Field Default Notes
Face the selected face A flat face. Positions are measured in its sketch coordinates.
Positions (0, 0) One row per hole, X and Y on the face, or sketch points picked in the view (see below).
Type Simple Simple, Counterbore or Countersink.
Diameter 6.6
Depth empty Empty goes through.
Counterbore Ø, Counterbore depth 11, 6.4 Counterbore only.
Countersink Ø, Countersink angle 13, 90° Countersink only.
Thread empty A tapped hole's thread, such as M6x1, for drawings' hole tables. The diameter is then the tap drill.

A face's sketch coordinates have their origin where the model origin projects onto the face, and their X axis along the model's X (or Y when X is normal to the face).

Holes at sketch points: sketch the hole centres first: points, circles (their centres) or lines (their ends), on the face or on a plane parallel to it. Finish the sketch, start Hole, pick the face, then click Pick sketch points under Positions. Every sketch shown in the view now marks its points; click the ones you want (click one again to take it out). Each appears in Positions as a chip, beside any typed rows. The hole follows its point when you change the sketch's dimensions. In code a picked point is written as its reference, for example points=["sketch_2.p1", "sketch_2.c1", "sketch_2.l1.start", (0, 0)]; points="sketch_2" drills at all of a sketch's points and circle centres.

Boundary fill

Fill or cut the regions that bodies and planes enclose between them: a pocket closed off by a plane, the space under a bridge down to a plane, or the slice of a body between two planes. Code: model.boundary_fill("boundary_fill_1", ["body_1"], planes="plane_1").

Field Default Notes
Bodies the selected bodies Click a face of each body that bounds the regions.
Plane None XY, XZ, YZ, a construction plane, or a picked flat face. It is extended across the whole model. In code planes=[…] takes several.
Regions empty A point (X, Y, Z) inside each region to use. Empty uses every enclosed region outside the bodies. The feature's details list every region with a point inside it, its volume and the body it lies in, so you can copy the point of the one you want.
Bodies afterwards Keep Keep the bodies, Remove them, or Include in the fill (they become part of it). The body the fill goes into always stays.
Operation Auto Auto joins the regions to the active body. Cut removes them from a body, New body makes them a body of their own.

When nothing is closed off the error says so: add a plane or body that closes the region, or use Extrude to grow a body up to a face. The fill's faces are named <id>.plane(<plane>) where they lie on a plane and <id>.face(<face name>) where they lie on a body's face, so later fillets and sketches can use them.

Primitive

The Primitive menu adds a solid shape without a sketch:

Command Fields (defaults) Code
Box Length (X) 40, Width (Y) 30, Height (Z) 20, Center (0, 0, 0), Operation model.box("box_1", 40, 30, 20)
Cylinder Radius 10, Height 20, Base center (0, 0, 0), Direction (0, 0, 1), Operation model.cylinder("cylinder_1", 10, 20)
Sphere Radius 10, Center (0, 0, 0), Operation model.sphere("sphere_1", 10)
Cone Base radius 10, Top radius 0, Height 20, Base center (0, 0, 0), Operation model.cone("cone_1", 10, 0, 20)
Torus Ring radius 20, Tube radius 4, Center (0, 0, 0), Operation model.torus("torus_1", 20, 4)
Text Text "STEVE", On XY (or the selected face), Size 10, Depth 1, Operation Raised or Engraved model.text("text_1", "STEVE", on="XY", size=10, depth=1)

Surface

The Surface menu makes surface bodies: thin sheets with no inside, for shapes a solid feature can't reach (a domed lid, a blend between two curves). Each is a body of its own in Bodies, with a sheet icon and its area instead of a volume, and the view draws it from both sides. Surfaces go into the STEP export. They have no volume or mass, so mesh exports (STL, 3MF), simulation and Manufacture leave them out and say so: thicken or solidify them first. The model's volume, surface area, mass and centre of mass are its solids' alone; Physical properties lists the surfaces apart, with their area. They can't be joined, cut or intersected with solids, filleted, chamfered, shelled or drafted, or picked as a machining target. A component made only of surfaces is marked "surface (not a part)" in the bill of materials and a drawing's parts list. A part or design made only of surfaces still builds, with a warning.

Fill's G1 makes a patch tangent to its neighbours, no more. G2 (curvature) continuity between faces and Class-A surface quality are beyond STEVE's modelling tools.

Fill closes a loop of edges or sketch curves with a patch. Code: model.fill("fill_1", boundary=["edge(a|b)", "edge(b|c)", …], continuity="G1", support=["extrude_1.side_faces"]).

Field Default Notes
Boundary the selected edges Edges or sketch curves that meet end to end all the way round.
Continuity Through the edges (G0) Tangent to the faces (G1) makes the patch tangent to the face each edge bounds.
Tangent to empty G1 only: the faces the patch is tangent to, needed where an edge lies between two faces (the rim of a shelled box).
Pass through empty Points (X, Y, Z) the patch also passes through, like the top of a dome.

The patch's face is fill_1.face. Its detail reports how closely it meets the boundary (g0_error_mm) and, for G1, its largest angle to the faces around it (g1_error_deg), both measured along the whole edge as the Surface tab's continuity check does. A G1 patch that isn't tangent within 0.57° is rebuilt finer, and g1_within_tolerance says whether it got there. In code, continuity can also be set per edge, {"edge(a|b)": "G1"}, and constraints= takes curves as well as points.

Boundary surface blends a surface through two or more curves, in order. Code: model.boundary_surface("surface_1", ["sketch_1", "sketch_2", "sketch_3"]).

Field Default Notes
Curves Sketches (or edges) in order; each is one curve set, open or closed.
Cross curves empty Curves running the other way: the first and last of both directions close a four-sided patch and the inner ones guide it, met within tolerance rather than exactly.
Straight between curves off Ruled spans between the curves (without cross curves).

Its faces are surface_1.face.

Thicken gives a surface a wall, making a solid: a domed lid from a fill, say. Code: model.thicken("thicken_1", "fill_1", 2).

Field Default Notes
Surface the selected faces A surface body's faces (the whole body becomes the solid), or faces of one solid (the wall joins it).
Thickness 2 The wall, in mm.
Side Along the normal Against the normal grows the wall the other way; Both ways (half each) centres it on the surface.
Operation Auto A surface makes a new body; faces of a solid join it.

Its faces are thicken_1.outer, thicken_1.inner and thicken_1.side (the rim). A wall that would reach past the centre of a curved face (thicker than the face's radius on that side) is refused, naming the face and its radius: thicken it the other way, thinner, or both ways.

Solidify sews surfaces that close a volume into one solid. Code: model.solidify("solid_1", ["fill_1", "fill_2", …]).

Field Default Notes
Surfaces Pick a face of each surface body.
Gap tolerance 0.01 Gaps up to this (mm) are closed when sewing.
Operation Auto

The solid's faces keep the surfaces' names. If the surfaces leave a gap, the error lists the open edges by surface and position: close it with a fill and solidify again.

Thicken and Solidify make ordinary solids that fillet, export, simulate and machine like any other. They follow the surfaces as they are: G2 (curvature) continuity and Class-A quality are still beyond these tools.

Modify

Fillet

Round edges. Shortcut Shift+F. Code: model.fillet("fillet_1", edges=[...], radius=2).

Field Default Notes
Edges the selected edges Pick edges, or a face for all its edges.
Radius 2
End radius empty A variable fillet: blends from Radius to this along each edge. Empty for a constant radius.
Flip direction off Only with an end radius: swaps which end gets which radius.

Chamfer

Bevel edges. Code: model.chamfer("chamfer_1", edges=[...], distance=1).

Field Default Notes
Edges the selected edges Or a face for all its edges.
Distance 1
Second distance empty For an unequal chamfer. Empty for equal distances.
Angle empty Distance and angle chamfer (0 to 90°) instead of a second distance.
Along face empty With a second distance or an angle: the face Distance runs along (each edge must touch one of them), so every edge in a ring is oriented the same way. Empty uses the edge's first face.
Flip side off With a second distance or an angle (and no Along face): measure the distance along the other face.

After a build, the chamfer's feature detail lists each edge's measured legs: which face each distance runs along, and how long it came out.

Shell

Hollow the body, opening the selected faces. Code: model.shell("shell_1", ["extrude_1.end"], 2).

Field Default Notes
Open faces the selected faces Faces to remove. None makes a closed hollow.
Wall 2 Wall thickness.

Draft

Taper faces for moulding. Code: model.draft("draft_1", [...], "XY", 3).

Field Default Notes
Faces the selected faces
Neutral plane XY An origin plane, a construction plane, or a picked flat face.
Angle 3 Degrees.

Move

Move/Copy: move, rotate or copy bodies; drag the handles in the view or type exact values. Shortcut Shift+M. Code: model.move("move_1", ["extrude_1"], translate=(10, 0, 0)).

Field Default Notes
Bodies the selected bodies Pick a body, or a face or edge of it.
X distance, Y distance, Z distance 0
Rotate about none X, Y or Z through the origin, an edge or a sketch line.
Angle 0 Applied before the move.
Create copy off Keep the originals and move new bodies.

In the view, drag an arrow to move along it, or a ring to rotate about the bodies' centre. Moved bodies keep their face names, so later features that refer to them still work.

Material

Opens the material library. See Materials and appearance.

Decal

Show an image (a logo, a label, markings) on a face, flat or curved, or across several faces of one body. Decals change only the appearance: geometry, mass, simulations and exports don't change. Code: model.decal("decal_1", image="img_…", on="extrude_1.end", width=40).

On one flat face the image lies on it. On a curved face (a cylinder, a cone, a loft's skin) or several faces it is projected, like a slide projector, onto the faces turned toward it: it runs on across the seams between faces, stops at its own edge and at the faces' borders, and never shows through on the far side. Code: model.decal("decal_2", image="img_…", on="loft_1.side_faces", width=120, direction=(0, 0, 1)).

Projection suits markings seen from one side. For a stripe, a band, a serial number or text running round a body, turn on Wrap around the surface: the image is laid along the skin like a vinyl sticker, so it keeps its size where the surface curves away instead of stretching. On a cylinder or a cone it wraps without distortion; a large decal on a doubly curved patch (a sphere, a nose cone's tip) has to stretch toward its edges, and the decal's step in the timeline says so. Code: model.decal("stripe", image="img_…", on="tank.side", width=100, height=10, wrap=True).

Field Default Notes
Image A PNG, JPEG or WebP image you upload.
Faces the selected faces One face or several of one body, flat or curved; the image shows on their outside.
Width 40
Height empty Empty keeps the image's proportions.
Center empty On one flat face, in its sketch coordinates. Empty: the middle of the (first) face. In code, a projected decal's at is a point (x, y, z) on or near the faces.
Rotation 0 Degrees, counter-clockwise seen from outside.
Wrap around the surface off Follows the surface like a sticker, for stripes and text running round a body.
Direction empty The side a projected image comes from. Empty: straight onto the face at its center.
Depth empty How far in front of and behind its center a projected image reaches. Empty: half its larger side. Not shown when wrapping.

Parameters

Opens the parameters table in the Inspector. See Parameters.

Pattern

Linear pattern

Repeat features along one or two directions. Code: model.linear_pattern("pattern_1", "X", 3, 10, features=["hole_1"]).

Field Default Notes
Features the last solid feature Click the features to repeat. A fillet or chamfer picked with them rounds each copy the same way.
Direction X X axis, Y axis, Z axis, or a picked edge or sketch line.
Count 3 Including the original.
Spacing 10
Second direction none Adds Second count (1) and Second spacing (10).

Circular pattern

Repeat features around an axis. Code: model.circular_pattern("pattern_1", "Z", 6, features=["hole_1"]).

Field Default Notes
Features the last solid feature
Axis Z Or a picked edge or sketch line (a selected edge fills it in).
Count 6
Total angle 360

Table pattern

Repeat features at positions you list, spaced however they are. Code: model.point_pattern("pattern_1", [(0, 0), (15, 0), (40, 10)], features=["hole_1"]).

Field Default Notes
Features the last solid feature
Positions (0, 0), (15, 0), (40, 10) Offsets from the features in mm: X, Y and optionally Z per row. (0, 0) is the original.
Polar (r, θ) off Each row is a radius, an angle in degrees and optionally Z; each copy turns by its angle about Z.
Absolute positions off Each row is a position instead of an offset: the first row is where the features are, and each other row gets a copy there.

The positions can also come from one of the design's tables, and each copy can be named after a column of it, like a pin or ball ID: model.point_pattern("pins", table("balls.csv", columns=("x", "y")), features=["pin"], absolute=True, labels=table("balls.csv", columns=("ball",))) names the copies' faces pins[A2].pin.wall(0) and so on (the original's too), instead of pins[2].pin.wall(0). A label is letters, digits and _, one per row, each different.

In a design with main.py open, the same command places a component at each row of one of the design's tables instead: see Patterns from a table.

Mirror

Mirror features across a plane or a flat face. Code: model.mirror("mirror_1", "YZ", features=["extrude_2"]).

Field Default Notes
Mirror plane YZ An origin plane, a construction plane, or a picked flat face.
Features the last solid feature

Construct

The Plane menu holds construction planes. A plane is a named reference you can sketch on, mirror across or use as a neutral plane.

Command What it makes
Offset plane A plane offset from a plane or flat face: From (XY), Offset (10), Tilt (0°). Code: model.plane("plane_1", on="XY", offset=10).
Construction plane Opens the Construction plane tool with Offset, Midplane and 3 points modes.
Midplane A plane centred between two parallel flat faces you select.
Plane through 3 points A plane through three vertices you select.

In the Construction plane tool, Offset takes Origin XY plane, Origin XZ plane, Origin YZ plane or Selected face, with an Offset distance slider and a Reverse normal switch. Planes are listed under Construction in the Browser, where you can hide them or start a sketch on them.

Commands that open other pages

  • Sketch: Parts, sketches and constraints.
  • Measure and Section: Measure and section.
  • Standard part and McMaster: Import parts.
  • Export: Export.

The complete list of commands, with their ids and shortcuts, is generated in the Commands reference.

Not shown for **Through all**. You can also drag the arrow in the view. **Operation** **Auto** See above. You can also right-click a sketch in the Browser and choose **Extrude…**. Revolve Spin a profile around an axis. Code: `model.revolve("revolve_1", "sketch_1", axis="Z")`. Field Default Notes **Profile** the last sketch  **Axis** Z **X axis**, **Y axis**, **Z axis**, or **Pick an edge or sketch line**: click a straight model edge, or a line of any sketch shown in the view (it's written as `"sketch_1.l3"`). While you pick, every sketch is drawn, even ones other features already use, and the chosen line is marked. A selected edge fills it in. **Angle** 360 Degrees. **Operation** **Auto**  Sweep Sweep a closed profile along a path. Code: `model.sweep("sweep_1", "sketch_1", "sketch_2")`. Field Default Notes **Profile** the last sketch  **Path**  A sketch whose curves form the path (construction lines count). **Orientation** **Default** How the profile turns along the path: **Default**, **Keep twist (Frenet)**, **Fixed direction** or **Guide curve**. **Direction** (0, 0, 1) With **Fixed direction**: a direction the profile keeps the same angles to all along, so it never twists. For a U-shaped path in one plane, use that plane's normal. On a path that turns toward the direction, the profile leans off square to the path. Code: `binormal=(0, 1, 0)`. **Guide curve**  With **Guide curve**: a sketch whose curves run beside the path from its start to its end (drawn in either direction). At each point the profile turns to face where the guide crosses it, and when the guide starts on the profile's outline the profile also grows or shrinks so the guide stays on its side (a widening guide widens the sweep; not with **More sections**). Code: `guide="sketch_3"`. **More sections** none Closed profiles after the first, in order along the path; the section blends from one to the next. Code: `sections=["sketch_4"]`, and optionally `positions=[0, 1]` to place each section (the first included) at a fraction of the path's length. **Corners** **Sharp** **Sharp**, **Round** or **Transformed**. **Operation** **Auto**  When a guide curve or sections can't be swept, the error says which one to fix (for example, a guide that doesn't run the
length of the path). Faces are named from the first profile. With any of these options the path runs from its end at
the profile, so `sweep_1.start` is the profile's end. The sweep's faces meet as the profile's curves and the path's segments meet: tangent where those are tangent. Sweeps
don't control or check curvature (G2) continuity, and Class-A surfacing is beyond these tools. Its faces are named `sweep_1.start`, `sweep_1.end` and `sweep_1.side(<profile curve>)`, and each side face also after the
path segment it runs along: `sweep_1.along(<path curve>)`, like `sweep_1.along(w.side0)` for a straight or
`sweep_1.along(bend1)` for a bend (a path given as edges counts them in order: `sweep_1.along(0)`, `sweep_1.along(1)`, …).
A drawing can dimension the path itself: refer to its sketch curves, like `"path.w.side0"` for a straight's length or
two of them for the angle of the bend between, and the drawing shows each one it measures as a centre line. Loft A smooth solid through two or more profiles, in order. Code: `model.loft("loft_1", ["sketch_1", "sketch_2"])`. Field Default Notes **Sections**  Click the sketches in order; each shows its number. A construction point can be the first or last section, closing the loft to a tip (a dome or a nose). **Straight sides** off Ruled surfaces between sections. **Smoothing** off Fairs the surface so it bulges less between unevenly spaced sections. Smooth lofts only. **Continuity** **Default** (C2) C1 keeps tangents through each section; C2 keeps curvature too. Applies inside the loft only, between its own sections, not where it meets other faces. Smooth lofts only. **Max degree** empty (8) 2 to 25: lower is stiffer, higher follows the sections more closely. Smooth lofts only. **Operation** **Auto**  Sections with different numbers of edges (a rectangle and a circle) are matched up before lofting, so the sides don't twist. **Continuity** shapes the loft's own surface; its start and end faces meet neighbouring faces with no continuity guarantee. G2 (curvature) continuity between separate faces and Class-A surface quality are beyond STEVE's modelling tools. A smooth loft through unevenly spaced sections (a few close together, then a long gap) can bulge well past them. When it does, the loft still builds and shows a warning; turn on **Smoothing** or **Straight sides**, or space the sections more evenly. Code: `model.loft("dome", ["base", "apex"], smoothing=True)` where `apex` is a construction point. Hole Simple, counterbored or countersunk holes normal to a flat face. Code: `model.hole("hole_1", on="extrude_1.end", points=[(0, 0)], diameter=6.6)`. Field Default Notes **Face** the selected face A flat face. Positions are measured in its sketch coordinates. **Positions** (0, 0) One row per hole, X and Y on the face, or sketch points picked in the view (see below). **Type** **Simple** **Simple**, **Counterbore** or **Countersink**. **Diameter** 6.6  **Depth** empty Empty goes through. **Counterbore Ø**, **Counterbore depth** 11, 6.4 Counterbore only. **Countersink Ø**, **Countersink angle** 13, 90° Countersink only. **Thread** empty A tapped hole's thread, such as M6x1, for drawings' hole tables. The diameter is then the tap drill. A face's sketch coordinates have their origin where the model origin projects onto the face, and their X axis along the model's X (or Y when X is normal to the face). **Holes at sketch points:** sketch the hole centres first: points, circles (their centres) or lines (their ends), on the face or on a plane parallel to it. Finish the sketch, start **Hole**, pick the face, then click **Pick sketch points** under Positions. Every sketch shown in the view now marks its points; click the ones you want (click one again to take it out). Each appears in Positions as a chip, beside any typed rows. The hole follows its point when you change the sketch's dimensions. In code a picked point is written as its reference, for example `points=["sketch_2.p1", "sketch_2.c1", "sketch_2.l1.start", (0, 0)]`; `points="sketch_2"` drills at all of a sketch's points and circle centres. ![The Hole options in the Dock for a hole on the plate's top face, with the hole previewed in the view.](../../../assets/design/feature-hole.png) Boundary fill Fill or cut the regions that bodies and planes enclose between them: a pocket closed off by a plane, the space under a
bridge down to a plane, or the slice of a body between two planes. Code:
`model.boundary_fill("boundary_fill_1", ["body_1"], planes="plane_1")`. Field Default Notes **Bodies** the selected bodies Click a face of each body that bounds the regions. **Plane** None **XY**, **XZ**, **YZ**, a construction plane, or a picked flat face. It is extended across the whole model. In code `planes=[…]` takes several. **Regions** empty A point (X, Y, Z) inside each region to use. Empty uses every enclosed region outside the bodies. The feature's details list every region with a point inside it, its volume and the body it lies in, so you can copy the point of the one you want. **Bodies afterwards** **Keep** **Keep** the bodies, **Remove** them, or **Include in the fill** (they become part of it). The body the fill goes into always stays. **Operation** **Auto** Auto joins the regions to the active body. **Cut** removes them from a body, **New body** makes them a body of their own. When nothing is closed off the error says so: add a plane or body that closes the region, or use **Extrude** to grow a
body up to a face. The fill's faces are named `<id>.plane(<plane>)` where they lie on a plane and
`<id>.face(<face name>)` where they lie on a body's face, so later fillets and sketches can use them. Primitive The **Primitive** menu adds a solid shape without a sketch: Command Fields (defaults) Code **Box** **Length (X)** 40, **Width (Y)** 30, **Height (Z)** 20, **Center** (0, 0, 0), **Operation** `model.box("box_1", 40, 30, 20)` **Cylinder** **Radius** 10, **Height** 20, **Base center** (0, 0, 0), **Direction** (0, 0, 1), **Operation** `model.cylinder("cylinder_1", 10, 20)` **Sphere** **Radius** 10, **Center** (0, 0, 0), **Operation** `model.sphere("sphere_1", 10)` **Cone** **Base radius** 10, **Top radius** 0, **Height** 20, **Base center** (0, 0, 0), **Operation** `model.cone("cone_1", 10, 0, 20)` **Torus** **Ring radius** 20, **Tube radius** 4, **Center** (0, 0, 0), **Operation** `model.torus("torus_1", 20, 4)` **Text** **Text** "STEVE", **On** XY (or the selected face), **Size** 10, **Depth** 1, **Operation** **Raised** or **Engraved** `model.text("text_1", "STEVE", on="XY", size=10, depth=1)` Surface The **Surface** menu makes surface bodies: thin sheets with no inside, for shapes a solid feature can't reach (a domed
lid, a blend between two curves). Each is a body of its own in **Bodies**, with a sheet icon and its area instead of a
volume, and the view draws it from both sides. Surfaces go into the STEP export. They have no volume or mass, so mesh
exports (STL, 3MF), simulation and Manufacture leave them out and say so: thicken or solidify them first. The model's
volume, surface area, mass and centre of mass are its solids' alone; **Physical properties** lists the surfaces apart,
with their area. They can't be joined, cut or intersected with solids, filleted, chamfered, shelled or drafted, or
picked as a machining target. A component made only of surfaces is marked "surface (not a part)" in the bill of
materials and a drawing's parts list. A part or design made only of surfaces still builds, with a warning. **Fill**'s G1 makes a patch tangent to its neighbours, no more. G2 (curvature) continuity between faces and Class-A
surface quality are beyond STEVE's modelling tools. **Fill** closes a loop of edges or sketch curves with a patch. Code:
`model.fill("fill_1", boundary=["edge(a|b)", "edge(b|c)", …], continuity="G1", support=["extrude_1.side_faces"])`. Field Default Notes **Boundary** the selected edges Edges or sketch curves that meet end to end all the way round. **Continuity** **Through the edges (G0)** **Tangent to the faces (G1)** makes the patch tangent to the face each edge bounds. **Tangent to** empty G1 only: the faces the patch is tangent to, needed where an edge lies between two faces (the rim of a shelled box). **Pass through** empty Points (X, Y, Z) the patch also passes through, like the top of a dome. The patch's face is `fill_1.face`. Its detail reports how closely it meets the boundary (`g0_error_mm`) and, for G1, its
largest angle to the faces around it (`g1_error_deg`), both measured along the whole edge as the Surface tab's
continuity check does. A G1 patch that isn't tangent within 0.57° is rebuilt finer, and `g1_within_tolerance` says
whether it got there. In code, `continuity` can also be set per edge,
`{"edge(a|b)": "G1"}`, and `constraints=` takes curves as well as points. **Boundary surface** blends a surface through two or more curves, in order. Code:
`model.boundary_surface("surface_1", ["sketch_1", "sketch_2", "sketch_3"])`. Field Default Notes **Curves**  Sketches (or edges) in order; each is one curve set, open or closed. **Cross curves** empty Curves running the other way: the first and last of both directions close a four-sided patch and the inner ones guide it, met within tolerance rather than exactly. **Straight between curves** off Ruled spans between the curves (without cross curves). Its faces are `surface_1.face`. **Thicken** gives a surface a wall, making a solid: a domed lid from a fill, say. Code:
`model.thicken("thicken_1", "fill_1", 2)`. Field Default Notes **Surface** the selected faces A surface body's faces (the whole body becomes the solid), or faces of one solid (the wall joins it). **Thickness** 2 The wall, in mm. **Side** **Along the normal** **Against the normal** grows the wall the other way; **Both ways (half each)** centres it on the surface. **Operation** **Auto** A surface makes a new body; faces of a solid join it. Its faces are `thicken_1.outer`, `thicken_1.inner` and `thicken_1.side` (the rim). A wall that would reach past the
centre of a curved face (thicker than the face's radius on that side) is refused, naming the face and its radius:
thicken it the other way, thinner, or both ways. **Solidify** sews surfaces that close a volume into one solid. Code: `model.solidify("solid_1", ["fill_1", "fill_2", …])`. Field Default Notes **Surfaces**  Pick a face of each surface body. **Gap tolerance** 0.01 Gaps up to this (mm) are closed when sewing. **Operation** **Auto**  The solid's faces keep the surfaces' names. If the surfaces leave a gap, the error lists the open edges by surface and
position: close it with a fill and solidify again. Thicken and Solidify make ordinary solids that fillet, export, simulate and machine like any other. They follow the
surfaces as they are: G2 (curvature) continuity and Class-A quality are still beyond these tools. Modify Fillet Round edges. Shortcut Shift+F. Code: `model.fillet("fillet_1", edges=[...], radius=2)`. Field Default Notes **Edges** the selected edges Pick edges, or a face for all its edges. **Radius** 2  **End radius** empty A variable fillet: blends from **Radius** to this along each edge. Empty for a constant radius. **Flip direction** off Only with an end radius: swaps which end gets which radius. Chamfer Bevel edges. Code: `model.chamfer("chamfer_1", edges=[...], distance=1)`. Field Default Notes **Edges** the selected edges Or a face for all its edges. **Distance** 1  **Second distance** empty For an unequal chamfer. Empty for equal distances. **Angle** empty Distance and angle chamfer (0 to 90°) instead of a second distance. **Along face** empty With a second distance or an angle: the face **Distance** runs along (each edge must touch one of them), so every edge in a ring is oriented the same way. Empty uses the edge's first face. **Flip side** off With a second distance or an angle (and no **Along face**): measure the distance along the other face. After a build, the chamfer's feature detail lists each edge's measured legs: which face each distance runs along, and how long it came out. Shell Hollow the body, opening the selected faces. Code: `model.shell("shell_1", ["extrude_1.end"], 2)`. Field Default Notes **Open faces** the selected faces Faces to remove. None makes a closed hollow. **Wall** 2 Wall thickness. Draft Taper faces for moulding. Code: `model.draft("draft_1", [...], "XY", 3)`. Field Default Notes **Faces** the selected faces  **Neutral plane** XY An origin plane, a construction plane, or a picked flat face. **Angle** 3 Degrees. Move **Move/Copy**: move, rotate or copy bodies; drag the handles in the view or type exact values. Shortcut Shift+M. Code: `model.move("move_1", ["extrude_1"], translate=(10, 0, 0))`. Field Default Notes **Bodies** the selected bodies Pick a body, or a face or edge of it. **X distance**, **Y distance**, **Z distance** 0  **Rotate about** none X, Y or Z through the origin, an edge or a sketch line. **Angle** 0 Applied before the move. **Create copy** off Keep the originals and move new bodies. In the view, drag an arrow to move along it, or a ring to rotate about the bodies' centre. Moved bodies keep their face names, so later features that refer to them still work. Material Opens the material library. See [Materials and appearance](/docs/design/materials/). Decal Show an image (a logo, a label, markings) on a face, flat or curved, or across several faces of one body. Decals change only the appearance: geometry, mass, simulations and exports don't change. Code: `model.decal("decal_1", image="img_…", on="extrude_1.end", width=40)`. On one flat face the image lies on it. On a curved face (a cylinder, a cone, a loft's skin) or several faces it is projected, like a slide projector, onto the faces turned toward it: it runs on across the seams between faces, stops at its own edge and at the faces' borders, and never shows through on the far side. Code: `model.decal("decal_2", image="img_…", on="loft_1.side_faces", width=120, direction=(0, 0, 1))`. Projection suits markings seen from one side. For a stripe, a band, a serial number or text running round a body, turn on **Wrap around the surface**: the image is laid along the skin like a vinyl sticker, so it keeps its size where the surface curves away instead of stretching. On a cylinder or a cone it wraps without distortion; a large decal on a doubly curved patch (a sphere, a nose cone's tip) has to stretch toward its edges, and the decal's step in the timeline says so. Code: `model.decal("stripe", image="img_…", on="tank.side", width=100, height=10, wrap=True)`. Field Default Notes **Image**  A PNG, JPEG or WebP image you upload. **Faces** the selected faces One face or several of one body, flat or curved; the image shows on their outside. **Width** 40  **Height** empty Empty keeps the image's proportions. **Center** empty On one flat face, in its sketch coordinates. Empty: the middle of the (first) face. In code, a projected decal's `at` is a point (x, y, z) on or near the faces. **Rotation** 0 Degrees, counter-clockwise seen from outside. **Wrap around the surface** off Follows the surface like a sticker, for stripes and text running round a body. **Direction** empty The side a projected image comes from. Empty: straight onto the face at its center. **Depth** empty How far in front of and behind its center a projected image reaches. Empty: half its larger side. Not shown when wrapping. Parameters Opens the parameters table in the Inspector. See [Parameters](/docs/design/history/#parameters). Pattern Linear pattern Repeat features along one or two directions. Code: `model.linear_pattern("pattern_1", "X", 3, 10, features=["hole_1"])`. Field Default Notes **Features** the last solid feature Click the features to repeat. A fillet or chamfer picked with them rounds each copy the same way. **Direction** X **X axis**, **Y axis**, **Z axis**, or a picked edge or sketch line. **Count** 3 Including the original. **Spacing** 10  **Second direction** none Adds **Second count** (1) and **Second spacing** (10). Circular pattern Repeat features around an axis. Code: `model.circular_pattern("pattern_1", "Z", 6, features=["hole_1"])`. Field Default Notes **Features** the last solid feature  **Axis** Z Or a picked edge or sketch line (a selected edge fills it in). **Count** 6  **Total angle** 360  Table pattern Repeat features at positions you list, spaced however they are. Code:
`model.point_pattern("pattern_1", [(0, 0), (15, 0), (40, 10)], features=["hole_1"])`. Field Default Notes **Features** the last solid feature  **Positions** (0, 0), (15, 0), (40, 10) Offsets from the features in mm: X, Y and optionally Z per row. (0, 0) is the original. **Polar (r, θ)** off Each row is a radius, an angle in degrees and optionally Z; each copy turns by its angle about Z. **Absolute positions** off Each row is a position instead of an offset: the first row is where the features are, and each other row gets a copy there. The positions can also come from one of the design's tables, and each copy can be named after a column of it, like a
pin or ball ID: `model.point_pattern("pins", table("balls.csv", columns=("x", "y")), features=["pin"], absolute=True,
labels=table("balls.csv", columns=("ball",)))` names the copies' faces `pins[A2].pin.wall(0)` and so on (the original's
too), instead of `pins[2].pin.wall(0)`. A label is letters, digits and `_`, one per row, each different. In a design with `main.py` open, the same command places a component at each row of one of the design's tables
instead: see [Patterns from a table](/docs/assemblies/add-components/#patterns-from-a-table). Mirror Mirror features across a plane or a flat face. Code: `model.mirror("mirror_1", "YZ", features=["extrude_2"])`. Field Default Notes **Mirror plane** YZ An origin plane, a construction plane, or a picked flat face. **Features** the last solid feature  Construct The **Plane** menu holds construction planes. A plane is a named reference you can sketch on, mirror across or use as a neutral plane. Command What it makes **Offset plane** A plane offset from a plane or flat face: **From** (XY), **Offset** (10), **Tilt** (0°). Code: `model.plane("plane_1", on="XY", offset=10)`. **Construction plane** Opens the **Construction plane** tool with **Offset**, **Midplane** and **3 points** modes. **Midplane** A plane centred between two parallel flat faces you select. **Plane through 3 points** A plane through three vertices you select. In the **Construction plane** tool, **Offset** takes **Origin XY plane**, **Origin XZ plane**, **Origin YZ plane** or **Selected face**, with an **Offset distance** slider and a **Reverse normal** switch. Planes are listed under **Construction** in the Browser, where you can hide them or start a sketch on them. Commands that open other pages **Sketch**: [Parts, sketches and constraints](/docs/design/sketches/). **Measure** and **Section**: [Measure and section](/docs/design/measure-section/). **Standard part** and **McMaster**: [Import parts](/docs/design/import/). **Export**: [Export](/docs/design/export/). The complete list of commands, with their ids and shortcuts, is generated in the [Commands reference](/docs/reference/commands/).

pages.title: Select faces, edges and bodies
pages.description: Click faces, edges, vertices and bodies in the 3D view, filter what a click picks, and use the selection with commands and references.
pages.html:
Goal: pick the geometry a command should work on.

Click to select

To Do this
Select one item Click it.
Add an item, or remove a selected one Ctrl+click, ⌘+click or Shift+click it.
Select a whole body or component Double-click any face of it.
Select something hidden behind other faces Press and hold on the spot (or right-click it and choose Select other…), then choose it from the list.
Clear the selection Click empty space, or press Esc.

As you move the pointer, the face, edge or vertex under it lights up and a tip names it, for example "Edge · Linear edge 10 mm". The status bar shows what is selected ("Nothing selected", "2 edges selected", or the item's name), and the Inspector shows its properties under Selection.

Lengths, areas and volumes show in millimetres. Click the "mm" chip at the right of the status bar to show them in inches, and click it again to go back. You can also set this in Settings → Display › Units. Only what's shown changes: the model and its code stay in millimetres.

Esc first closes the open tool or the section view, if any; once nothing else is open, it clears the selection.

A sketch shown in the view is picked whole. Inside a feature, its parts can be picked too: with a Hole's Pick sketch points on, click its points, circle centres and line ends; with an Axis or Direction field's Pick an edge or sketch line on, click one of its lines. While you pick, every sketch is drawn, even ones other features already use.

The selection filter

The selection filter in the status bar (bottom right) sets what a click picks:

Filter Picks
Auto (default) Sketches, vertices, edges and faces, whichever is under the pointer; double-click selects the whole component.
Components Whole bodies and components.
Faces Faces only.
Edges Edges only.
Vertices Vertices only.

Changing the filter clears the selection.

Select other: what lies behind

A click picks what is nearest. To reach a face, edge or vertex behind it (a back face, an edge inside a pocket, a face of a body hidden by another), press and hold the mouse button on the spot without moving it, for half a second. A list opens of everything under the pointer at any depth, nearest first, each named with its kind and its body or component, for example "Cylindrical face · Body 1". Point at a row (or use the arrow keys) and the item lights up in the view (an edge or vertex shows through the faces in front of it; in the X-ray display style, a face behind others does too); click it (or press Enter) to choose it, or press Esc to close the list.

Choosing a row does what clicking the item would: it selects it, or, with a feature dialog or tool open (Fillet, Extrude, Measure and others), fills the dialog's field with it. Hold Shift, Ctrl or ⌘ as you press to add the item to the selection. The list follows the selection filter (with Edges, only edges are listed) and leaves out hidden bodies and the cut-away side of a section. Right-click the spot and choose Select other… for the same list; on a phone or tablet, touch and hold to open the menu.

Select first, then command

Most commands start from the selection:

  • a flat face, then Sketch: the sketch goes on that face;
  • edges, then Fillet or Chamfer: those edges are filled in (a face gives all its edges);
  • a face, then Hole, Shell, Decal or Offset plane;
  • one straight edge, then Revolve or Circular pattern: the edge becomes the axis;
  • a body, a face or an edge of it, then Move.

You can also select inside a feature's dialog: its geometry fields fill from the picks you make while it is open. See Modelling features.

The right-click menu

Right-click in the view for commands that fit what is under the pointer. The item you right-click is selected first. In a part, the menu offers:

  • always: Zoom to selection, Fit all and Show all;
  • on the model: Select other…, the list of everything under the pointer at any depth (see Select other);
  • on a face or an edge: Show in source (the code that made it) and Measure from here;
  • on anything with a row in the browser: Show in tree, which opens the browser at that body (in a design, inside its component), node or link, unfolding the groups above it, selects it there and scrolls it into view;
  • on a body's face or edge: Hide body, Isolate body (when the part has several bodies) and Material…;
  • on a face: Fillet its edges…, Decal on this face…, Shell, opening this face… and Move/Copy body…; on a flat face also Sketch on this face, Hole on this face…, Offset plane from here… and Section at this face;
  • on an edge: Fillet…, Chamfer… and Pattern around this edge…;
  • once the document is saved and something is selected: Comment on selection….

Hide and show

Command Key Effect
Hide selected H Hides the selected bodies, components, sketch or construction plane.
Hide / show selected Space Hides the selection, or shows it again; the selection stays, so Space again undoes it.
Isolate selected I Shows only the selected components (in a design).
Show all Shift+H Shows everything again.
Zoom to selection Z Frames the selection.

The eye beside an item in the Browser hides or shows it too.

See-through components

In a design, the cube button next to a shown component's eye (or link's, or placed instance's) makes it see-through: it is drawn faint in its own colours, so you can see how it meets the parts around and inside it while they stay solid. Click it again to make it opaque. Right-click a component in the Browser or in the view for Make see-through / Make opaque; the view's menu also offers Make all opaque while anything is see-through. See-through components can still be picked and measured. Like hiding, it only changes the view: it is never saved in the design, and it stays as you left it when the design rebuilds. The X-ray display style makes everything see-through at once.

How a pick becomes a reference

STEVE names every face, edge and vertex by the history that made it, not by a number. A face made by an extrude is called, for example, extrude_1.end (its far end) or extrude_1.side(r1.left) (the side made from the sketch line r1.left). An edge is named by its two faces: edge(extrude_1.side(r1.bottom)|extrude_1.side(r1.right)). Feature dialogs show these as short chips, such as "side r1.bottom ∩ side r1.right".

These names are written into the code, and they keep working when you change a dimension, because they don't depend on face order. If a later change removes the geometry a name points at, the feature that uses it fails with a message such as "Reference 'extrude_1.end' no longer exists: an earlier change removed that face." and is marked as failed in the timeline. Edit the feature and pick the geometry again.

To use a reference yourself, right-click an item in the Browser or the timeline and choose Copy reference, then paste it into Source or into a message to STEVE.

Common problems

  • A click selects a face when you wanted its edge. Move the pointer onto the edge until it lights up, or set the selection filter to Edges.
  • The edge you need is behind the model. Press and hold on the spot and choose it from the list (see Select other), or orbit (or click Orbit left 90° beside the view cube) until you can see it; the selection is kept while you move the view.
  • "Regenerate to pick references". The model on screen was built before its faces had names. Click Update model (Ctrl+Enter) and pick again.

The status bar shows what is selected ("Nothing selected", "2 edges selected", or the item's name), and the **Inspector** shows its properties under **Selection**.
