You can also set this in **Settings → Display › Units**. Only what's shown changes: the model and its code stay in millimetres. Esc first closes the open tool or the section view, if any; once nothing else is open, it clears the selection. A sketch shown in the view is picked whole. Inside a feature, its parts can be picked too: with a Hole's **Pick sketch points** on, click its points, circle centres and line ends; with an Axis or Direction field's **Pick an edge or sketch line** on, click one of its lines. While you pick, every sketch is drawn, even ones other features already use. ![Two vertical edges of a plate selected in the 3D view, drawn in blue, with "2 edges selected" in the status bar.](../../../assets/design/selecting-edges.png) The selection filter The selection filter in the status bar (bottom right) sets what a click picks: Filter Picks **Auto** (default) Sketches, vertices, edges and faces, whichever is under the pointer; double-click selects the whole component. **Components** Whole bodies and components. **Faces** Faces only. **Edges** Edges only. **Vertices** Vertices only. Changing the filter clears the selection. Select other: what lies behind A click picks what is nearest. To reach a face, edge or vertex behind it (a back face, an edge inside a pocket, a face of a body hidden by another), press and hold the mouse button on the spot without moving it, for half a second. A list opens of everything under the pointer at any depth, nearest first, each named with its kind and its body or component, for example "Cylindrical face · Body 1". Point at a row (or use the arrow keys) and the item lights up in the view (an edge or vertex shows through the faces in front of it; in the **X-ray** display style, a face behind others does too); click it (or press Enter) to choose it, or press Esc to close the list. Choosing a row does what clicking the item would: it selects it, or, with a feature dialog or tool open (Fillet, Extrude, Measure and others), fills the dialog's field with it. Hold Shift, Ctrl or ⌘ as you press to add the item to the selection. The list follows the selection filter (with **Edges**, only edges are listed) and leaves out hidden bodies and the cut-away side of a section. Right-click the spot and choose **Select other…** for the same list; on a phone or tablet, touch and hold to open the menu. Select first, then command Most commands start from the selection: a flat face, then **Sketch**: the sketch goes on that face; edges, then **Fillet** or **Chamfer**: those edges are filled in (a face gives all its edges); a face, then **Hole**, **Shell**, **Decal** or **Offset plane**; one straight edge, then **Revolve** or **Circular pattern**: the edge becomes the axis; a body, a face or an edge of it, then **Move**. You can also select inside a feature's dialog: its geometry fields fill from the picks you make while it is open. See [Modelling features](/docs/design/features/#how-every-feature-dialog-works). The right-click menu Right-click in the view for commands that fit what is under the pointer. The item you right-click is selected first. In a part, the menu offers: always: **Zoom to selection**, **Fit all** and **Show all**; on the model: **Select other…**, the list of everything under the pointer at any depth (see [Select other](#select-other-what-lies-behind)); on a face or an edge: **Show in source** (the code that made it) and **Measure from here**; on anything with a row in the browser: **Show in tree**, which opens the browser at that body (in a design, inside its component), node or link, unfolding the groups above it, selects it there and scrolls it into view; on a body's face or edge: **Hide body**, **Isolate body** (when the part has several bodies) and **Material…**; on a face: **Fillet its edges…**, **Decal on this face…**, **Shell, opening this face…** and **Move/Copy body…**; on a flat face also **Sketch on this face**, **Hole on this face…**, **Offset plane from here…** and **Section at this face**; on an edge: **Fillet…**, **Chamfer…** and **Pattern around this edge…**; once the document is saved and something is selected: **Comment on selection…**. Hide and show Command Key Effect **Hide selected** H Hides the selected bodies, components, sketch or construction plane. **Hide / show selected** Space Hides the selection, or shows it again; the selection stays, so Space again undoes it. **Isolate selected** I Shows only the selected components (in a design). **Show all** Shift+H Shows everything again. **Zoom to selection** Z Frames the selection. The eye beside an item in the Browser hides or shows it too. See-through components In a design, the cube button next to a shown component's eye (or link's, or placed instance's) makes it see-through: it is drawn faint in its own colours, so you can see how it meets the parts around and inside it while they stay solid. Click it again to make it opaque. Right-click a component in the Browser or in the view for **Make see-through** / **Make opaque**; the view's menu also offers **Make all opaque** while anything is see-through. See-through components can still be picked and measured. Like hiding, it only changes the view: it is never saved in the design, and it stays as you left it when the design rebuilds. The **X-ray** display style makes everything see-through at once. How a pick becomes a reference STEVE names every face, edge and vertex by the history that made it, not by a number. A face made by an extrude is called, for example, `extrude_1.end` (its far end) or `extrude_1.side(r1.left)` (the side made from the sketch line `r1.left`). An edge is named by its two faces: `edge(extrude_1.side(r1.bottom)|extrude_1.side(r1.right))`. Feature dialogs show these as short chips, such as "side r1.bottom ∩ side r1.right". These names are written into the code, and they keep working when you change a dimension, because they don't depend on face order. If a later change removes the geometry a name points at, the feature that uses it fails with a message such as "Reference 'extrude_1.end' no longer exists: an earlier change removed that face." and is marked as failed in the timeline. Edit the feature and pick the geometry again. To use a reference yourself, right-click an item in the Browser or the timeline and choose **Copy reference**, then paste it into **Source** or into a message to STEVE. Common problems *A click selects a face when you wanted its edge.* Move the pointer onto the edge until it lights up, or set the selection filter to **Edges**. *The edge you need is behind the model.* Press and hold on the spot and choose it from the list (see [Select other](#select-other-what-lies-behind)), or orbit (or click **Orbit left 90°** beside the view cube) until you can see it; the selection is kept while you move the view. *"Regenerate to pick references".* The model on screen was built before its faces had names. Click **Update model** (Ctrl+Enter) and pick again.

pages.title: Edit features and the history
pages.description: Use the timeline to edit, rename, suppress, roll back and delete features, and drive the part with named parameters.
pages.html:
A part is its features, in order. The Timeline along the bottom of the canvas shows them as steps, left to right, in the order they run; the Browser lists the same sketches, bodies and planes by kind.

Edit a feature

  1. Double-click the feature's step in the timeline. For a sketch, double-click it in the timeline or in the Browser.
  2. The feature's dialog opens in the Dock titled "Edit" and the feature's name, filled with its current values. A sketch opens in the sketch editor.
  3. Change what you need. The model previews as you type.
  4. Click OK (Enter) to update the feature, or Cancel (Esc) to leave it as it was.

You can also right-click the step and choose Edit (Edit sketch for a sketch). Features that the dialogs can't represent (for example code with a loop) show "This feature is edited in Source." or "written as custom code"; change them in Source.

Clicking a step once shows the feature in the Inspector: its code, and the buttons Edit, Code (open it in Source), Suppress and Delete.

The step menu

Right-click a step in the timeline, or a sketch, body or plane in the Browser, for its menu:

Command What it does
Edit / Edit sketch Opens the feature's dialog, or the sketch editor.
Rename (F2) Changes the name shown in the timeline and the Browser. The feature's id, and every reference to it, stays the same.
Suppress / Unsuppress Skips the feature in the build without deleting it (suppressed=True in the code).
Show in source Opens Source at the feature's code.
Copy reference Copies the feature's id for use in code or in a message to STEVE.
Roll back to here / Roll to end Moves the history marker (timeline only; see below).
Delete Removes the feature's code. Not available while another feature names it directly, such as an extrude naming its sketch: the menu says which ("Used by …").

A sketch's menu also has Hide/Show, Extrude… and Revolve…; a construction plane's has New sketch on this plane and Hide/Show.

In the Browser, double-click a sketch, body or plane name (or press F2) to rename it.

Roll back the history

The history marker is the handle after the last step of the timeline. Drag it back between two steps to see the model as it was at that point: the later features are skipped for the display only, and the saved code doesn't change.

  • With the marker focused, the arrow keys move it one step, and Home and End move it to the start and the end.
  • While the marker is back, new features go in at the marker, and the marker moves past them. This is how you add a feature early in the history.
  • To see every step again, drag the marker to the end, double-click it, choose Roll to end on a step's menu, or click "Show every step again".

Parameters

Parameters are named numbers that drive the part, such as width, thickness or hole_count. Use them in any dimension or feature field, alone or in expressions like width / 2 + 3. Change a parameter and everything that uses it follows. A length parameter (unit mm, or none) can be typed with a unit, such as 1in or 3cm; it's kept in millimetres (25.4).

In the code they are plain assignments before model = Model(), with an optional unit and description in the comment:

width = 80          # mm Plate width
thickness = 6       # mm
hole_d = 6.6        # mm M6 clearance

Add a parameter

  1. Click Parameters on the ribbon (or the + beside Parameters in the Browser). The Parameters table opens in the Inspector.
  2. Click Add.
  3. Type a name, a value or expression, choose a unit (mm, deg, count, in, or none), and optionally a description.
  4. Click Add parameter (or press Enter).

Change a parameter

  1. In the Parameters table, click the parameter's value.
  2. Type a new value or expression and press Enter.

The model rebuilds. Uses shows how many features use the parameter; hover over the count to see which. A parameter in use can't be deleted until you remove its uses.

To rename a parameter, double-click it in the Browser (or right-click it and choose Rename): STEVE renames it everywhere it is used.

Undo

Inside a sketch, Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z undo and redo. Outside a sketch, every change is an edit of the code. While the Source tab is open, its editor records the tools' edits too, so Ctrl+Z in the editor undoes them one by one. Otherwise, go back to a saved revision in Versions (see Collaborate).

Common problems

  • A step is marked as failed. Hover over it to read why. A common cause is a reference to a face or edge that an earlier change removed; edit the feature and pick the geometry again.
  • Delete is greyed out. Another feature names this one or uses its faces or edges; delete or change that feature first.
  • A later feature fails after a delete. Code you wrote by hand chose faces or edges of the feature you deleted in a way STEVE can't trace. Edit it and pick the geometry again, or go back to the last saved revision.
  • A new feature appears in the middle of the history. The history marker was rolled back. Drag it to the end.

pages.title: The code view
pages.description: Read and edit a part's CadQuery code in the Source tab, and how your edits and the modelling tools' edits stay in step.
pages.html:
Every part is Python code that runs on CadQuery. The Source tab of the Dock shows it, and you can edit it there. The code and the model are the same thing seen two ways: there is nothing else stored.

Open it with Source in the Dock, or Source editor in the command palette (Ctrl+E).

How the tools and the code stay in step

The tools write code. Each modelling action writes or replaces one statement:

You do The code gets
Finish a sketch A with model.sketch("sketch_1", on=..., name=...) as s: block of s.<shape>(...), constraint and dimension calls.
Add a feature One call, model.<feature>("<id>", ...), such as model.extrude("extrude_1", "sketch_1", distance=10).
Edit a feature The same call, with the new values; its id stays.
Rename a feature Its name="…". The id never changes, so references to it don't break.
Rename a body A model.body_name("<body id>", "<name>") line.
Suppress a feature suppressed=True on its call.
Add or change a parameter A line such as width = 80 # mm Plate width before model = Model().
Assign a material A model.material(...) statement.

Feature ids look like extrude_1 and are never reused or renumbered. The last line is always result = model.result().

Your code edits reach the tools. When you change the code, STEVE reads it again and the Browser, timeline and dialogs follow. A feature call stays editable in its dialog as long as its arguments are numbers, parameter names, arithmetic of those, reference names (strings) or lists of them. Anything else, such as a loop, a function or plain CadQuery, still runs, and shows as a read-only feature: you edit it here, in the code.

Write a dimension as an expression of a parameter, for example distance=thickness * 2, and the dialogs keep the expression.

Building

With Live on (the switch at the bottom of the tab, on by default), the model rebuilds a moment after you stop typing. Code with a syntax error isn't built until you fix it. With Live off, build with Update model (Ctrl+Enter). The status beside the switch says Up to date, Building…, Waiting to build…, Changes not built yet or Build failed. The same switch is Build as you type (Live) in Settings → Code editor.

Errors appear under the line they come from, in plain words, with Fix with STEVE. The Output strip at the bottom of the tab shows what the build printed.

Edits in the code are part of the document like any other change: save them with Save (Ctrl+S).

Find your way

  • The bar at the top of the tab names the file (model.py for a part). Outline lists the parameters and features; choose one to jump to its code.
  • Put the cursor in a feature's code and its faces light up in the model. Select a feature in the model or the timeline and its code is tinted.
  • Ctrl+click (⌘+click on a Mac) a parameter or a feature id to go to where it is defined.
  • Show in source on a feature's or a face's menu opens the tab at the code that made it.
  • Expand the editor gives a wide editor beside the model, with the outline as a column. Esc returns to the side panel.

Change numbers quickly

  • The parameters appear as a small form above the code; change a value there.
  • Alt+drag a number in the code sideways to change it, with a live preview. Hold Shift for steps ten times larger, Ctrl for ten times smaller.

Ask STEVE about the code

Select some code to get Explain and Change… (and Fix when the selection has an error), or press Ctrl+K (⌘K) at the cursor. A change runs as a normal STEVE conversation (it appears in the STEVE tab). When STEVE has edited the file, the editor shows each change inline: Keep or Undo it, one at a time or all at once.

Other tools in the tab

  • Samples: open an example part or design, or one of the reference designs in a new tab.
  • Download .py: the code as a file (also Download source under Export).

Older OCP calls keep working

Code can call OCP, the OpenCASCADE Python bindings CadQuery is built on, directly. Designs written with the names older OCP versions used, such as TopoDS.Face_s(shape), TColgp_Array1OfPnt, TopTools_ListOfShape, BRepTopAdaptor_FClass2d or Bnd_Box.Get(), still build: those calls work as they did. New code can use the current names: TopoDS.Face(shape), and the collection classes in OCP.collections (Array1_gp_Pnt, List_TopoDS_Shape).

Common problems

  • A feature you wrote by hand has no dialog. Its arguments aren't plain values (see above), or it isn't a model.<feature>(...) call. It still runs; edit it in the code, or ask STEVE to rewrite it as a feature call.
  • The model doesn't change while you type. Live is off, or the code has a syntax error. Look at the status beside the switch.
  • The editor is read-only. A build is running with Live off; wait for it to finish.

pages.title: Materials and appearance
pages.description: Assign an engineering material to a part or to some of its bodies, choose a finish or a colour, read the mass it gives, or set an appearance with no material.
pages.html:
Goal: give a part, or some of its bodies, a real material, so its mass, its simulation inputs and its look follow from it.

A material is a statement in the code, not a feature: it has no id and no timeline step, and it versions, branches and merges with the design.

model.material("aluminum-6061-t6")                                       # the whole part
model.material("stainless-304", bodies=["extrude_2"], finish="brushed")  # some bodies
model.material("abs", bodies=["boss"], color="#1f2328")                  # with a colour

Before you start

A part with at least one body.

Assign a material to the whole part

  1. Click Material on the ribbon's Modify group. (Or, in the Inspector with nothing selected, click Assign material, or Change on the current material.) The Materials library opens.
  2. Find the material: choose a category on the left, or type in the search box a name, a grade or a standard, such as 6061, 1.4301 or PEEK.
  3. Click the material. The right side shows its description, its properties with their sources, and the mass it gives the part ("Mass here").
  4. Optionally choose a Finish (the finishes offered depend on the material) and a colour: Tint, or Paint color for painted finishes. Use the material’s color undoes a colour.
  5. Under Assign to, leave Whole part.
  6. Click Assign (or press Enter). Double-clicking a material in the list assigns it at once.

A message confirms the assignment, for example "Aluminum 6061-T6 → the part", and the model rebuilds with the material's appearance.

Assign a material to some bodies

  1. Select the bodies (click them in the view or in the Browser under Bodies), then click Material. Or right-click a body and choose Material….
  2. Choose the material, as above.
  3. Under Assign to, choose Bodies and click the bodies' chips to choose which ones take it.
  4. Click Assign.

A body's own material overrides the part's, whatever the order of the statements.

Remove a material

Open the library for the part or the body and click Remove material (for the whole part) or Use part material (for bodies).

What you should see

The Inspector, with nothing selected, shows the part's material card (name, finish, Young's modulus and yield strength), its Density, Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, Yield strength, Tensile strength, Thermal conductivity and Thermal expansion, and, under Physical properties, the part's Mass computed from the exact volume and the density. Without a material the card says No material and "Mass needs a density".

Select a body to see its own Volume, Mass and Density.

Finishes and colours change only the look

A finish (for example polished, brushed, anodized, painted, matte) and a colour change how the body renders. They don't change the mass, the simulation inputs or the exported geometry.

The same is true of decals: images on a face, flat or curved, or across several faces, projected or wrapped round a body like a sticker, for appearance only.

Appearance without a material

To show paint, glazing or a presentation colour on geometry whose material isn't modelled (an exterior shell, a concept model, a proxy), give it an appearance instead of a material. An appearance never sets a density: the mass stays "—" until a body has a real material, and simulations ignore it.

  1. Click Appearance on the ribbon's Modify group, or right-click a body and choose Appearance…. Its options open in the right-hand panel.
  2. Under Apply to, choose Whole part, or Bodies and the bodies' chips.
  3. Set any of Color, Finish, Opacity, Roughness and Metalness (switch a value on to set it; one left off comes from the material, if there is one).
  4. Click OK. Clear appearance removes it.

In the code it is model.appearance(...):

model.appearance(color="#1c1c1e", finish="matte")                                     # the whole part
model.appearance(color="#9ec5e8", opacity=0.35, roughness=0.05, bodies=["canopy"])  # glazing

When a body has both, the appearance wins for the look and the material still gives the mass. Exported STEP files carry the appearance colour. Select a body to see its Appearance in the Inspector.

Some faces of a body

To paint a band, a trim or one side of a part without splitting the solid, give some faces their own appearance:

  1. Open Appearance and choose Faces under Apply to.
  2. Pick the faces in the viewport (Shift adds more). The panel lists their names.
  3. Set the look and click OK.

In the code the faces are named by their references, so the look follows the geometry when it changes:

model.appearance(color="#c8102e", finish="painted", faces=["strut.side_faces"])  # a red band
door_inner = ["door.end", "door_lip.faces"]                                       # a named set of faces
model.appearance(color="#2b2b2b", finish="matte", faces=door_inner)

A face's appearance wins over its body's. The geometry, the number of solids and the mass don't change, and STEP files carry the face colours. If a reference no longer names a face after an edit, the build says so and the faces keep their body's look.

The library

The library holds a few hundred engineering materials from open datasets (FreeCAD, physicallybased.info, Wikidata, Ultimaker and the USDA Wood Handbook). Every value has its unit and source; hover over a property to see where it comes from. Simulate reads the same materials.

Your own materials

Keep materials the library doesn't have, or a library material with the values from your supplier's data sheet. They are yours alone: nobody else sees them, and the shared library doesn't change.

  • Copy and change a library material: click the material, then Copy to my materials. Change its name, values or colour, and click Add to my materials. The copy is marked Modified; the original stays in the library, so you can assign either one.
  • Make a new one: click New material above the list, choose its category and enter the values you know (leave the others empty).
  • Find them: choose My materials on the left. Your materials also show in their categories and in searches, marked Modified or Mine.
  • Edit or delete one: click it, then Edit or Delete. A design that uses it rebuilds with the new values.

Assign them like any other material. Their ids start with my:, for example model.material("my:bronze-c932"). The density gives the mass; simulations use the stiffness, strength and thermal values (solving again uses the material's current values; earlier results keep the values they were solved with). Code that names a material you deleted reports it as unknown.

Common problems

  • The Material button is greyed out. There is no geometry yet; add a feature first. In a design, select a component (or open its file) first: materials belong to components.
  • Mass shows "—". No material is assigned, so there is no density.
  • An unknown material id in the code. It is reported and ignored; the build doesn't fail. Choose the material again from the library.

pages.title: Measure and section
pages.description: Measure distances, angles, radii and areas between faces, edges and vertices, and cut the model with a section plane to see inside.
pages.html:
Measure

Goal: read a size off the model.

  1. Click Measure on the ribbon's Inspect group, or on the view bar, or press M. The Measure panel opens in the Dock with two slots, "Pick an entity".
  2. Click a face, an edge or a vertex. The panel shows what it is and its sizes.
  3. Click a second one. The panel shows the measurement between the two, and the view draws it.
  4. Click Close (or press Esc) when you are done.

A third pick starts a new measurement. Click a picked item again to remove it; Clear empties both slots. You can also right-click a face or edge and choose Measure from here.

What one pick shows:

Pick Shows
Flat face Area and Normal.
Cylindrical face Area, Radius, Diameter, Axis, Axis through (a point on the axis) and Length along axis.
Conical face Area, Half angle, Axis and Apex.
Spherical face Area, Radius, Diameter and Center.
Toroidal face Area, Major radius, Minor radius, Axis and Center.
Other curved face (B-spline, lofted, swept) Area.
Edge Length; for arcs and circles Radius, Diameter and Center; Continuity "Tangent" for a smooth edge.
Vertex Its X, Y and Z.
Component Its Extents (X × Y × Z).

What two picks show (the rows that apply):

Rows When
Minimum distance Always: the shortest distance between the two picks (not for two circles in the same plane).
Distance and Angle "0° (parallel)" Two parallel flat faces.
Angle Two flat faces at an angle; two axes or straight edges (cylinders, cones, circles); an axis and a flat face.
Axis to axis Two cylinders, cones, circular edges or tori with parallel axes: the distance between the axes ("coaxial" at 0); with axes at an angle, how near the two axes come ("closest approach"). A straight edge's line counts as an axis: Axis to line, Line to axis.
Line to line Two parallel straight edges: the distance between them.
Axis to plane (or Line to plane) A cylinder or cone whose axis (or a straight edge) runs parallel to a flat face.
Center to plane, Apex to plane, Point to plane A sphere's, torus's or circle's centre, a cone's apex, or a vertex, to a flat face.
Center to axis, Point to axis A sphere's centre or a vertex to the axis of a cylinder, cone, torus or circle.
Center distance, Point to center Between two centres (spheres, tori, circles), or from a vertex to one.
Edge gap Two circles in the same plane: the gap between them.
ΔX, ΔY, ΔZ Two vertices.

Areas, radii, axes, centres, angles and the distances between them come from the model's exact geometry. A Minimum distance that involves a curved face or edge (or a flat face with a curved outline) is measured on the displayed model, which only approximates curves: it reads "≈" (hover it to see why). Between flat faces with straight edges, straight edges and vertices it is exact. Length along axis reads "≈" for the same reason; for the exact spacing of round features, use their axes and centres (Axis to axis, Center to plane and the like) with their radii.

Measure follows the selection filter in the status bar: with Auto it picks faces, edges and vertices; with Faces it picks faces only, which helps with a narrow face such as a small fillet.

All lengths are in millimetres, areas in mm² and angles in degrees. Measuring changes nothing in the design.

Physical properties

For sizes of the whole part, look at the Inspector with nothing selected: Dimensions (the overall X, Y and Z extents), Volume, Mass (with a material), Surface area, Center of mass and the number of Solids.

Section analysis

Goal: cut the model with a plane to see inside it.

  1. Click Section on the ribbon's Inspect group, or Section analysis on the view bar, or press X. The model is cut by the origin plane that faces you most directly, and the near half is removed. Cut faces are capped and hatched where there is solid material.
  2. In the Section analysis panel in the Dock, choose the Plane normal: X, Y or Z.
  3. Move the plane with the Offset slider, or type the position in millimetres. The range of the model along that axis is shown under the slider.
  4. Flip side keeps the other half.
  5. Click Close (or press Esc) to show the whole model again.

To cut through a particular flat face, right-click it and choose Section at this face.

The section is a view only: it changes nothing in the design, and exports are always of the whole model.

Save a section view

Goal: keep a cut so you can see it again later.

  1. Set up the cut in the Section analysis panel.
  2. Type a name in Save as (or keep the one suggested) and click Save. The cut is added to the code as one line, section_view("section_1", axis="x", at=12.5), so it's kept with the revision and follows branches and history.
  3. The saved cut is listed under Sections in the Browser. Click it to show that cut again, fixed: no plane to drag and no panel. Click it again, or press Esc, to show the whole model.

Right-click a saved section for Edit section… (opens Section analysis at that cut; Update saves it back, under a new name too), Show in source and Delete. A saved section stays at the same millimetres when the model changes; if it's now outside the model, its row is dimmed and its tooltip says so.

Common problems

  • Measure and Section are greyed out. There is no geometry yet.
  • A click on a narrow curved face, such as a small fillet, picks the edge beside it. Zoom in, or set the selection filter in the status bar to Faces.
  • "Click faces to measure. Edge and vertex picking needs topology from a newer build — regenerate to enable it." The model on screen was built by an older version of STEVE. Click Update model (Ctrl+Enter) to rebuild it.

pages.title: Sheet metal
pages.description: Model bent sheet-metal parts with a base flange and flanges, see the flat pattern, and export it as DXF with its bend table.
pages.html:
Sheet-metal parts are ordinary parts: each sheet-metal command writes one call into the code, in the same history as any other feature. The Sheet metal ribbon of the Design workspace holds the commands.

How a sheet works

A sheet starts with a Base flange (or a Rolled sheet, or Convert to sheet metal on a plate). That first feature sets the sheet's rules, which every later flange and bend follows:

  • Thickness (default 1.5 mm);
  • Bend radius, the inside bend radius (default 1.5 mm; about 1× the thickness suits most steel and aluminium);
  • K-factor, where the neutral layer sits in a bend (0 to 1, usually 0.3 to 0.5; default 0.44, a common air-bending estimate). It sets the flat length, so use your shop's value;
  • Source, an optional note of where the numbers come from (a shop chart, a test bend). It travels with the DXF.

Instead of typing values, you can choose Named rule and use a rule declared in the file (Sheet metal rules on the ribbon manages them; a rule can come from a gauge table or a bend table).

Make a bracket from a base flange and a flange

  1. Choose File → New part (Alt+N), then choose Sheet metal in the tools menu beside the Design workspace menu.
  2. Click Sketch and draw a closed outline on XY, for example a rectangle 80 × 40 mm. Click Finish (Ctrl+Enter). See Parts, sketches and constraints.
  3. Click Base (Base flange). Profile is your sketch. The sketch is the sheet's top face; the material goes below it. Leave Rules on Values, or type your Thickness, Bend radius and K-factor.
  4. Click OK.
  5. Click Flange (Edge flange), then click a straight outer edge of the sheet (its top or bottom edge, or the side face between them).
  6. Set Length (default 20) and Angle (default 90°; negative bends the other way). Measured to sets which length you mean (Tangent, Inner sharp or Outer sharp); Position sets where the wall sits relative to the edge (Bend outside, Material inside, Material outside or Centered).
  7. Click OK.

More options on the flange adds its own Bend radius and K-factor, an Edge offset, Inset start and Inset end, a Bend relief (None, Rectangular or Round) and a Miter gap.

The commands

The ribbon shows short names (Base, Flange, Contour, Flat, DXF and so on); hover over a button for its full name.

Group Command What it does
Rules Sheet metal rules Named rules sheets can share: thickness, bend radius and K-factor, or a gauge or bend table.
Create Base flange A flat sheet from a closed sketch; sets the sheet's rules.
Edge flange A wall bent up from a straight outer edge.
Contour flange Several walls off one edge in one step (an L, U, Z or hat section): a list of up to 32 segments, each a length after a bend angle.
Hem Folds an edge back on itself with a gap (Length 6, Gap 1, Fold Up or Down).
Jog Two opposed bends: a step up or down to a parallel panel (Offset 10, Length 15, Angle 45°).
Tab Cuts a U around a rectangle in a panel and bends it out.
Rolled sheet An open cylinder (a shroud, a guard, a sleeve) with an angular seam (Width 40, Wrap 340°).
Modify Sheet cut Cuts closed sketch shapes straight through one flat panel, so the flat pattern keeps them. Sketch on the panel's face first.
Relief Notches a panel with sketched shapes open to its edge (corner and bend reliefs).
Sketched bend Bends a flat panel along a line.
Corner Closes the corner between two 90° walls with a Gap (0.5).
Rip Opens the sheet with a gap: Slit a panel, Split a bend into two bodies, or Open a tube's seam so it unfolds.
Unfold Unfold Lays the sheet flat in the model, so you can sketch and cut across bends.
Refold Folds it back up, keeping cuts made in the flat.
Form Form Presses a form tool (lance, louver, emboss or dimple) into a flat panel.
Form tools Define reusable form tools, then place them with Form.
Convert Convert to sheet metal Makes a flat, uniform-thickness solid (a plate, or an imported STEP) into a sheet: pick its top face.
Flat pattern Flat pattern Shows the flat pattern beside the folded part.
Export flat pattern (DXF) Downloads the flat pattern files (below).

The Create, Modify, Unfold and Form commands, except Base flange, Rolled sheet and Rip, need a base flange first; until then their tooltip says "Make a base flange first." Flat pattern and Export flat pattern (DXF) need a built sheet-metal part ("Generate a sheet-metal part first."). The dialogs work like the Solid features: pick in the view, preview, OK. See Modelling features.

The flat pattern

Click Flat pattern (Flat on the ribbon) to show the developed blank in a panel over the canvas, beside the folded part: its developed size (for example "103.39 × 40 mm"), the bend lines (solid for Bend up, dotted for Bend down), the number of bends and the area. It updates with every change. Hover over a bend line to read its angle, direction, radius and bend allowance.

Export the flat pattern

  1. Click Export flat pattern (DXF) (DXF on the ribbon).
  2. STEVE builds the part fully if needed, and downloads a ZIP.

For each sheet body the ZIP holds a layered DXF in millimetres with exact arcs (layers CUT, BEND_UP, BEND_DOWN and ROLL), its bend table as CSV, an SVG illustration and a manifest. Bodies with forms add a forming DXF and a form table.

To put the blank on a shop drawing, add a Flat pattern view to a drawing sheet (see Views): it is the same development as the DXF, with its bend lines, bend notes and overall size.

Common problems

  • The sheet-metal buttons are greyed out with "Make a base flange first." Add a Base flange (or a Rolled sheet or Convert to sheet metal) first.
  • "Pick the edge of the sheet to bend from". A flange needs a straight outer edge of the sheet: its top or bottom edge, or the side face between them.
  • "The flat pattern can’t be exported yet". A sheet-metal feature failed; the message names it. Fix that feature first.
  • In a design, sheet metal is modelled in a component's file: open the component first.

Set **Length** (default 20) and **Angle** (default 90°; negative bends the other way). **Measured to** sets which length you mean (**Tangent**, **Inner sharp** or **Outer sharp**); **Position** sets where the wall sits relative to the edge (**Bend outside**, **Material inside**, **Material outside** or **Centered**). Click **OK**. ![A sheet-metal bracket with one flange bent up, and its flat pattern beside it with the bend line.](../../../assets/design/sheet-metal.png) **More options** on the flange adds its own **Bend radius** and **K-factor**, an **Edge offset**, **Inset start** and **Inset end**, a **Bend relief** (**None**, **Rectangular** or **Round**) and a **Miter gap**. The commands The ribbon shows short names (**Base**, **Flange**, **Contour**, **Flat**, **DXF** and so on); hover over a button for its full name. Group Command What it does **Rules** **Sheet metal rules** Named rules sheets can share: thickness, bend radius and K-factor, or a gauge or bend table. **Create** **Base flange** A flat sheet from a closed sketch; sets the sheet's rules.  **Edge flange** A wall bent up from a straight outer edge.  **Contour flange** Several walls off one edge in one step (an L, U, Z or hat section): a list of up to 32 segments, each a length after a bend angle.  **Hem** Folds an edge back on itself with a gap (**Length** 6, **Gap** 1, **Fold** **Up** or **Down**).  **Jog** Two opposed bends: a step up or down to a parallel panel (**Offset** 10, **Length** 15, **Angle** 45°).  **Tab** Cuts a U around a rectangle in a panel and bends it out.  **Rolled sheet** An open cylinder (a shroud, a guard, a sleeve) with an angular seam (**Width** 40, **Wrap** 340°). **Modify** **Sheet cut** Cuts closed sketch shapes straight through one flat panel, so the flat pattern keeps them. Sketch on the panel's face first.  **Relief** Notches a panel with sketched shapes open to its edge (corner and bend reliefs).  **Sketched bend** Bends a flat panel along a line.  **Corner** Closes the corner between two 90° walls with a **Gap** (0.5).  **Rip** Opens the sheet with a gap: **Slit a panel**, **Split a bend** into two bodies, or **Open a tube**'s seam so it unfolds. **Unfold** **Unfold** Lays the sheet flat in the model, so you can sketch and cut across bends.  **Refold** Folds it back up, keeping cuts made in the flat. **Form** **Form** Presses a form tool (lance, louver, emboss or dimple) into a flat panel.  **Form tools** Define reusable form tools, then place them with **Form**. **Convert** **Convert to sheet metal** Makes a flat, uniform-thickness solid (a plate, or an imported STEP) into a sheet: pick its top face. **Flat pattern** **Flat pattern** Shows the flat pattern beside the folded part.  **Export flat pattern (DXF)** Downloads the flat pattern files (below). The **Create**, **Modify**, **Unfold** and **Form** commands, except **Base flange**, **Rolled sheet** and **Rip**, need a base flange first; until then their tooltip says "Make a base flange first." **Flat pattern** and **Export flat pattern (DXF)** need a built sheet-metal part ("Generate a sheet-metal part first."). The dialogs work like the Solid features: pick in the view, preview, **OK**. See [Modelling features](/docs/design/features/#how-every-feature-dialog-works). The flat pattern Click **Flat pattern** (**Flat** on the ribbon) to show the developed blank in a panel over the canvas, beside the folded part: its developed size (for example "103.39 × 40 mm"), the bend lines (solid for **Bend up**, dotted for **Bend down**), the number of bends and the area. It updates with every change. Hover over a bend line to read its angle, direction, radius and bend allowance. Export the flat pattern Click **Export flat pattern (DXF)** (**DXF** on the ribbon). STEVE builds the part fully if needed, and downloads a ZIP. For each sheet body the ZIP holds a layered DXF in millimetres with exact arcs (layers CUT, BEND_UP, BEND_DOWN and ROLL), its bend table as CSV, an SVG illustration and a manifest. Bodies with forms add a forming DXF and a form table. To put the blank on a shop drawing, add a **Flat pattern** view to a drawing sheet (see [Views](/docs/drawing/views/#flat-pattern-view)): it is the same development as the DXF, with its bend lines, bend notes and overall size. Common problems *The sheet-metal buttons are greyed out with "Make a base flange first."* Add a **Base flange** (or a **Rolled sheet** or **Convert to sheet metal**) first. *"Pick the edge of the sheet to bend from".* A flange needs a straight outer edge of the sheet: its top or bottom edge, or the side face between them. *"The flat pattern can’t be exported yet".* A sheet-metal feature failed; the message names it. Fix that feature first. *In a design*, sheet metal is modelled in a component's file: open the component first.

pages.title: Import parts
pages.description: Bring STEP files, Autodesk Fusion designs, McMaster-Carr parts and open-source standard parts into a new part or into the part you have open.
pages.html:
Imported geometry is referenced from the code, so the code stays the whole design. STEVE keeps one copy of each file you import, and the part gets a call such as

model.import_step("import_1", "<the file's id>", name="bracket")

Imported faces get names in file order (import_1.face(12), or import_1.solid(2).face(3) when the file has several solids), so you can sketch on them, fillet their edges and cut into them like any other geometry.

Import a STEP or Fusion file

  1. Choose File → Import… (also in the command palette), and choose a .step, .stp or .f3d file. You can also drop the file anywhere on the STEVE window.
  2. The Import dialog uploads the file and checks it. It then shows how many solids the file holds, its size and its number of faces.
  3. Choose what to do with it:
    • New part from this file: opens a new tab with the model and this import, ready to save.
    • "Insert into" (the open part's name): adds the solids as new bodies after the last feature.
    • In a design: A component of this design (or Components in this design, one file per solid), or Link into this design (or One linked part per solid), which creates part documents and links them.
  4. Click the button at the bottom (Create part, Insert, Add component or Create and link).

When you insert into a part, STEVE builds it and opens Move/Copy on the new bodies: drag the arrows to place them, then click OK. Save the part to keep the import.

Fusion designs (.f3d)

A design exported from Autodesk Fusion as an .f3d file (in Fusion: File, Export, Fusion archive) comes in as its exact solids, at the size you modelled them. STEVE checks every solid against the shape Fusion itself displays for the design and refuses the file if they disagree, so what you import is what you saw in Fusion.

  • What comes in: the bodies of the design, each as a solid, in millimetres.
  • What doesn't: the Fusion timeline. Sketches, extrudes, revolves and other features aren't rebuilt as STEVE features, so the imported solids don't change when you edit a parameter.
  • The parameters and features are listed: STEVE reads the design's user and model parameters (name, expression, value, unit, comment) and its timeline features (type, name, description). Ask STEVE, or your AI agent, to rebuild the design as code from them when you want it parametric again (see Coming from Fusion).
  • Fusion archives of several designs (.f3z) can't be imported: export each design as .f3d, or the assembly as STEP.
  • Designs made of flat, cylindrical, conical, spherical and toroidal faces import today. Rounded blends that Fusion stores as procedural surfaces (many fillets) aren't read yet: the file fails with a message that names what couldn't be read. Export STEP from Fusion and import that instead.
  • A body that doesn't match Fusion's display of it fails the same way, with a message that says why.
  • Show every body in Fusion before you export: a body without a display in the file can't be checked, and the file is refused.

Limits and errors

The size limit for one file is listed in Limits. Errors the dialog can show:

  • File too large: simplify the model or export fewer bodies.
  • Not a file STEVE can import: only .step, .stp and .f3d files can be imported. Dropping another kind of file says "Only STEP and Fusion files can be imported".
  • A file with surfaces but no closed solids fails with "The STEP file has no solids".
  • Couldn’t import this Fusion design: the message says what STEVE couldn't read or check in the .f3d file.

Choose another file starts again.

Insert a standard part

STEVE can search about 17,000 open-source STEP models of bought-in parts from step.parts (MIT licensed): bearings, fasteners, motors, pulleys, extrusions, connectors and more.

  1. Click Standard part on the ribbon's Parts group (or File → Standard parts…).
  2. Type what you need in the search box, for example "608 bearing", "M3 socket head 10", "NEMA 17" or "GT2 pulley". Narrow it with the category chips.
  3. Click a part to select it. Its link to step.parts appears at the bottom.
  4. Click the button at the bottom right, which names where the part goes: "Insert into" the open part, "Add to" the open design, or Insert as a new part when nothing is open. Double-clicking a part does the same.

STEVE downloads the part, checks it like an imported STEP file ("Checking the part…"), and inserts it as above.

If nothing matches, try the designation without a vendor prefix, or the standard's number (ISO 4762, DIN 912).

Insert a McMaster-Carr part

STEVE never contacts McMaster-Carr itself: you download the part's file, and STEVE keeps a copy in your McMaster parts.

  1. Click McMaster on the ribbon's Parts group (or File → McMaster-Carr…).
  2. Click Open McMaster-Carr, or type a part number (such as 91251A540) and click Open on McMaster. McMaster-Carr opens in its own window.
  3. On McMaster-Carr, choose the part's 3-D STEP and download it.
  4. Drop the downloaded STEP or ZIP file on the dialog, or click to choose it from your downloads.
  5. Check the Part number (taken from the file name; type it if the file name has none) and the Description.
  6. Click the insert button ("Insert into" the open part, "Add to" the open design, or Insert as a new part).

The part is inserted named by its part number. Parts you have inserted before are listed under Your McMaster parts: search them and click Insert to use one again without downloading it.

Coming from Fusion

An imported STEP file is the shape only, without Fusion's parameters or timeline. An imported .f3d file is the shape too, with its parameters and features listed (see Fusion designs (.f3d)), but its timeline isn't rebuilt. To get an editable STEVE part with the same parameters and features, an AI agent connected to both Fusion and STEVE can rebuild the design: see Move designs from Fusion into STEVE.

Common problems

  • The insert button names the wrong place. It inserts into the active document tab. Switch tabs first, or close the document to make a new part.
  • "One moment — Wait for the current operation to finish." A build is running; insert again when the status bar says the model is ready.
  • Standard part search fails. The step.parts catalogue isn't reachable from STEVE right now; try again later, or download the part's STEP yourself and use Import….

pages.title: Surfaces and surface analysis
pages.description: The Surface tab of the Design workspace, its surfacing commands, and zebra stripes, curvature, draft and continuity checks for curved parts.
pages.html:
Freeform parts (a moulded enclosure, a handle, a lid that flows into its sides) live or die by how smoothly their faces meet. The Surface ribbon of the Design workspace gathers the commands that make curved faces and the tools that check them. Click Surface in the tab bar above the ribbon, beside Solid and Sheet metal.

The ribbon shows only commands that work today. More surfacing commands join it as they are added to STEVE.

The commands

Group Commands What they do
Create Sketch, Sweep, Loft, Fill, Boundary surface Draw the curves, then make faces from them. Sweep, loft, fill and boundary surface are the same commands as on the Solid ribbon: a sweep along a path (with a guide curve or a fixed direction), a smooth loft through sections, a patch closing a loop of edges, and a surface blended through curves. See Modelling features.
Analyze Zebra, Curvature, Draft, Continuity, Measure, Section Display-only checks of the model, described below, and distances, angles and a cut through it (Measure and section).

A Modify group appears once its commands (turning surfaces into solids) are part of STEVE.

Each command opens its options in the panel on the right, where you pick edges, curves and faces in the view and see the result before you apply it. Editing a Fill or a Boundary surface from the timeline opens this tab.

Surface bodies (from Fill and Boundary surface) have no inside. The view draws them in their own sand colour and from both sides, with their open edges in orange, and the model browser lists them under Surfaces, apart from the solid Bodies.

Check a surface

Each check colours the model in place of its usual look; its options and legend are in the panel on the right. Only one shows at a time: the buttons at the top of the panel switch between them, and Close (or clicking the same ribbon button again) brings the model's own look back. Nothing is written into your design, and the checks leave the model, its exports and its drawings unchanged.

Zebra stripes

Zebra stripes reflects a pattern of black and white stripes in the model, the way a car's paint reflects the strip lights of a showroom. Turn the view and watch the stripes where two faces meet:

  • stripes that run on across the edge in a smooth line: the faces are tangent, or better;
  • stripes that run on but bend sharply at the edge: the faces are tangent, but their curvature changes there;
  • stripes that kink into a corner at the edge: a crease (the faces meet at an angle);
  • stripes that jump sideways: a gap or step between the faces.

Stripes sets how many stripes there are, and Direction whether they run Vertical or Horizontal.

Curvature map

Curvature map colours the model by how tightly it curves: red where it bulges out (convex), blue where it curves in (concave), and grey where it is flat. Show chooses Mean curvature (how much it bends, on average) or Gaussian curvature (positive on a dome, zero on a cylinder or a cone, negative on a saddle). Full colour at radius sets the radius (mm) that shows at full colour; it starts at a twentieth of the model's size.

The values are estimated from the model as displayed (≈): close on a finely displayed model, not exact. On a smooth surface the colours change gradually; a sudden change of colour where two faces meet is a change of curvature there.

Draft analysis

Draft analysis colours each face by its draft against the direction the part leaves its mould:

  • green: draft of the minimum or more, towards the pull direction;
  • yellow: less than the minimum, such as vertical walls that need draft;
  • red: facing away from the pull direction, which is the other half of the mould, or an undercut.

Pull direction is X, Y or Z, and Reverse turns it round. Minimum draft (degrees) is the least draft that is enough; 1° is a common minimum for moulded plastics, more for textured faces. To add draft to faces, use Draft on the Solid ribbon.

Continuity check

Continuity check shows how two faces meet along an edge. Click an edge between two faces in the view, and the panel shows:

Value What it means
Largest gap (G0) The largest distance between the two faces along the edge. Faces that share an edge touch: 0 mm.
Largest angle (G1) The largest angle between the faces along the edge. 0° means they are tangent there.
Curvature change (G2) The largest difference between how tightly each face curves across the edge (per mm, and as a share of the larger).

Above them, the panel names the best continuity the faces meet: G2 (curvature continuous), G1 (tangent), G0 (touching, with a crease) or apart. They meet G0 within 0.01 mm, G1 within 0.1°, and G2 when their curvature across the edge matches within 5 %. An orange mark in the view shows where along the edge it is worst.

Where the build measured the edge itself, every value is exact: read from the faces' own geometry at points along the edge, and marked "Exact B-rep". It does that for every smooth edge (a fillet against its faces, a blend) and for the open edges of a surface body against the face of another body that continues it, such as a Fill patch against the walls it closes; pick either edge. Where two faces meet at a crease, the values come from the model as displayed and show ≈: close, not exact. An open edge that no other face continues has nothing to meet.

What STEVE's surfacing can and can't do

The analysis measures continuity, including curvature (G2) continuity, between any faces. STEVE's modelling tools don't make it: a loft is smooth through its own sections, and Fill can be tangent (G1) to the faces around it, but G2 continuity between faces and Class-A surface quality are beyond STEVE's modelling tools. Use the checks to find where a model creases or steps, and change the curves or the features that made those faces.

pages.title: Export
pages.description: Download a part as STEP, STL or 3MF, an image of the view as PNG, or its CadQuery source.
pages.html:
Goal: get your part out of STEVE, for another CAD program, a 3D printer, a document or a script.

Where the exports are

  • The Export button at the right of the top bar. Its main part repeats the last format you used (STEP until you choose another; remembered in this workspace). The arrow beside it lists every format.
  • File → Export.
  • Export on the ribbon's Export group.
  • A body's menu in the Browser (right-click it) offers that body alone as 3MF or STL.

Exports need geometry: with an empty part they are greyed out ("There’s no geometry yet.").

Formats

Menu item Command What you get
STEP Export STEP The complete CAD model as STEP AP214, including hidden bodies and components, as a .step file.
3MF Export 3MF For your slicer: millimetres, each body a named object placed as modelled. The selection if there is one, otherwise the whole model.
STL Export STL One binary STL in millimetres, bodies placed as modelled. The selection if there is one, otherwise the whole model.
Image (PNG) Capture image The 3D view as it is now, as <document name>.png. Also the camera button on the view bar.
Source (.py) Download source The part's CadQuery code as <document name>.py.

Designs add Selected component (STEP), Selected component (3MF) and Print set exports (see Assemblies), and parts and designs with a drawing add Drawing (PDF), Drawing (view · print) and Drawings (SVG · DXF) (see Drawings). Sheet-metal flat patterns are exported from the Sheet metal tab: see Sheet metal.

STEP, STL and 3MF come from a full build of the model. If the model on screen is a quick preview, STEVE makes the full build first, which can take a few seconds longer. The STEP file is made when you export, send or download it; large assemblies can take a few minutes. The status bar shows "Making STEP file…" with its progress, and the download starts by itself when the file is ready. If it can't be made, STEVE says why and offers "Retry". You don't need to save first: the export is of what you see.

Export a STEP file

  1. Click Export STEP in the top bar (or choose STEP from its menu).
  2. The first time, STEVE makes the STEP file ("Making STEP file…"); then choose a local destination for a .step file, and a message says "Exporting STEP".

Open the file in any CAD program that reads STEP. To check it in STEVE, import it into a new part: File → Import…, then New part from this file (see Import parts).

Export only some bodies as STL or 3MF

  1. Select the bodies, or faces of them, in the view or the Browser.
  2. Open the menu beside Export and choose STL or 3MF; the menu marks them "Selection".

To export the whole model, clear the selection first (Esc). The message after the export says what was exported, for example "The whole model: 1 body as one binary STL in millimetres."

Resolution Surface within What it's for
Fine (default) 0.02 mm The smoothest mesh, finer than any printer needs.
Medium 0.05 mm Still smooth for most prints, in a smaller file.
Coarse 0.1 mm The smallest file; small holes and fillets show their facets.

The choice applies to 3MF, STL and the Print set, and stays chosen in this workspace. The message after the export names the resolution, the number of triangles and the file's size. The first export at a new resolution takes a moment longer while STEVE meshes the model again.

Capture an image

  1. Set up the view: orbit, choose the display style, hide what you don't want.
  2. Click the camera button on the view bar (Capture image), or choose Image (PNG) from the Export menu.

The PNG is the 3D view at the size it has on your screen.

Common problems

  • "Nothing to export as STL". The selection has no bodies. Clear it to export the whole model.
  • The STL or 3MF is huge. Choose Medium or Coarse under Mesh resolution in the Export menu.
  • The STEP file has bodies you hid. STEP always holds the complete model, including hidden components. Use STL or 3MF with a selection for part of it.
  • The export waits. The full build is queued behind other work, or the STEP file is still being made; the status bar shows its place and progress.

pages.title: Assemblies
pages.description: Designs made of components and linked parts, placed together, connected by joints and moved.
pages.html:
An assembly in STEVE is a design document: several components and linked documents placed together in one coordinate frame. Joints connect them so they can move, and the build reports a bill of materials and the results of any collision or fit checks you ask for.

Everything you do here is written as Python into the design's files, mostly main.py. The tools in the app write the same calls you could type yourself, so the code and the model always agree.

Pages

Concepts

  • Designs and parts: what a design is, how it differs from a part, and its files, components, links and instances.

Building an assembly

  • Add components and linked parts: new components, linked parts and designs, imported and standard parts, patterns.
  • Place components: the Place tool and at=.
  • Fasteners and standard parts: bought-in parts, and declared screw joints that every build checks.

Making it move

  • Joints: revolute, slider, cylindrical and fixed joints, with axes and limits.
  • Gears and couplings: gear meshes, rack and pinion, belts and custom couplings.
  • Move a mechanism: the Motion ribbon, dragging parts, joint sliders, motors and poses.
  • Animations: keyframes between poses on a timeline.
  • Export motion: an animated GLB, a video, or a MuJoCo simulation model.

Checking it

  • Collision and fit checks: collision checks on motors and animations, collision studies across several joints, and fit checks for interference and clearance.
  • Exploded views: spread the components apart on screen, or make a step-by-step explode that plays on the timeline.
  • Bill of materials: what the design is made of, with quantities.

Single parts (sketches and features) are covered in Design parts. Every command named here is listed in the commands reference.

pages.title: Add components and linked parts
pages.description: Add new components, link saved parts and designs, and repeat instances in a design.
pages.html:
Goal: put geometry into a design, either as components that belong to it or as links to parts and designs you have already saved.

Prerequisites

  • A design open in the Design workspace (File → New design, or open a saved one).
  • To link a document: the part or design you want to link is saved at least once.

Add a new component

  1. In the model tree, under Components, click New component. (In an empty design you can also click Create component in the middle of the viewport.)
  2. Type a name, for example lid, and press Enter.

STEVE creates components/lid.py with an empty Component, imports it into main.py and places it there with design.add(lid). The new file opens, so the sketch and feature tools now work inside that component. Spaces and hyphens in the name become underscores and capitals become lowercase; the result must start with a letter. A name that is already used is refused with "There is already a component named lid."

To edit a component later, double-click it in the tree, or right-click it and choose Edit component. Placement (main.py) and Shared parameters (params.py) sit below the components in the same group.

Link a saved part or design

  1. On the Solid ribbon, in the Design group of the ribbon, click Link (the command palette calls it Link a design or part).
  2. In Link a part, design or circuit board, find the document. Type in Search designs to filter.
  3. Select it and click Link and place (or press Enter).
  4. The Place tool opens on the new instance. Move it where it belongs and click the panel's OK button, or cancel to leave it at the origin. See Place components.

What you should see: the document appears under Links in the model tree with its pinned revision, and main.py gains two lines:

from links import hinge_pin
design.add(hinge_pin())

The link's name comes from the document's name in lowercase with underscores (a document called "Hinge pin" becomes hinge_pin). A design can't link itself, and STEVE refuses a link that would loop back to the design.

Your own libraries

Keep the parts you reuse (hardware, fixtures, house standards) as ordinary parts and designs in a folder, and mark the folder as a library so it's one click away:

  1. File → Open…, right-click the folder in the folder list and choose Use as library. A small library mark appears beside its name. (Stop using as library turns it back into an ordinary folder; nothing in it changes.)
  2. With a design open, File → Libraries lists your libraries. Pick one: the Link dialog opens inside it, listing the documents in it and in its subfolders.
  3. Select a part and click Link and place, as above.

The Libraries button in the Parts group and Libraries… in the command palette open your first library; the others carry the library mark in the dialog's folder list. In a part, Libraries is unavailable: libraries are linked into designs. Library parts are always links, pinned to a revision with their own parameters per use, never copies. STEVE and your AI agents see which folders are libraries too, so they look there before making a new part.

Set a linked document's parameters

A linked part's parameters are its top-level numbers (for example length = 40); a linked design's are the values in its params.py. Override them where the link is placed, in main.py:

design.add(hinge_pin(length=60), at=(0, 50, 40))
design.add(hinge_pin(length=30), at=(0, -50, 40))

Each distinct set of overrides builds once and becomes its own row in the bill of materials. An override that the linked document doesn't have fails the build with a message listing the parameters it does have.

Update a link to a newer revision

A link stays at the revision you linked until you update it. When the linked document has been saved again, its row under Links shows a button such as rev 3 → 5.

  1. Click that button to update one link, or click Update in the Design group (Update links) to update every link that is behind.

The design rebuilds with the new revision. Right-clicking a link offers the same as Update to revision 5.

Open the document behind a link

  1. Select the linked instance in the viewport.
  2. In the Assemble group, click Open link (Open linked document).

The document opens in a new tab. Right-clicking the link in the tree offers Open linked document too.

Add bought-in and imported parts

  • Standard parts: in the Parts group, click Standard part, search (for example "608 bearing" or "M3 socket head 10"), select a part and click Add to your design's name. See Fasteners and standard parts.
  • McMaster-Carr: in the Parts group, click McMaster, download a part's 3-D STEP file there and drop it on STEVE.
  • A STEP or Fusion file: File → Import…, or drop the file on the window. In a design you can add each solid as Components in this design (one file per solid) or create One linked part per solid.

Repeat a component

Placing the same component or link again makes another instance. In main.py:

design.add(wheel, at=(-40, 0, 0))
design.add(wheel, at=(40, 0, 0))            # a second instance, named wheel_2
design.pattern(spoke, count=6, axis="Z")    # six instances around Z: spoke_1 ... spoke_6
design.pattern(slat, count=4, direction=(1, 0, 0), spacing=25)   # four in a row, 25 mm apart
  • design.pattern(component, count, axis="Z", angle=360.0) spreads instances evenly around an axis through the origin. With the default full turn, the last instance doesn't repeat the first.
  • design.pattern(component, count, direction=(x, y, z), spacing=mm) places them in a line.
  • design.pattern(component, points=[(x, y), (x, y, z), ...]) places one instance at each point, spaced however you like (mm). Add polar=True to give points as (radius, angle in degrees) or (radius, angle, z); each instance turns by its angle, as in a circular pattern.
  • at= on a pattern places the whole pattern; name= sets the base name (<name>_1, <name>_2, ...).

Patterns from a table

When the positions come as a table, keep it in the design: in the Source panel, open the file switcher and choose Import table…, then pick a .csv file (a spreadsheet saves one with Save As → CSV) or an Excel workbook (.xlsx). It is saved beside main.py, as holes.csv for example, and you can edit it there.

Without writing code: with main.py open, choose Pattern → Table pattern on the ribbon. In its panel pick the Component, then the Table (or Import table… to add one there), and optionally the Columns to read, Polar (r, θ), Move pattern and a Name. The preview shows the instances; OK writes the design.pattern(...) line below into main.py. Or read the table in main.py yourself:

from steve import Design, table

design.pattern(hole_insert, points=table("holes.csv"))              # x, y (and z) per row
design.pattern(post, points=table("posts.csv"), polar=True)          # radius, angle per row
design.pattern(pin, points=table("pins.csv", columns=("x", "y")))   # pick columns by their header names

Commas, semicolons or tabs all work, and a first row of column names is recognised. Importing a table of the same name again replaces it (history keeps the old one).

An .xlsx workbook is turned into a .csv in your browser, and only that .csv is saved: STEVE keeps no link to the workbook, so after changing it, import it again. The first sheet is used; when there are several, pick one. Only cell values come across: a formula brings the value Excel last saved with it (it isn't recalculated), dates arrive as Excel's day numbers, and hidden sheets, macros, links, comments, charts and formatting are left behind. Macro-enabled (.xlsm), binary (.xlsb) and old (.xls) workbooks aren't read: save them as Excel Workbook (.xlsx) or as CSV. A workbook can be up to 10 MB and its sheet up to 200,000 cells.

Remove a component

Right-click the component in the tree and choose Delete component. STEVE deletes its file, its import and its design.add(...) lines in main.py. If a joint, another component or a placement inside a loop still uses it, the command is unavailable and says where it is used ("Used in ...: remove those uses first.").

Common problems

  • Link is unavailable: the open document is a part. Links belong to designs; open or create a design.
  • A linked part's face can't be picked as a joint axis: joint axes come from components' geometry. Use a datum axis, or a face on a component; see Joints.
  • "Link ... isn't part of this design": main.py imports a link that the design doesn't list. Add it with Link rather than typing the import by hand.

pages.title: Animations
pages.description: Make a keyframed animation between named poses, then play, scrub and retime it on the timeline.
pages.html:
Goal: show a mechanism moving through a sequence, for example a lid that opens, holds and closes, as a repeatable animation you can check for collisions and export.

An animation (design.animation) lists keys: a pose and the time it is reached. Between keys every joint and coupling moves from one key's value to the next.

Prerequisites

  • A design with joints and at least two saved poses. See Move a mechanism to save poses.

Make an animation

  1. On the Motion ribbon, in the Animate group, click Animation (New animation), or click New animation in the timeline under the viewport.
  2. Type a Name (lowercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter; the default is animation_1).
  3. Edit the keys. The panel starts with three: your first pose at 0 s, your second at 2 s, and the first again at 4 s. For each key, choose a pose and type its time in seconds. Earlier and Later swap a key's pose with its neighbour's, keeping the times; the bin button removes a key (an animation keeps at least two). Add key adds a key one second after the last.
  4. Choose Easing: Smooth (each move starts and stops gently) or Linear (constant speed between keys).
  5. Set Loop (on by default in this panel) and, optionally, Check collisions.
  6. Click OK (Save animation).

What you should see: the timeline under the viewport shows the animation with a diamond for each key, the animation is listed under Joints in the model tree with its number of keys and length, and main.py gains:

design.animation("open_close", [("closed", 0), ("open", 2), ("open", 3), ("closed", 5)], loop=True)

The same pose twice in a row holds it: above, the lid stays open from 2 s to 3 s.

Use the timeline

The timeline appears under the viewport on the Motion ribbon.

  • Choose an animation in the list at its left, and click the play button (Play animation) to play it from the playhead; click again to pause. The time shows as now / length s.
  • Scrub: press on the track and drag; the mechanism follows the playhead.
  • Retime a key: drag its diamond. It stays between its neighbours and snaps to 0.1 s (hold Shift for 0.01 s).
  • Change a key: right-click its diamond and choose another pose, Edit animation… or Remove key. Double-click a diamond to edit the whole animation.
  • Add a key at the playhead: click the + button (Add key) and choose the pose it reaches there, or Save the current pose… first.
  • Loop: the loop button switches between Looping and Plays once.
  • Collision check: the radar button turns the build's collision sweep of this animation on or off. Collisions show as red spans on the track, and the parts turn red while the playhead is in one.

Every change on the timeline rewrites the design.animation(...) call in main.py and rebuilds.

You can also play an animation from the Animate group's Play button, from the Inspector's Motion section (each animation has a play and an edit button), or by right-clicking it in the tree (Play, Edit animation…, Show in source, Delete).

In code

design.animation(name, keys, loop=False, easing="ease", check=False, samples=48)
  • keys: at least two (pose, seconds) pairs in time order. A pose is a name from design.pose(...) or a dict of joint and coupling values, such as {"hinge": 30}. What a key doesn't name keeps its value from the key before (the code's pose at the start). The last key must be later than the first.
  • easing: "ease" (smoothstep: a smooth start and stop, as the viewer plays it) or "linear".
  • loop=True plays it over and over. In code the default is False; the panel's default is on.
  • check=True sweeps the animation at each build with exact solids, at samples times across its length (2 to 360).

Common problems

  • New animation is unavailable: "Save two poses first (Pose)."
  • "Give the last key a later time than the first." All keys are at the same time.
  • A pose can't be deleted: an animation moves through it. Edit or delete the animation first.

Related

  • Export motion: an animated GLB or a video of the animation.
  • Presentation view: play the animation full screen, with nothing else on the screen.
  • Collision and fit checks

pages.title: Bill of materials
pages.description: Where a design's bill of materials comes from, what each row means, and how printed parts, fasteners and cables appear in it.
pages.html:
Goal: see what a design is made of, with quantities, for ordering, printing or a drawing's parts list.

Every build of a design computes its bill of materials from main.py. You don't maintain it by hand: add, link or remove instances and it follows.

Prerequisites

  • A generated design with at least one placed instance.

See the bill of materials

  1. Open the Inspector (the right-hand panel) with nothing selected.
  2. Scroll to the Bill of materials section.

The table has three columns:

Column Shows
Item The component's or linked document's name. A link placed with parameter overrides lists them under its name, such as length=60.
Qty How many instances use it.
Source component for a component of this design; kind · rev n for a linked part, design or circuit, with its pinned revision; the kind and standard for declared hardware; and printed (FDM, PETG) style notes for parts marked as printed.

How rows are counted

  • Components: one row per component, counting its instances (design.add twice, or a pattern of six, gives a quantity of 2 or 6).
  • Links: one row per linked document and distinct set of overrides. hinge_pin(length=60) and hinge_pin(length=30) are two rows.
  • Printed parts: instances placed with print={...} (below) are rows of their own per print settings, listing their instances.
  • Declared fasteners: each design.fasten(...) adds its screw (by standard, size and length, such as "ISO 4762 M3×8"), and its washer, nut or heat-set insert when it has one. A placed screw part that a fastener names with instance= is counted once, as the fastener's screw. See Fasteners and standard parts.
  • Cables: each design.cable(...) is a row with its diameter and, when the build measured it, its cut length (the longest path checked through the motion, plus its slack, rounded up).
  • Bodies that aren't parts have no row. See Mark a component as not hardware.

Mark a component as not hardware

Some components exist only for analysis or layout: the air or liquid a flow study needs as a body, or a keep-out volume. Declare it once, in the component's file:

air_path = Component("air_path", name="Air path", hardware=False)

It still builds, shows in the viewer, stays in the design's STEP file, and a simulation study can use it as its body. It is left out of:

  • the bill of materials, and a drawing's parts list, cut list and balloons;
  • the design's volume, mass and centre of mass in the Inspector (the extent still includes it);
  • fit checks, motion and collision checks, cable checks and fastener checks;
  • the print meshes (STL and 3MF export, Export print set), the one-STEP-per-component download and the manufacturing checks.

It can't be marked as printed (print=), and a screw can't clamp or thread into it.

Mark parts as 3D-printed

Add print= to a placement in main.py:

design.add(bracket, print={"build_direction": "+Z", "material": "petg"})
design.pattern(clip, count=4, axis="Z", print={"process": "fdm"})
  • process: "fdm" (default), "sla", "sls" or "mjf".
  • build_direction: the part's own axis that points up on the printer: "+Z" (default), "-Z", "+X", "-X", "+Y" or "-Y".
  • Optional material (a filament or resin, such as "petg"), group (a variant group) and notes.

Then Export → Export print set downloads a zip with one 3MF per unique printed part, standing on its bed in millimetres, with quantities, a print list and a manifest tied to the revision. Identical instances with the same settings share one file.

The zip also has plates (plates/plate_1.3mf, …): every copy the quantities ask for, laid out side by side on a print bed, so a plate opens in your slicer ready to slice. Choose the bed in the same menu under Print bed (180 × 180 up to 350 × 350 mm; remembered in this workspace). Each plate holds one process and one material, and parts sit 5 mm apart by their bounding boxes, so your slicer's arrange can pack them tighter. A part too big for the bed gets a plate of its own, and the print list marks it "bigger than the bed". Each plate is a standard 3MF, one per plate, which every slicer opens.

Use the bill of materials elsewhere

  • A drawing's parts list and balloons come from the same rows. See Drawings.
  • AI agents get it, with each link's update status, from read_design. See AI agents and the design tools reference.

Common problems

  • No Bill of materials section: the design has no placed instances yet, or hasn't been generated.
  • A linked part appears twice: it is placed with two different sets of overrides, or linked at two revisions.
  • Export print set is unavailable: "Mark parts as printed first: design.add(part, print={"build_direction": "+Z"}) in main.py."

Related

  • Designs and parts
  • Add components and linked parts
