pages.title: Collision and fit checks
pages.description: Find parts that collide while a design moves, across combinations of joints, or that overlap or sit too close as modeled.
pages.html:
Goal: find out whether the parts of a design run into each other, and where.

STEVE has three kinds of check, all computed at the build with the exact solids:

Check Question it answers How you add it
Collision check Does anything collide along this motor's or animation's motion? Collisions on the Motion ribbon, or check=True
Collision study Which combinations of several joints collide? design.collision_study(...) in main.py
Fit check Do the parts overlap or come closer than a clearance, as modeled, at poses and through their motion? design.fit_check(...) in main.py

Collision checks and studies test every two instances that move relative to each other; a fit check tests every two instances. Faces that only touch have no common volume, so they don't count as a collision. Pairs that already overlap in the code's pose are listed as "Already overlapping at rest (not counted)" in the motion checks.

Prerequisites

  • A design with joints, and a motor or an animation for the collision check. See Move a mechanism and Animations.

Check a motor or an animation for collisions

  1. On the Motion ribbon, show the animation on the timeline, or select the joint whose motor you want to check (with neither, the first motor is used).
  2. In the Check group, click Collisions. It stays highlighted while the check is on.

The tool writes check=True on the design.drive(...) or design.animation(...) call and rebuilds. The same switch is Check collisions in the Motor, Joint and Animation panels, and the radar button on the timeline. Click Collisions again to turn it off.

What you should see, in the Inspector's Motion section:

  • for a motor: "joint: no collisions across range (n poses checked)", or one line per colliding pair, "a hits b at values", with a show button that moves the mechanism there;
  • for an animation: red spans on the timeline where parts collide.

While the motion plays or you scrub it, colliding parts turn red, and the motor's player over the viewport names them.

The build checks a motor at 24 values across its range (or -180° to 180° for a continuous one) and an animation at 48 times across its length; samples= (2 to 360) changes that. In the preview made as you save, each check stops after 25 seconds and says how many poses it covered. A full build (the toolbar's build) gives the checks a share of its own time limit, so they cover many more poses.

Study combinations of joints

A motor or animation checks one path. Arms, legs and pan-tilt heads often collide only when two joints move together. A collision study samples several joints at once:

design.collision_study("reach", joints=["shoulder", "elbow"], sampling="grid", steps=5)
design.collision_study("sweep", joints=["shoulder", "elbow", "wrist"], samples=800, seed=1, clearance=1.0)
design.collision_study("log", sampling="poses", poses=["home", {"shoulder": 30, "elbow": -45}])
design.collision_study("walk", sampling="animation", animation="walk_sit", at="keys", pairs=[("thigh", "pack")])
  • joints: the joints or couplings that vary, over their limits or ranges={"elbow": (-90, 0)}. Everything else stays at hold (a pose name or values; default the code's pose).
  • sampling: "random" (default: samples poses, 400 by default, reproducible with seed), "grid" (steps in degrees or mm, one number or one per joint), "poses" (a list of pose names or value dicts, such as a recorded motion) or "animation" (an animation as it plays: at="keys" at its keys, at=[seconds, ...], or samples times evenly across it, optionally between=(start, end) seconds). Following an animation with pairs=[...] also reports each listed pair's closest approach over the motion and when it happens; it's a lighter, more focused alternative to the animation's own check=True on a large design.
  • ignore=[("a", "b")] skips designed contacts; pairs=[...] checks only those pairs.
  • clearance (mm) also reports near misses closer than that.
  • map=(a, b) maps which pair collides over two joints (the default for a two-joint grid); boundary=(a, b) finds b's first contact at boundary_values values of a (default 11), to tolerance (default 0.1).

A study checks at most 2000 poses, within 25 seconds in a preview or its share of a full build's time. Its report in the Inspector's Motion section gives the share of poses that collide, each pair with how much of the space it blocks and how deep it overlaps (with a show button for its deepest pose), arrows to step through the colliding poses (the pair turns red and a yellow dot marks the overlap's centre), the map, and Download results for the full JSON.

design.collision_shape(instance, "box" | "sphere" | "capsule", ...) gives an instance simple shapes, as a physics simulator would use; a study scores them against the exact solids (detection rate, false alarms, deepest missed overlap).

Check fit and clearance

A fit check answers "does what I changed still fit its neighbours" at every build:

design.clearance(0.5, pairs={("plug", "shell"): 1.0})    # gaps required, in mm
design.contact("lid", "base", "seated")                  # a contact that is meant to exist
design.contact("pin", "bushing", "press_fit", max_overlap_mm3=2)
design.fit_check()                                       # every pair, as modeled and through every joint
design.fit_check("lid_fit", instances=["lid"], poses=["open"], motion=False)
  • design.fit_check(name="fit", instances=None, poses=None, motion=True, samples=24, refine=0.1) checks every two instances (or each listed instance against everything) as modeled, at each named pose in poses, and, with motion=True, through every joint or coupling that moves one of them, refined between samples until a step moves the parts at most refine mm.
  • Each pair that overlaps, or comes closer than its clearance, is reported with the overlap volume or the gap, and the pose where it is worst.
  • design.clearance(default=0.0, pairs=None) sets the gap required between instances with no declared contact.
  • design.contact(a, b, kind="seated", max_overlap_mm3=None) declares contacts that are meant to exist: "seated" (face to face), "press_fit" (no overlap unless you allow some) or "threaded" (a screw in its hole: any overlap unless you give a limit). Declared contacts are listed apart and fail only past their allowance. Parts fastened with a fixed joint are not a contact and still may not overlap.

The Inspector's Motion section shows each fit check: "name: fits: no overlaps or tight gaps in n pairs", or the pairs that overlap or are too close, each with show to move to where it's worst. Where no clearance is kept, a "Touching" line lists the pairs that touch without overlapping (with no contact declared), so a seated part and one just clear of its seat no longer look the same; touching never fails the check.

AI agents can compare a fit check with an earlier revision: inspect_model with checks=["interference"] reports each pair as new, worse, unchanged or resolved against options={"base_revision": N} (default: the previous revision), and passes when nothing is new or worse and the check reached every requested pose and sweep. See AI agents and the design tools reference.

Common problems

  • Collisions is unavailable: "Add a motor or an animation first."
  • Incomplete, "Stopped after ... poses (time budget 25 s, a preview's ...)": the check ran out of time in a preview. It shows how many of the requested poses it checked (and, for a fit check, which poses and sweeps it didn't reach) and is never reported as clear, by the panel or to AI agents. Run a full build to check every pose, or lower samples, check fewer pairs, or split a study. If a full build's check still stops ("this full build's share of its time limit"), do the same.
  • A result says "approximate" or "the exact check failed": an instance isn't a valid closed solid (often an imported mesh-like part), so its overlaps can't be computed exactly. A failed check is never reported as clear.

Related

  • Fasteners and standard parts: declared screws have their own clash checks.
  • Export motion: collision shapes in the simulation model.

alternative to the animation's own `check=True` on a large design. `ignore=[("a", "b")]` skips designed contacts; `pairs=[...]` checks only those pairs. `clearance` (mm) also reports near misses closer than that. `map=(a, b)` maps which pair collides over two joints (the default for a two-joint grid); `boundary=(a, b)` finds
b's first contact at `boundary_values` values of a (default 11), to `tolerance` (default 0.1). A study checks at most 2000 poses, within 25 seconds in a preview or its share of a full build's time. Its report in the Inspector's **Motion** section
gives the share of poses that collide, each pair with how much of the space it blocks and how deep it overlaps (with a
**show** button for its deepest pose), arrows to step through the colliding poses (the pair turns red and a yellow dot
marks the overlap's centre), the map, and **Download results** for the full JSON. `design.collision_shape(instance, "box" | "sphere" | "capsule", ...)` gives an instance simple shapes, as a physics
simulator would use; a study scores them against the exact solids (detection rate, false alarms, deepest missed
overlap). Check fit and clearance A fit check answers "does what I changed still fit its neighbours" at every build: design.clearance(0.5, pairs={("plug", "shell"): 1.0})    # gaps required, in mm
design.contact("lid", "base", "seated")                  # a contact that is meant to exist
design.contact("pin", "bushing", "press_fit", max_overlap_mm3=2)
design.fit_check()                                       # every pair, as modeled and through every joint
design.fit_check("lid_fit", instances=["lid"], poses=["open"], motion=False)
 `design.fit_check(name="fit", instances=None, poses=None, motion=True, samples=24, refine=0.1)` checks every two
instances (or each listed instance against everything) as modeled, at each named pose in `poses`, and, with
`motion=True`, through every joint or coupling that moves one of them, refined between samples until a step moves the
parts at most `refine` mm. Each pair that overlaps, or comes closer than its clearance, is reported with the overlap volume or the gap, and the
pose where it is worst. `design.clearance(default=0.0, pairs=None)` sets the gap required between instances with no declared contact. `design.contact(a, b, kind="seated", max_overlap_mm3=None)` declares contacts that are meant to exist: `"seated"`
(face to face), `"press_fit"` (no overlap unless you allow some) or `"threaded"` (a screw in its hole: any overlap
unless you give a limit). Declared contacts are listed apart and fail only past their allowance. Parts fastened with
a fixed joint are not a contact and still may not overlap. The Inspector's **Motion** section shows each fit check: "*name*: fits: no overlaps or tight gaps in *n* pairs", or the
pairs that overlap or are too close, each with **show** to move to where it's worst. Where no clearance is kept, a
"Touching" line lists the pairs that touch without overlapping (with no contact declared), so a seated part and one
just clear of its seat no longer look the same; touching never fails the check. AI agents can compare a fit check with an earlier revision: `inspect_model` with `checks=["interference"]` reports each
pair as new, worse, unchanged or resolved against `options={"base_revision": N}` (default: the previous revision), and
passes when nothing is new or worse and the check reached every requested pose and sweep. See [AI agents](/docs/agents/) and the [design tools reference](/docs/reference/mcp-tools/designs/). Common problems *Collisions is unavailable*: "Add a motor or an animation first." *Incomplete*, "Stopped after ... poses (time budget 25 s, a preview's ...)": the check ran out of time in a preview.
It shows how many of the requested poses it checked (and, for a fit check, which poses and sweeps it didn't reach)
and is never reported as clear, by the panel or to AI agents. Run a full build to check every pose, or lower
`samples`, check fewer pairs, or split a study. If a full build's check still stops ("this full build's share of its
time limit"), do the same. *A result says "approximate" or "the exact check failed"*: an instance isn't a valid closed solid (often an
imported mesh-like part), so its overlaps can't be computed exactly. A failed check is never reported as clear. Related [Fasteners and standard parts](/docs/assemblies/fasteners/): declared screws have their own clash checks. [Export motion](/docs/assemblies/export-motion/): collision shapes in the simulation model.

pages.title: Designs and parts
pages.description: How a design differs from a part, and how its files, components, links and instances fit together.
pages.html:
STEVE has two kinds of CAD document. A part is one piece of geometry defined by one file of code. A design is several components designed together and placed in one coordinate frame: an assembly. You choose the kind when you create the document (File → New part or New design, or New and then Part or Design), and it can't be changed after you save.

Part Design
Files One file of code (model = Model()) main.py, params.py and one file per component in components/
Geometry Its bodies Components and linked documents, each placed with design.add(...)
Motion None Joints, couplings, motors, poses and animations
Tabs in the Design workspace Solid, Sheet metal, Drawing Solid, Sheet metal, Motion, Drawing
Inspector Dimensions and physical properties Also Motion and Bill of materials

The files of a design

A design is a small codebase. A new design starts with two files:

# main.py: places the components
from steve import Design

design = Design()

result = design.result()

# params.py
# Shared parameters: every component imports what it needs from here.
  • main.py (shown as Placement in the model tree) places components and linked documents, and holds the joints and motion. It ends with result = design.result().
  • params.py (Shared parameters) holds numbers that several components use. When another design links this one, these are the parameters it can override.
  • components/<name>.py holds one component: its own sketches, features and bodies, written with the same modeling calls as a part. Each file defines exactly one Component; a second component in the same file, or one defined in main.py, is reported as a problem.

A typical main.py:

from steve import Design
from components.base import base
from components.lid import lid
from links import hinge_pin          # a saved part, linked at a pinned revision

design = Design("Box")
design.add(base)
design.add(lid, at=(0, 0, 40))
design.add(hinge_pin(length=60), at=((0, 50, 40), ("Y", 90)))
design.revolute("lid_hinge", "base", "lid", axis=base.face("hinge_bore.side(c1)"), limits=(0, 110))
result = design.result()

Components, links and instances

  • A component is geometry that belongs to this design, in its own file. Components are modeled in the design's coordinate frame, so one component can reference another's faces and edges (base.face("rim.end")) to fit against it. A component's id is lowercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter.
  • A link is another saved document used inside this design: a part, a design or a circuit board. A link is pinned to a revision: it keeps building from that revision until you update it, so changes to the source never move your assembly by surprise. A link to a part or design can override that document's parameters per use (hinge_pin(length=60)): a part's top-level number assignments, or a design's params.py. A circuit board link takes no overrides. The design keeps each link's document and pinned revision with its files (the Links group of the model tree lists them), and main.py imports it with from links import <name>. A linked part's faces and edges keep their own names (plate.face("extrude_1.end"); in a linked design, gearbox.face("housing:extrude_1.end")): joints and fasteners on them follow where the link is placed, and a component can sketch on one or project its edges by giving the same placement, plate.face("extrude_1.end", at=(50, 0, 0)).
  • An instance is one placement of a component or link. design.add(...) makes one; placing the same component again makes another instance of it, not a copy. Instances are named after their component (wheel, then wheel_2, wheel_3, ...) unless you pass name=. Joints, placements and the bill of materials refer to instances by these names.

An instance that no joint moves is grounded: it stays where main.py puts it. The Motion section of the Inspector lists the grounded instances.

How a design builds

Each component builds on its own, and STEVE reuses a component's result until its file or a file it imports changes, so editing one component rebuilds that component and main.py only. Joints never change geometry: the build places every instance as written (every joint at its value in the code, 0 unless you set value=), and the viewer moves the parts when you move a joint. STEP export keeps the structure, with one named node per instance.

A part (a single file with model = Model()) stays a part. Earlier documents of the retired assembly kind open as designs whose main.py links their parts.

Related

  • Add components and linked parts
  • Place components
  • Joints
  • Design parts for the modeling calls inside a component

pages.title: Exploded views
pages.description: Spread a design's parts apart on screen with Quick explode, or make a named, step-by-step explode that plays on the timeline.
pages.html:
Goal: see every part of a design separately, for example to check what sits inside an enclosure, or show how it comes apart, step by step, for assembly instructions, a teardown video or a presentation.

STEVE has two exploded views. Both are display only: neither changes the placements, the STEP export, the bill of materials or any check.

  • Quick explode spreads every part away from the centre with one slider, for a quick look. It isn't saved.
  • Explode steps makes a named explode, saved in main.py as design.explode(...): parts move in steps, in the order you choose, and it plays on the Motion timeline like an animation. You can scrub it, loop it, export it as a video or an animated GLB, and agents can look at any moment of it.

Prerequisites

  • A generated design. (Both tools are available for designs only.)

Quick explode

  1. On the Solid ribbon, in the Assemble group, click Quick explode.
  2. The components spread apart as the view zooms to fit them, and the Quick explode panel opens.
  3. Drag Explode distance to spread them more or less. Distance shows the amount as a percentage (0 % to 150 %; the tool opens at 55 %).
  4. Click Collapse to bring them back together while keeping the tool open, or Close (or Esc) to leave it.

What you should see: each instance moves away from the design's centre in proportion to how far out it sits, so stacked parts keep their order and separate evenly; a part at the centre stays put. A linked design's own parts spread less, around that instance's centre.

Export → Capture image saves the view as a PNG.

Make an explode with Explode steps

  1. On the Motion ribbon, in the Animate group, click Explode steps (also in the Solid ribbon's Assemble group). The Explode steps panel opens on the right with a new explode named explode_1; type another Name if you like (lowercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter).
  2. Click the parts that come off first (Shift-click for more, or pick them in the model tree), then click Add step. The step starts by lifting them along +Z, and arrows appear on them.
  3. Drag an arrow to move the step's parts along that axis: red is X, green Y, blue Z. Moves snap to 1 mm; hold Shift for 10 mm or Alt for 0.1 mm. Or type the move in the step's X, Y and Z fields (mm, in the design's frame).
  4. While a step is open, click a part in the viewport to add it to the step, or click it again to take it out (Alt-click picks a part inside a linked design). Add selected adds what you picked in the tree. Every part in a step moves together.
  5. Set the step's length in seconds and the hold after it (the second field; the defaults are 1 s and 0.25 s).
  6. Click Add step again for the next step. Click a step's header to open it; the parts show where that step leaves them. Use the arrow buttons (Earlier, Later) to reorder steps and the bin (Remove step) to delete one.
  7. Turn on Loop to play it over and over, and click the play button (Play the explode) to watch it before saving.
  8. Click OK.

What you should see: the explode is listed on the timeline and in the model tree's Explodes group, and main.py gains something like:

design.explode("explode_1", [
    {"move": ["lid", "knob"], "by": (0, 0, 40)},
    ("knob", (0, 0, 25)),
])

Moves add up: above, the knob rises 40 mm with the lid, then 25 mm more on its own.

To change an explode later, choose it on the timeline and click the pencil (Edit explode), double-click it in the tree, or right-click it there (Edit explode…). Delete in the panel removes it.

Automatic

Click Automatic in the panel to let STEVE work the steps out from the geometry. It writes design.explode("explode_1", auto=True) and builds, then shows the steps it found:

  • with assembly steps, the reverse of them: the last step's parts come off first, each step's screws before its other parts; the largest part of the first step stays;
  • without them, layer by layer: every placed screw first, then the parts that can lift straight off, then the ones under them, the largest part staying;
  • screws come out along their own axes; every other part moves along X, Y or Z, the way it is free to slide out past what is still assembled, pointing away from the rest;
  • each part goes past everything in its way, with a gap (5 % of the design's size, at least 2 mm), so the parts that come off first end furthest out and no two parts overlap at the end.

It is worked out again at each build, so it follows your changes. Clearance is judged on the parts' bounding boxes, which can space parts further apart than they need; the way a part is free to go is checked on its exact shape. Click Edit as steps to turn the result into steps you can change; OK then writes them out.

Play an explode

On the Motion ribbon, choose the explode in the timeline's list (it shows as explode with its length) and click the play button (Play explode). Each step shows as a bar on the track; click a bar to see where that step leaves the parts, or press on the track and drag to scrub.

  • The trails button (Trails shown / Trails hidden) draws a dashed line from where each part sits in the design to where the explode has it now.
  • The loop button switches between Looping and Plays once (it rewrites loop=True in main.py).
  • Play in the Animate group plays the explode shown on the timeline; the Inspector's Motion section lists explodes with play and edit buttons too.
  • Export → Animated GLB and Video export the explode shown on the timeline, like an animation (the video dialog's Motion lists explodes too). See Export motion.
  • Presentation view plays explodes on its player, full screen.

On a phone, the timeline plays explodes the same way; making and editing them is best done on a tablet or a computer.

In code

design.explode(name, steps=None, auto=False, duration=1.0, hold=0.25, easing="ease", loop=False, gap=None)

  • steps, in order. Each is one of:

    • {"move": instances, "by": (x, y, z)}: a move in mm, in the design's frame;
    • {"move": instances, "along": "+Z", "distance": 40}: along "+X", "-X", "+Y", "-Y", "+Z", "-Z" or a direction (dx, dy, dz);
    • {"move": screws, "out": True}: screws placed with design.fasten(..., instance=...) out along their own axis, by 1.5 times their length, or "out": 12 for 12 mm;
    • {"moves": {"lid": (0, 0, 30), "tray": (40, 0, 0)}}: parts going different ways in one step;
    • (instances, (x, y, z)): the short form of the first.

    instances is an instance name, a pattern such as "screw_*", a fastener's name (its placed screw), an instance inside a linked design by path ("gearbox/housing", or "gearbox/*"), or a list of them. A step can also give its own "duration", "hold" (seconds) and "name".

  • auto=True: the steps are worked out from the geometry instead (see Automatic); gap sets the space between parts in mm.

  • duration and hold: each step's move and pause, in seconds, unless the step says otherwise.

  • easing: "ease" (each move starts and stops gently) or "linear".

  • loop=True: plays over and over.

An explode plays from the code's pose (every joint at its value=) and only moves the instances it names: a joint's child doesn't follow its parent, so name both to move them together. Animations and explodes share the timeline, so their names must differ.

For agents

inspect_model draws a moment of an explode: explode="teardown" with t (seconds) or step (the moment that step has finished moving; 0 is at rest), with any view and show or hide. summary.posed.moved gives each moved instance's offset in mm. read_design lists the explodes in main.py, and its detail="kinematics" gives each step's moves.

Common problems

  • Quick explode or Explode steps is unavailable: the open document is a part, or the design has no geometry yet.
  • "… matches no instance of this design": a step names an instance that isn't placed; the message lists the instances.
  • "out moves placed screws along their axes": out is for screws placed as a fastener's instance=; move other parts with by or along.
  • Two parts overlap at the end of my own steps: only Automatic spaces parts apart; give one of them a longer move.

Related

  • Animations, the timeline's other kind of motion
  • Export motion
  • Fasteners, for assembly steps and placed screws
  • Place components, which changes where parts really are

between parts in mm. `duration` and `hold`: each step's move and pause, in seconds, unless the step says otherwise. `easing`: `"ease"` (each move starts and stops gently) or `"linear"`. `loop=True`: plays over and over. An explode plays from the code's pose (every joint at its `value=`) and only moves the instances it names: a joint's
child doesn't follow its parent, so name both to move them together. Animations and explodes share the timeline, so
their names must differ. For agents `inspect_model` draws a moment of an explode: `explode="teardown"` with `t` (seconds) or `step` (the moment that step
has finished moving; 0 is at rest), with any view and `show` or `hide`. `summary.posed.moved` gives each moved
instance's offset in mm. `read_design` lists the explodes in `main.py`, and its `detail="kinematics"` gives each step's
moves. Common problems *Quick explode or Explode steps is unavailable*: the open document is a part, or the design has no geometry yet. *"… matches no instance of this design"*: a step names an instance that isn't placed; the message lists the
instances. *"out moves placed screws along their axes"*: `out` is for screws placed as a fastener's `instance=`; move other
parts with `by` or `along`. *Two parts overlap at the end of my own steps*: only Automatic spaces parts apart; give one of them a longer move. Related [Animations](/docs/assemblies/animations/), the timeline's other kind of motion [Export motion](/docs/assemblies/export-motion/) [Fasteners](/docs/assemblies/fasteners/), for assembly steps and placed screws [Place components](/docs/assemblies/place-components/), which changes where parts really are

pages.title: Export motion
pages.description: Export a design's motion as an animated GLB, an MP4 video, or a MuJoCo simulation model.
pages.html:
Goal: take a mechanism's motion out of STEVE, for a slide deck, a web page, or a physics simulator.

Prerequisites

  • A generated design with a motor, an animation or an explode (for the GLB and the video), or at least one revolute, slider or cylindrical joint (for the simulation model). See Move a mechanism and Animations.

Export an animated GLB

  1. On the Motion ribbon, choose what to export: show an animation or an explode on the timeline, or, with neither shown, select the joint whose motor you want (otherwise the first motor is used).
  2. In the Export group, open Export and click Animated GLB.

What you get: <design>-<animation or joint>.glb, the design as glTF with one animation channel per moving part, sampled at 30 frames a second. glTF viewers, PowerPoint and web pages play it. It covers the shown animation or explode, or one cycle of a motor: a sweep there and back over its range (or its joint's limits), or one full turn for a motor nothing bounds.

Export a video

A video shows the motion exactly as the view does: the same camera, display style, materials and grid, with nothing selected or highlighted. It's made frame by frame in your browser, so no frame is dropped however heavy the design, and you can switch to another tab while it records.

  1. Frame the view the way you want the video to look. Presentation view shows the clean picture full screen.
  2. Open the options: on the Motion ribbon, in the Export group, open Export and click Video; or click Record video… (the red dot) on presentation view's player.
  3. Choose the options (they are remembered for next time):
    • Motion: which animation, explode or motor, when the design has several. It starts as the one on show.
    • Size: Viewport (the view's own size in pixels, up to 4K), 720p, 1080p, 1440p or 4K. With a size, Frame chooses Like the view (the view's shape, as big as fits that size) or 16:9 (everything the view shows, with more around it to fill the wider or taller picture).
    • Frame rate: 30 fps or 60 fps.
    • Quality: Standard, High or Maximum; the bitrate shows beside it.
    • Format: MP4 (H.264, plays everywhere) or WebM.
    • Speed: from ¼× to 4×.
    • Plays: how many times the motion plays in a row.
    • Hold at start and Hold at end: seconds the first and last pose stand still.
    • Turntable: degrees the camera turns about the middle of the view over the whole video (360 for a full turn, negative the other way); 0 keeps the camera still.
  4. Click Record. The dialog shows the frame being encoded, how far it is and how long is left; Cancel stops it. The view stays as it was meanwhile.

What you get: <design>-<animation or joint>.mp4 (or .webm) in your downloads, and a summary of its codec, size, length and file size. A motion that plays once ends on its last pose. A video can be up to 10 minutes long.

The view cube and axis triad are in the video when presentation view shows them (its Picture menu), so a video made outside presentation view leaves them out.

If the browser can't encode H.264 at the size you chose, the video is saved as WebM (VP9) instead, and the dialog says so. A browser that can't encode video frame by frame at all records the view live, as WebM, while the motion plays; keep its tab in front.

Export a simulation model (MuJoCo)

  1. Assign materials to the parts that move, so the model gets their masses (see Design parts). Parts without a material are listed in the report and left out of the mass.
  2. On the Motion ribbon, in the Export group, open Export and click Simulation model (MuJoCo).

What you get: <design>-mjcf.zip, made in your browser from the design's latest generated model:

  • The MJCF model, model.xml, with one body per link (instances joined by fixed joints move as one link). The grounded instances form the base, welded to the world. Revolute joints become hinges, sliders become slides, a cylindrical joint becomes a hinge and a <joint>_travel slide. Limits become ranges, couplings become joint equality constraints, and the code's pose and every named pose become keyframes. Lengths are in metres and angles in radians; joint position 0 is the design as modeled.
  • meshes/: one STL per body, in its link's frame.
  • inventory.json: the same links, joints, bodies (material, volume, mass, centre of mass, inertia), couplings and poses as plain data.
  • report.json: a check of the export against the design (forward kinematics at zero and with each joint moved a little, the exported mass against the bodies' sum, poses outside limits) and what wasn't exported.
  • manifest.json: the document, revision, branch and build it came from, and each file's SHA-256.

Each body collides as its mesh's convex hull unless you give it simplified shapes. A joint geared by two couplings is reported, not exported.

Physical properties in code

These calls in main.py change only the simulation export (and the build reports them):

Call What it does
design.fill(instances, fraction) Scales printed parts' mass and inertia by an infill fraction (0.4 for 40 %).
design.mass(instances, grams, center=None) Sets a datasheet mass for an envelope model; no material needed.
design.measured_mass(instances, grams) Scales a set of instances to a weighed total, keeping its centre of mass.
design.lumped_mass(name, on, grams, at=(0, 0, 0), box=None) Adds a mass that isn't modeled (a battery, ballast) to an instance's link.
design.site(name, at, x_dir=None) A named frame (sensor, tool tip) exported as a <site>.
design.collision_shape(instance, "box" | "sphere" | "capsule", ...) A simple collision shape used instead of the mesh hull.
design.collision_filter(instances, contype=1, conaffinity=1, ...) MuJoCo contact bit masks, group, condim and friction.
design.contact_pair(a, b) / design.contact_exclude(a, b) Force or forbid contacts between two instances' links.

instances takes names or patterns such as "servo_*".

Common problems

  • The export buttons are unavailable: "Add a motor or an animation first." (GLB and video), or "Add a revolute or slider joint first." (simulation model).
  • "Nothing moves in this motion": the motion's joints don't move any part.
  • The video would be too long: more than 10 minutes, counting the plays, holds and speed. Play it fewer times, shorten the holds or raise the speed.
  • "This GPU draws at most … pixels a side" or "This browser can't encode a … video": choose a smaller size.

Related

  • Animations
  • Presentation view
  • Collision and fit checks, where collision shapes are also scored

pages.title: Fasteners and standard parts
pages.description: Add bought-in parts to a design, and declare screw joints that every build measures and lists in the bill of materials.
pages.html:
Goal: put real hardware into a design (bearings, motors, screws) and have STEVE check that each screw actually fits the holes, threads and parts it goes through.

There are two separate things here:

  • Standard parts are geometry: STEP models of bought-in parts, added to the design as components.
  • Declared fasteners (design.fasten) are screw joints: a description of a screw, what it clamps and what it threads into. Every build measures them on the geometry as built and lists the hardware in the bill of materials.

Add a standard part

  1. Open the design.
  2. In the Parts group of the Solid ribbon, click Standard part (Standard parts…).
  3. Search the catalog, for example "608 bearing", "M3 socket head 10", "NEMA 17" or "GT2 pulley", or pick a category.
  4. Select a part and click Add to your design's name (or press Enter, or double-click the part).

The catalog is step.parts: about 17,000 open-source STEP models of bought-in parts. STEVE downloads the chosen file, checks it like an imported STEP file ("Checking the part…"), and adds it to the design as a component, with a comment above the import naming the catalog part, its page, its license and its checksum. Place it with the Place tool.

McMaster in the same group opens McMaster-Carr in its own window: download a part's 3-D STEP file there and drop it on STEVE.

Declare a fastener

Write the declaration in main.py, after the instances it names:

design.fasten("lid_screw_1", "ISO 4762 M3x8", axis=lid.face("screw_hole.wall(0)"),
              head_on=lid.face("lid_plate.end"), clamps=["lid"], into="base", thread="thread_forming")
design.fasten_pattern("corner", "ISO 7380 M4x10", axes=frame.face("corner_holes.wall"),
                      head_on=frame.face("frame.end"), clamps=["panel"], thread="nut")
Argument Meaning
screw Standard, size and length: ISO 4762 / DIN 912 (socket head), ISO 7380 (button), ISO 10642 / DIN 7991 (countersunk), ISO 4017 / DIN 933 (hex), ISO 7045 (pan); M2 to M12.
axis A hole wall or circular edge, or ((x, y, z), (dx, dy, dz)).
head_on The flat face the head (or washer) rests on; it sets the direction. A countersunk head sits flush with it.
clamps The instances the screw passes through, head side first.
into The instance it threads into (none for a nut).
thread "tapped" (default), "thread_forming" (a pilot hole in plastic), "insert" (heat-set; insert=(bore_mm, length_mm) overrides the standard one) or "nut" (on the far side).
washer=True An ISO 7089 washer under the head.
fit Clearance holes per ISO 273: "close", "normal" (default) or "loose".
through=True Lets the tip come out of the far side.
step, driver Add the driver-access and insertion checks (see below).
instance A placed screw part that is this fastener: it isn't clashed against itself and is counted once in the bill of materials.
rules Overrides for this fastener, as design.fastener_rules.

design.fasten_pattern(name, screw, axes, ...) declares the same fastener on every hole of a pattern, named <name>_1, <name>_2, .... A design checks at most 1000 fasteners.

What every build checks

Check Default rule
Clearance hole At least the ISO 273 clearance for the fit, less 0.1 mm; oversized holes are flagged for review
Concentric The hole's offset from the screw axis is less than the radial clearance
Head seat The head (or washer) bears on material; not proud of a counterbore; a countersink within 0.1 mm
Engagement Tapped 1.5 × d, thread-forming 2 × d, the full insert length, or through the nut
Tapped hole, pilot, insert bore Tap drill to d; pilot 0.8–0.9 × d; insert bore ± 0.1 mm and at least the insert's length deep
Bottoming The tip stops at least 0.5 mm short of a blind hole's floor
Breakthrough The tip stays inside the part it threads into, unless through=True
Wall At least 1.6 mm around the hole in parts marked as FDM-printed, otherwise 1.0 mm
Clashes The head, screw and nut share no volume with parts they aren't declared to pass through; two screws closer than 0.5 mm are flagged for review
Moving Its parts aren't moved by different joints
Driver access, insertion The driver's shaft is clear for its free length (L-key 20 mm, screwdriver and nut driver 45 mm), and the head's way in is clear

Each failing length also suggests a standard length that would pass. Change the rules for a whole design with design.fastener_rules(min_engagement_d=..., pilot_ratio=..., min_wall_mm=..., bottom_gap_mm=..., screw_gap_mm=..., head_proud_mm=..., hole_tolerance_mm=...).

Driver access and insertion are checked only when you declare the assembly order with design.assembly_steps([("frame", ["base", "frame"]), ("lid", ["lid", "lid_screw_*"])]), or when a fastener names a driver ("hex_2.5", "ph2", "socket_7", or a profile from design.tool(name, shaft_d, min_free_mm=20)).

All fastener checks share 25 seconds of each preview, and a share of a full build's own time limit when you build (the toolbar's build); fasteners past that are reported as unchecked. STEVE doesn't check preload, torque, joint strength or thread stripping beyond the engagement rule.

See the results

  • The bill of materials lists the screws by standard, size and length, and any washers, nuts and inserts.
  • The check results (pass, review or fail per fastener, with measured values and the holes each part needs) are read with inspect_model and checks=["fasteners"] ({"fastener": name or pattern} in options picks some). AI agents call it over MCP, and STEVE, the in-app assistant, can run it for you. See AI agents and the design tools reference.
  • STEVE never cuts holes for you behind the scenes: each fastener's report gives the hole(...) arguments, and you or STEVE write them into the part's own component file as ordinary features.

Common problems

  • A standard part fails to insert: the catalog file couldn't be read as solids, or the catalog can't be reached right now; the dialog shows the reason.
  • "There is already a fastener named ...": fastener names are unique in a design.

Related

  • Collision and fit checks: design.contact(..., "threaded") for screws in a fit check.
  • Bill of materials

pages.title: Gears and couplings
pages.description: Make joints move together in fixed ratios with gear meshes, rack and pinion, belts and custom couplings.
pages.html:
Goal: tie two or more joints together, so turning one turns (or slides) the others, as gears, a rack and pinion or a belt do.

All four tools write a coupling: one input value that moves several joints in fixed ratios.

design.couple("mesh", {"input_shaft": 1, "output_shaft": -0.5})  # 20 : 40 teeth, external

At coupling value x, each joint it gears moves by x × its ratio, on top of the joint's own value. Turning motions are in degrees and sliding motions in mm, so a rack's ratio is mm per degree. A cylindrical joint's two motions are named <joint>.turn and <joint>.travel.

Prerequisites

  • A design with at least two revolute, slider or cylindrical joints (one for Coupling). See Joints.

Gear two joints by their teeth

  1. On the Motion ribbon, in the Gears & links group, click Gears (Gear mesh).
  2. Check Driver. The tool fills both lists with the first turning joints it finds and waits for a click: click the part the driving joint moves in the viewport, or choose the joint from the list. If the list already shows the right joint, go on.
  3. Set Driven the same way.
  4. Under Set by, keep Teeth and type both tooth counts (driver first; defaults 20 and 40). Choose Mesh: External for spur gears side by side (they turn opposite ways) or Internal for a gear inside a ring gear (same way). Or choose Ratio and type how far the driven gear turns per degree of the driver (negative turns the other way).
  5. Check Name (default mesh_1; a rack starts as rack_1 and a belt as belt_1).
  6. Read the summary line, for example "output_shaft turns 0.5× input_shaft, the other way (2 : 1 reduction)".
  7. Click OK.

What you should see: a coupling appears under Joints in the model tree, and main.py gains a design.couple(...) line with a comment such as # 20 : 40 teeth, external.

The driven joint's ratio is driver teeth ÷ driven teeth, negative for an external mesh.

Rack and pinion

  1. In Gears & links, click Rack (Rack and pinion).
  2. Set Pinion (a turning joint) and Rack (a slider or cylindrical joint).
  3. Type the pinion's Pitch radius in mm (default 10). One turn moves the rack 2πr.
  4. Turn on Reverse if the rack moves the wrong way.
  5. Click OK.

The rack's ratio is πr ÷ 180 mm per degree of the pinion.

Belt or chain

  1. In Gears & links, click Belt (Belt or chain).
  2. Set Driver and Driven (both turning joints).
  3. Type the two pulley Diameters in mm (defaults 30 and 60).
  4. Turn on Crossed belt for a crossed belt, which turns the pulleys opposite ways.
  5. Click OK.

The pulleys turn the same way, the driven one by driver diameter ÷ driven diameter.

  1. In Gears & links, click Coupling (in the panel it's the Custom choice).
  2. For each joint, choose it in the list and type its ratio. Add joint adds a row; the bin button removes one.
  3. Type a Name and click OK (Save coupling).

Each joint may appear once, and ratios are nonzero numbers.

Switch on Joints only follow when the coupling's joints should never be set on their own, as with the two outputs of a mixer (two couplings that each gear both joints). It writes follow=True into each joint's line, for example design.revolute("wheel_l", "chassis", "left_wheel", axis="Y", follow=True). A follower:

  • moves only through its couplings. Its own value stays as written;
  • shows Follows couplings in the Inspector, with a read-only slider. Move its couplings' sliders instead;
  • moves its coupling when you drag it, if exactly one coupling gears it. With two or more, dragging it does nothing and a note says which couplings to move;
  • can't be set by a pose, animation key, motor, collision study or simulation pose. The build reports an error such as "joint 'wheel_l' follows forward and steer; set those instead". A follower that no coupling gears is an error too.

Build a gear train

When one of the two joints you pick is already geared by a coupling, the panel shows Add to coupling, switched on. The new joint then joins that coupling at the right ratio, so one input turns the whole train. Switch it off to make a separate coupling instead.

Edit or remove a coupling

Select the coupling in the tree. The Inspector shows its Position slider and its Gears (each joint with its ratio, Limits and the Range it can move through). Edit gears opens it as a custom coupling, Add motor drives it, and Show code goes to its line. Right-click it in the tree for Edit coupling…, Play drive and Show in source. To remove a coupling, delete its line in main.py; deleting a joint also removes it from the couplings that gear it.

How couplings behave

  • Bounds: design.couple(name, gears, limits=(min, max)) bounds the coupling. The limits of every joint it gears bound it too: a pinion geared to a rack with travel limits can only turn as far as the rack can slide.
  • Units: a coupling's value is degrees when every joint it gears turns. Otherwise it takes the unit of the joint it gears at ×1 (a rack and pinion's value is the pinion's angle, in degrees), mm when every joint it gears slides, and no unit of its own when it mixes both with no joint at ×1. Each joint moves by the value times its ratio.
  • Driving and posing: a motor, pose or animation can name a coupling like a joint (design.drive("mesh", speed=90), design.pose("open", mesh=45)).
  • Dragging back-drives: dragging a geared part on the canvas moves its coupling, so the whole train follows. This works for a joint geared by one coupling; a joint in two couplings moves on its own, unless it only follows them (see above).
  • Joint labels: a geared joint shows Driven by coupling in the Inspector.
  • Gear meshes are kinematic only: STEVE doesn't model tooth contact, backlash or forces.

Common problems

  • The Gears & links buttons are unavailable: "Add a revolute or slider joint first."
  • "... slides; the driving joint of a gear turns (revolute or cylindrical)." Choose a turning joint as driver.
  • "... doesn't slide; a rack is a slider (or cylindrical) joint." Choose a slider for Rack.
  • "... already gears both joints." Both joints are already in that coupling; edit it instead.

  • Joints
  • Move a mechanism

pages.title: Joints
pages.description: Connect two instances of a design with a revolute, slider, cylindrical or fixed joint, with an axis from geometry and optional limits.
pages.html:
Goal: let one instance move on another, the way a hinge, a drawer or a shaft in a bushing does.

A joint has a parent (the instance that stays) and a child (the instance that moves on it). Joints never change geometry: the build places every instance as modeled, and the viewer moves the child when you move the joint.

Type Moves Value unit Code
Revolute Turns about the axis, like a hinge or a wheel degrees, right-handed design.revolute(name, parent, child, axis, limits=None, value=0)
Slider Slides along the axis, like a drawer or a piston mm design.slider(name, parent, child, axis, limits=None, value=0)
Cylindrical Turns about and slides along the axis, like a shaft in a bushing degrees and mm design.cylindrical(name, parent, child, axis, limits=None, slide_limits=None, value=0, slide=0)
Fixed (rigid) Nothing: the child moves with the parent design.rigid(name, parent, child)

Prerequisites

  • A design with at least two placed instances, generated (press Update model or Ctrl+Enter if the preview is out of date).
  • For an axis taken from geometry: a pin, bore, flat face or edge on a component of the design. Faces of linked documents can't be used as axes yet; use a datum axis for those.

Add a joint

  1. Choose Motion in the tools menu (beside the Design workspace menu, at the top left).
  2. In the Joints group, click the joint type: Revolute joint, Slider joint, Cylindrical joint or Fixed joint. The panel calls a fixed joint Rigid. (On any tab of a design, J opens the same tool as a revolute joint; see Keyboard shortcuts.)
  3. Check Parent and Child. The tool fills them in for you: a component you selected beforehand becomes the child. To change one, choose it from the list, or click the crosshair button next to it and then click the instance in the viewport.
  4. Set the Axis (not needed for a fixed joint). The tool starts out waiting for it: click a face or edge in the viewport.
    • A cylindrical face (a pin or a bore) gives its axis.
    • A flat face gives its normal, through the face's centre.
    • A straight or circular edge gives its line or its centre axis.
    • Or choose X axis, Y axis or Z axis from the list. These datum axes pass through the design's origin.
  5. Optional: turn on Limits and type the minimum and maximum (degrees for turning, mm for sliding). A cylindrical joint also has Travel limits in mm. While a limit field of an existing joint has focus, the part shows at that limit.
  6. Optional: turn on Drive to add a motor with a Speed, and Check collisions to sweep it at every build. See Move a mechanism.
  7. Check Name (lowercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter; the default is hinge, slide, shaft or fixed).
  8. Click OK.

What you should see: the joint appears under Joints in the model tree, the design rebuilds, and main.py gains a line such as:

design.revolute("hinge", "base", "lid", axis=base.face("hinge_bore.side(c1)"), limits=(0, 110))

The panel's hint shows what it will write before you click OK.

Edit, rename or remove a joint

Click a joint in the tree to select it. The Inspector shows its type, Position slider, and Definition: Parent, Child, Axis (a direction), Through (a point on the axis, mm), Limits and Driven by. From there:

  • Edit joint reopens the joint tool with the joint's values.
  • Add motor (or Edit motor) opens the motor tool for it.
  • Show code goes to its line in main.py.

Right-click the joint in the tree for Edit joint…, Rename (F2, or double-click), Play drive when it has a motor, Show in source and Delete. Renaming or deleting a joint also updates the drives, poses and couplings that name it.

How joints behave

  • Values are absolute. 0 is the geometry as modeled. value= (and slide= for a cylindrical joint) sets the joint's position in the code's pose, which is where Rest pose returns to.
  • Axes ride on the parent. A face reference is resolved on the instance that owns it (the parent or child when it's their component), so the joint acts where that instance is placed. When the parent moves on its own joint, the child's axis moves with it.
  • One parent joint per instance. An instance can be the child of only one joint ("child is already moved by joint ..."), and joints may not form a closed loop yet (four-bar linkages aren't supported). Make extra connections fixed joints on other instances, or remove them.
  • Grounded instances are those no joint moves.
  • Limits are (min, max) with min < max. A joint whose value in the code is outside its limits is reported as an error of the build.
  • Faces of a component placed several times: wheel.face(...) is taken from the parent or child that is that component; otherwise from its first instance. Name instances explicitly ("wheel_2") for parent and child.

You can also give an axis as a literal line, axis=((x, y, z), (dx, dy, dz)), or as "X", "Y" or "Z".

Common problems

  • "Place two instances first": a joint needs two placed instances.
  • "Pick the axis: a pin or bore, a flat face (its normal), an edge, or a datum axis." The axis is still empty.
  • "Joint axes come from a component's geometry; linked documents can't be referenced yet." You clicked a linked part. Pick a face on a component, or use a datum axis.
  • "That geometry has no reference name yet. Regenerate the model, then pick it." Press Update model and try again.
  • The part turns about the wrong place with a datum axis: X axis, Y axis and Z axis pass through the design's origin, not through the part. Pick a pin, bore or edge on the part instead.

Related

  • Gears and couplings: make joints move together.
  • Move a mechanism: drag parts, sliders, motors and poses.
  • Collision and fit checks

pages.title: Move a mechanism
pages.description: Move a design's joints by dragging parts or with sliders, add motors, save named poses and return to rest.
pages.html:
Goal: see how a design moves, drive it with a motor, and save the positions you want to come back to.

Moving the mechanism in the viewer never changes the code: the code's pose stays as written until you save a pose or change a joint's value=.

Prerequisites

  • A design with at least one revolute, slider or cylindrical joint. See Joints.

Drag a part

  1. Choose Motion in the tools menu (beside the Design workspace menu, at the top left).
  2. Press on a moving part in the viewport and drag.

The part turns or slides only the way its joint allows, and stops at the joint's limits. A geared part moves its coupling, so the parts geared to it follow. Pressing on a grounded part orbits the view as usual, and a press without a drag selects the part and its joint. On a cylindrical joint, a drag turns the part; hold Alt while dragging to slide it.

Dragging works on the Motion ribbon with the select tool active. On the Solid ribbon the same press selects or orbits.

Move joints with sliders

  1. Open the Inspector (the right-hand panel) with nothing selected.
  2. In the Motion section, drag a joint's slider or type its value. Couplings have their own sliders above the joints.

A slider covers the joint's limits; without limits, a turning joint covers -180° to 180° and a sliding one about the size of the design either way. Clicking a joint's name selects it and shows its own Inspector page. The Motion section also lists the Grounded instances.

Add a motor

A motor (design.drive) plays a joint or coupling at a speed.

  1. On the Motion ribbon, in the Drive group, click Motor.
  2. Choose what it Drives: a joint or a coupling.
  3. Set Speed in degrees per second for turning (default 90) or mm per second for sliding (default 20), and the Direction: Forward is positive about the joint's axis, right-handed.
  4. Choose Motion: Continuous turns on and on (only a turning joint or coupling without limits can), Back & forth sweeps the Range and back. The range starts at the joint's limits, or at the range a coupling can move through.
  5. Optional: turn on Check collisions to sweep the motion with exact solids at every build. See Collision and fit checks.
  6. Click OK (Save motor).

What you should see: main.py gains a line such as design.drive("hinge", speed=45, range=(0, 110)), and the Motion section of the Inspector gets a Play button. To change or remove a motor, open Motor on the same joint (or Edit motor in its Inspector page): the panel shows Edit joint and a Remove button.

In code, a motor without speed= plays at 90°/s for a turning joint, or crosses half its range per second for a slider. A slider needs limits or range= to be driven.

Play and stop

  • Play in the Animate group of the Motion ribbon plays the animation shown on the timeline, or else the first motor. Click it again to pause.
  • In the Inspector's Motion section, Play plays the first motor (the button names it when there are several), and the play button on a joint's row plays that joint's motor. ¼×, ½×, 1× and 2× set the playing speed.
  • While a motor plays, a small player over the viewport shows the joint, its live value and any parts in collision, with buttons to pause and to stop and return to rest.

Save a pose

A pose is a named set of joint and coupling values, such as "open" and "closed". Animations move between poses.

  1. Move the mechanism where you want it (drag parts or use the sliders).
  2. On the Motion ribbon, in the Drive group, click Pose (Save pose), or click Save pose among the pose buttons in the Inspector.
  3. Type a Name (letters, digits, spaces, hyphens and underscores; the default is pose_1).
  4. Each joint and coupling is listed with its current value. Switch off the ones the pose shouldn't set, or adjust a value.
  5. Click OK (Save pose).

What you should see: main.py gains design.pose("open", hinge=80), and a button for the pose appears in the Inspector's Motion section.

Move to a pose, or back to rest

  • Click a pose's button in the Inspector to move there. Right-click it for Move to pose, Update or rename…, Show code and Delete pose.
  • Rest in the Animate group (Rest pose in the Inspector) puts every joint back where the code has it: each joint's value=, 0 unless set.

A pose that an animation uses can't be deleted ("pose is in use"); edit or delete the animation first.

Switch between modes

A mode is a named set of tighter limits, for a mechanism with selectable stops or travel ranges (a full and a limited range, a parking lock). Declare it in main.py; the joints' own limits stay the default:

design.mode("limited", limits={"hinge": (0, 60)})   # joints or couplings; travel_limits= for a cylindrical joint's slide
design.drive("hinge", speed=30, mode="limited")     # motors, poses, animations, collision studies and fit checks take mode=

In the Inspector's Motion section, Mode (above the joints) switches between Default and each mode. The sliders cover that mode's limits and the mechanism moves within them at once, without a rebuild. Playing a motor, moving to a pose or playing an animation switches to its own mode, and a pose saved with Pose is saved in the selected mode. Shares that let visitors move the mechanism offer the same selector.

Common problems

  • Motor, Pose and the Gears & links tools are unavailable: "Add a revolute or slider joint first."
  • Play is unavailable: "Add a motor or an animation first."
  • Dragging orbits instead of moving the part: the part is grounded (no joint moves it), or you are on the Solid ribbon.
  • "Drive: slider ... needs limits or a range to sweep": give the slider limits= or the motor a range.

Related

  • Animations
  • Gears and couplings
  • Export motion

drag selects the part and its joint. On a cylindrical joint, a drag turns the part; hold Alt while dragging to slide it. Dragging works on the **Motion** ribbon with the select tool active. On the **Solid** ribbon the same press selects or
orbits. Move joints with sliders ![The Motion section of the Inspector: Play, Rest pose, speeds, saved poses, a collision check result, an animation and the coupling and joint sliders.](../../../assets/assemblies/motion-inspector.png) Open the **Inspector** (the right-hand panel) with nothing selected. In the **Motion** section, drag a joint's slider or type its value. Couplings have their own sliders above the
joints. A slider covers the joint's limits; without limits, a turning joint covers -180° to 180° and a sliding one about the
size of the design either way. Clicking a joint's name selects it and shows its own Inspector page. The **Motion**
section also lists the *Grounded* instances. Add a motor A motor (`design.drive`) plays a joint or coupling at a speed. On the **Motion** ribbon, in the **Drive** group, click **Motor**. Choose what it **Drives**: a joint or a coupling. Set **Speed** in degrees per second for turning (default 90) or mm per second for sliding (default 20), and the
**Direction**: **Forward** is positive about the joint's axis, right-handed. Choose **Motion**: **Continuous** turns on and on (only a turning joint or coupling without limits can), **Back & forth**
sweeps the **Range** and back. The range starts at the joint's limits, or at the range a coupling can move
through. Optional: turn on **Check collisions** to sweep the motion with exact solids at every build. See
[Collision and fit checks](/docs/assemblies/collision-checks/). Click **OK** (**Save motor**). ![The Motor panel driving a coupling back and forth, with Check collisions on.](../../../assets/assemblies/motor-panel.png) What you should see: `main.py` gains a line such as `design.drive("hinge", speed=45, range=(0, 110))`, and the
**Motion** section of the Inspector gets a **Play** button. To change or remove a motor, open **Motor** on the same
joint (or **Edit motor** in its Inspector page): the panel shows **Edit** *joint* and a **Remove** button. In code, a motor without `speed=` plays at 90°/s for a turning joint, or crosses half its range per second for a
slider. A slider needs limits or `range=` to be driven. Play and stop **Play** in the **Animate** group of the **Motion** ribbon plays the animation shown on the timeline, or else the first
motor. Click it again to pause. In the Inspector's **Motion** section, **Play** plays the first motor (the button names it when there are several),
and the play button on a joint's row plays that joint's motor. **¼×**, **½×**, **1×** and **2×** set the playing
speed. While a motor plays, a small player over the viewport shows the joint, its live value and any parts in collision,
with buttons to pause and to stop and return to rest. Save a pose A pose is a named set of joint and coupling values, such as "open" and "closed". Animations move between poses. Move the mechanism where you want it (drag parts or use the sliders). On the **Motion** ribbon, in the **Drive** group, click **Pose** (**Save pose**), or click **Save pose** among the
pose buttons in the Inspector. Type a **Name** (letters, digits, spaces, hyphens and underscores; the default is `pose_1`). Each joint and coupling is listed with its current value. Switch off the ones the pose shouldn't set, or adjust a
value. Click **OK** (**Save pose**). What you should see: `main.py` gains `design.pose("open", hinge=80)`, and a button for the pose appears in the
Inspector's **Motion** section. Move to a pose, or back to rest Click a pose's button in the Inspector to move there. Right-click it for **Move to** *pose*, **Update or rename…**,
**Show code** and **Delete pose**. **Rest** in the **Animate** group (**Rest pose** in the Inspector) puts every joint back where the code has it: each
joint's `value=`, 0 unless set. A pose that an animation uses can't be deleted ("*pose* is in use"); edit or delete the animation first. Switch between modes A mode is a named set of tighter limits, for a mechanism with selectable stops or travel ranges (a full and a limited
range, a parking lock). Declare it in `main.py`; the joints' own limits stay the default: design.mode("limited", limits={"hinge": (0, 60)})   # joints or couplings; travel_limits= for a cylindrical joint's slide
design.drive("hinge", speed=30, mode="limited")     # motors, poses, animations, collision studies and fit checks take mode=
 In the Inspector's **Motion** section, **Mode** (above the joints) switches between **Default** and each mode. The
sliders cover that mode's limits and the mechanism moves within them at once, without a rebuild. Playing a motor,
moving to a pose or playing an animation switches to its own mode, and a pose saved with **Pose** is saved in the
selected mode. Shares that let visitors move the mechanism offer the same selector. Common problems *Motor, Pose and the Gears & links tools are unavailable*: "Add a revolute or slider joint first." *Play is unavailable*: "Add a motor or an animation first." *Dragging orbits instead of moving the part*: the part is grounded (no joint moves it), or you are on the
**Solid** ribbon. "Drive: slider ... needs limits or a range to sweep": give the slider `limits=` or the motor a range. Related [Animations](/docs/assemblies/animations/) [Gears and couplings](/docs/assemblies/gears-and-couplings/) [Export motion](/docs/assemblies/export-motion/)

pages.title: Place components
pages.description: Move and turn a component or linked part in a design with the Place tool, which writes at= into main.py.
pages.html:
Goal: put an instance where it belongs in the design, by dragging or by typing its position and rotation.

Prerequisites

  • A design that has been generated, with at least one instance placed by a plain design.add(...) call in main.py.

Place an instance

  1. On the Solid ribbon, click the instance in the viewport to select it.
  2. In the Design group of the ribbon, click Place.
  3. The Place instance panel opens, and a handle with arrows, squares and rings appears at the instance's centre. Either:
    • drag an arrow to move along one axis, a square to move in a plane, or a ring to turn; or
    • type X, Y and Z (mm), choose an axis under Turn about (X, Y or Z) and type the Angle (degrees).
  4. Click OK (or press Enter).

What you should see: the instance stays where you put it, a message says "Placed instance", and its design.add call in main.py carries the placement, for example:

design.add(lid, at=(0, 0, 40))                           # moved only
design.add(lid, at=((0, 0, 40), ("X", -90)))             # moved, then turned -90° about X

Cancel (or Esc) puts the instance back where it was. Linking a part opens this tool on the new instance automatically.

How placement works

  • at=(x, y, z) moves the instance by that many millimetres from where its geometry is modeled.
  • at=((x, y, z), (axis, degrees)) first turns it about axis through the origin of the design, then moves it by (x, y, z). axis is "X", "Y", "Z" or a direction such as (0, 1, 1); degrees are right-handed. When a drag turns an instance about a direction that isn't one of the main axes, Turn about shows Custom and the code gets the direction.
  • While you drag, positions snap to a step a few pixels long at the current zoom (1, 2 or 5 × a power of ten mm), and angles snap to whole degrees. Type a value for anything finer.
  • The Place tool edits only the design.add(...) call that made the instance. The handle sits at the centre of the instance's bounding box, but the numbers are the placement written in at=.
  • Placement doesn't change the component's geometry or its joints. A joint's axis rides on its parent instance, so placing a parent moves the joint too.

Common problems

  • Place is unavailable: select a component or linked part first, and make sure the open document is a design.
  • "name is one of the pattern base: place the whole pattern with its at= in main.py." Instances made by design.pattern(...) move together: edit the pattern's at= in main.py.
  • "Couldn't find the design.add(…) that places name in main.py." The instance is placed by code the tool can't edit (inside a loop, or built by a helper). Edit its placement in main.py.

Related

  • Add components and linked parts
  • Joints, which move instances without changing their placement
  • Exploded views, which spread instances apart on screen only

pages.title: Drawings
pages.description: Engineering drawings of parts and designs, made in the Drawing ribbon and written as Drawing(...) code.
pages.html:
An engineering drawing in STEVE is one or more sheets of a part or a design: ISO or ANSI (ASME) sheets with orthographic and isometric views, section and detail views, dimensions with tolerances and fits, GD&T, notes, item balloons, a parts list, hole tables, a revision table and a title block. You print them to PDF or download them as SVG and DXF.

Each sheet is a Drawing(...) call in the code: in a part's code, or in a design's main.py. The Drawing ribbon's tools write the same call you could type, and STEVE edits it the same way, so the drawing is saved with the design's history, branches and versions, and a sheet made by hand, by STEVE or by an AI agent is the same sheet.

What STEVE places itself (dimension values, tolerance frames, datums, balloons, notes, weld symbols and hole tags) keeps clear of other text, the views' lines, section cutting planes, the title block and the tables: a value moves along its dimension line, a frame or balloon goes further out, and frames on one feature stack on one leader. What you place yourself, at a position or an offset you give, stays there.

An AI agent sees each sheet as a picture, the same sheet you see, with a list of what's hard to read on it: text over other text, over the title block or a table, or crossed by a view's lines. It can look closer at part of a crowded sheet, so it can fix the layout before it tells you the drawing is done.

The Drawing ribbon

In the Design workspace, Drawing in the tools menu (with Solid, Sheet metal and Motion) shows the sheets in the centre. It works like the drawing workspace of a desktop CAD program:

  • The ribbon holds the tools, one a button, in five groups: Sheet, Views, Annotate, Tables and Export.
  • The tools are used on the sheet: you click the edges, circles and corners of a view, and where the result goes. The open tool's options, with OK and Cancel, are in the right-hand panel.
  • The left-hand panel lists the drawing as a tree: each sheet, its views, what's on each view, its tables, notes and title block.
  • What you select, on the sheet or in the tree, shows its properties in the Inspector.
  • Right-click anything on the sheet or in the tree for what you can do with it.

The Drawing ribbon is for tablets and desktops. On a phone, open the sheets from Export.

Pages

  • Sheets: add a sheet, set its format and title block, use templates, and manage several sheets.
  • Views: base, projected, section and detail views; moving and lining them up.
  • Dimensions: dimension the model's geometry on a view, with tolerances and ISO 286 fits.
  • GD&T: datum feature symbols and feature control frames.
  • Notes and balloons: notes placed on the sheet or listed, and a design's item balloons.
  • Tables: the parts list, hole tables, the revision table and the cut list.
  • Select and edit: the drawing tree, the Inspector, dragging, right-click menus and keys.
  • Print and export: PDF, SVG and DXF.

You can also ask STEVE to make or change a drawing ("an A3 drawing with a section through the bore"); it writes the same Drawing(...) code.

pages.title: Sheets
pages.description: Add a drawing sheet, set its standard, size, scale and title block (or your company's own), reuse templates, and manage several sheets.
pages.html:
Goal: start a drawing of a part or design and set up its sheet.

Prerequisites

  • An open part or design that builds without errors.

Add a sheet

  1. Click the Drawing ribbon.
  2. Click New sheet (in the middle of the tab on a model with no drawing yet, or in the Sheet group of the ribbon). The New sheet tool opens in the right-hand panel.
  3. Choose the standard, Size, Orientation and the rest of the sheet format, or a saved template under Templates (Use for the new sheet). You can save the setup as a new template there too.
  4. In a design, choose what to Draw: the whole design, or one of its components on its own.
  5. Leave Start with the standard views off for a blank sheet, or turn it on for front, top, right and isometric views.
  6. Click OK. Cancel (Esc) writes nothing.

What you should see: a sheet with its border and title block, titled with the document's (or component's) name, and no views yet: click Base view to place the first one. In the code, a new line Drawing(result, standard="ISO", title=..., views=[]) (no views with the standard views). A new sheet takes the standard of the last sheet (ISO for the first).

Set the sheet format

  1. Click Format in the Sheet group. The Sheet format tool opens in the right-hand panel.
  2. Choose the standard: ISO or ANSI / ASME. Switching keeps the matching size (A3 becomes B, and back).
  3. Set Size (ISO A4 to A0, ANSI A to E), Orientation (Landscape or Portrait), Projection (the standard's own: first angle for ISO, third angle for ASME; or either one), Scale (Largest that fits, or an ISO 5455 scale from 50:1 to 1:1000) and Units (millimetres or inches; the standard's own by default).
  4. Turn Hidden lines dashed, Shaded views and Overall dimensions on or off for every view. Shaded views fill the faces in greys under their lines; section views stay hatched, and the DXF keeps the lines only.
  5. Click OK (or press Enter). Cancel (Esc) leaves the sheet as it was.

Nothing is written until OK: then the sheet is redrawn. The same settings are in the Inspector when you select the sheet in the drawing tree, where each change is written at once.

Fill in the title block

  1. Click Title block in the Sheet group.
  2. Type the Title and the fields: Drawing no., Owner, Drawn, Checked, Approved, Date, Material, Finish, General tolerances and Revision (left empty, the revision table's last row is shown).
  3. To add another field (a customer, a project), type its name in the New field box and click Add field.
  4. Click OK.

Text is one line, up to 200 characters.

Use your company's title block

A sheet can have its own title block in place of the standard one: your company's rows and cells, with your labels, sizes and fixed text (the company name, for example).

  1. Ask STEVE for it: describe your title block, or drop a picture of it in the chat, and ask STEVE to use it on the sheet. STEVE writes it into the sheet's code as title_block=[...].
  2. Click Title block in the Sheet group. It now lists the fields your layout shows, beside the Title. Fill them in and click OK.
  3. Save the sheet as a template (below) to start every new sheet with your title block.

In the code, title_block is a list of rows, bottom row first. Each row has a height and cells, and each cell a width (both in mm), and optionally a label, a field (a field's name like number or customer, or title, revision, scale, sheet, size, units or projection, which the sheet fills in), fixed text (one line, or a list of up to 12 lines), and a text_height. Up to 12 rows of 12 cells, each row 2.5 mm or taller. Lines aren't wrapped: give a long statement's cell a tall enough row (or rows span) for its lines. The parts list, revisions and other tables above the title block take its width.

A cell can also have:

  • rows: how many rows it spans upward, drawn as one box with no row lines through it. The rows above place their cells to the right of it.
  • align (left, centre or right) and valign (top, middle or bottom) for its value or text, and label_align and label_valign for its label.
  • bold: True draws its value or text in bold, like a "PROPRIETARY AND CONFIDENTIAL" header or a revision letter; label_bold: True does the same for its label. Bold shows in the SVG, the PDF and the DXF (as an Arial Bold text style).
  • label_height: the label's text height in mm. A field cell shows the field's own label (DRAWING NO., REV…) unless you give one; "label": "" shows none, which suits low rows.
  • image: your company logo in place of a value, like "image": "logo.png". Add the logo first: open the Source panel's file switcher, click Import logo… and pick a PNG or JPEG (at most 512 KB and 4096 pixels a side; SVG isn't taken). It's scaled to fit the cell with its proportions kept, placed by align and valign (centred by default), with padding (mm, default 1) around it. Up to 4 cells a title block can hold a logo. It's embedded in the sheet (SVG and printed PDF), and drawings.zip holds the image file beside the DXFs, which reference it.
{"height": 14, "cells": [{"width": 50.8, "image": "logo.png"}, {"width": 130, "field": "title"}]}

Drawing(result, fields={"number": "BRK-001", "customer": "Globex"}, title_block=[
    {"height": 14, "cells": [{"width": 130, "label": "PART NAME", "field": "title"},
                             {"width": 50, "field": "number", "align": "centre"}]},
    {"height": 9, "cells": [{"width": 80, "text": "ACME ENGINEERING LTD"}, {"width": 50, "label": "CUSTOMER", "field": "customer"},
                            {"width": 25, "field": "scale"}, {"width": 25, "field": "revision"}]},
    {"height": 3.2, "cells": [{"width": 60, "rows": 2, "text": ["PROPRIETARY: do not copy", "without written consent"],
                               "align": "centre", "valign": "middle"},
                              {"width": 120, "field": "material", "label": "", "text_height": 2}]},
    {"height": 3.2, "cells": [{"width": 120, "field": "finish", "label": ""}]},
])

Reuse a sheet setup as a template

A template keeps a sheet's standard, size, orientation, projection, units, title block fields and layout, and notes, for every drawing in your account (up to 20 templates).

  1. Open Format, or select the sheet in the drawing tree.
  2. Under Templates, type a name in the Template name box and click Save as template.
  3. To use it: New sheet from template opens New sheet set up that way; Apply to this sheet puts it on the shown sheet (its views, scale, title, revisions and dimensions stay).

A template is copied into the code when you use it, so changing or deleting it later doesn't change sheets already made.

Several sheets

Each Drawing(...) call is one sheet, numbered in the order the code declares them; the title block's SHEET cell shows 1/2, 2/2 on its own. With more than one sheet, the sheets are listed above the paper: click one to show it. In the drawing tree, right-click a sheet for Rename, Duplicate, Move up, Move down and Delete sheet (which asks first). See Select and edit.

To reorder sheets, drag a sheet's tab above the paper to its new place, or right-click the tab for Move left and Move right. The sheet's Drawing(...) statement moves in the code, with the comment lines directly above it and the statements that only build it (a dims = [...] list no other code reads), as one edit. The sheets, the drawing tree, the PDF and STEVE all follow the new order. A move that could change what the code does is refused, and the menu says why: sheets made in a loop, a function or an if block, other code between the sheets, or a sheet that uses a name another one defines (sheet_a = Drawing(...) read by a later sheet). Reorder those in the code.

Common problems

  • "The views are larger than the sheet" in the bar above the sheet: the chosen scale doesn't fit. Choose a smaller scale, Largest that fits, or a larger size.
  • The Drawing ribbon shows nothing to edit: the sheets are declared in another file of a design. Edit them there, or ask STEVE.
  • A setting shown as written in the code (a variable or an expression) isn't changed by the tools: change it in the code, or ask STEVE.

Related

  • Views
  • Print and export
