sheet. STEVE writes it into the sheet's code as `title_block=[...]`. Click **Title block** in the **Sheet** group. It now lists the fields your layout shows, beside the **Title**. Fill
them in and click **OK**. Save the sheet as a template (below) to start every new sheet with your title block. In the code, `title_block` is a list of rows, bottom row first. Each row has a `height` and `cells`, and each cell a
`width` (both in mm), and optionally a `label`, a `field` (a field's name like `number` or `customer`, or `title`,
`revision`, `scale`, `sheet`, `size`, `units` or `projection`, which the sheet fills in), fixed `text` (one line, or
a list of up to 12 lines), and a `text_height`. Up to 12 rows of 12 cells, each row 2.5 mm or taller. Lines aren't
wrapped: give a long statement's cell a tall enough row (or `rows` span) for its lines. The parts list,
revisions and other tables above the title block take its width. A cell can also have: `rows`: how many rows it spans upward, drawn as one box with no row lines through it. The rows above place their
cells to the right of it. `align` (`left`, `centre` or `right`) and `valign` (`top`, `middle` or `bottom`) for its value or text, and
`label_align` and `label_valign` for its label. `bold`: `True` draws its value or text in bold, like a "PROPRIETARY AND CONFIDENTIAL" header or a revision letter;
`label_bold`: `True` does the same for its label. Bold shows in the SVG, the PDF and the DXF (as an Arial Bold text
style). `label_height`: the label's text height in mm. A field cell shows the field's own label (DRAWING NO., REV…) unless
you give one; `"label": ""` shows none, which suits low rows. `image`: your company logo in place of a value, like `"image": "logo.png"`. Add the logo first: open the Source
panel's file switcher, click **Import logo…** and pick a PNG or JPEG (at most 512 KB and 4096 pixels a side; SVG
isn't taken). It's scaled to fit the cell with its proportions kept, placed by `align` and `valign` (centred by
default), with `padding` (mm, default 1) around it. Up to 4 cells a title block can hold a logo. It's embedded in
the sheet (SVG and printed PDF), and drawings.zip holds the image file beside the DXFs, which reference it. {"height": 14, "cells": [{"width": 50.8, "image": "logo.png"}, {"width": 130, "field": "title"}]}
 Drawing(result, fields={"number": "BRK-001", "customer": "Globex"}, title_block=[
    {"height": 14, "cells": [{"width": 130, "label": "PART NAME", "field": "title"},
                             {"width": 50, "field": "number", "align": "centre"}]},
    {"height": 9, "cells": [{"width": 80, "text": "ACME ENGINEERING LTD"}, {"width": 50, "label": "CUSTOMER", "field": "customer"},
                            {"width": 25, "field": "scale"}, {"width": 25, "field": "revision"}]},
    {"height": 3.2, "cells": [{"width": 60, "rows": 2, "text": ["PROPRIETARY: do not copy", "without written consent"],
                               "align": "centre", "valign": "middle"},
                              {"width": 120, "field": "material", "label": "", "text_height": 2}]},
    {"height": 3.2, "cells": [{"width": 120, "field": "finish", "label": ""}]},
])
 Reuse a sheet setup as a template A template keeps a sheet's standard, size, orientation, projection, units, title block fields and layout, and notes,
for every drawing in your account (up to 20 templates). Open **Format**, or select the sheet in the drawing tree. Under **Templates**, type a name in the **Template name** box and click **Save as template**. To use it: **New sheet from template** opens **New sheet** set up that way; **Apply to this sheet** puts it on the shown
sheet (its views, scale, title, revisions and dimensions stay). A template is copied into the code when you use it, so changing or deleting it later doesn't change sheets already
made. Several sheets Each `Drawing(...)` call is one sheet, numbered in the order the code declares them; the title block's `SHEET` cell
shows `1/2`, `2/2` on its own. With more than one sheet, the sheets are listed above the paper: click one to show
it. In the drawing tree, right-click a sheet for **Rename**, **Duplicate**, **Move up**, **Move down** and
**Delete sheet** (which asks first). See [Select and edit](/docs/drawing/select-and-edit/). To reorder sheets, drag a sheet's tab above the paper to its new place, or right-click the tab for **Move left** and
**Move right**. The sheet's `Drawing(...)` statement moves in the code, with the comment lines directly above it and
the statements that only build it (a `dims = [...]` list no other code reads), as one edit. The sheets, the drawing
tree, the PDF and STEVE all follow the new order. A move that could change what the code does is refused, and the menu
says why: sheets made in a loop, a function or an `if` block, other code between the sheets, or a sheet that uses a
name another one defines (`sheet_a = Drawing(...)` read by a later sheet). Reorder those in the code. Common problems *"The views are larger than the sheet"* in the bar above the sheet: the chosen scale doesn't fit. Choose a smaller
scale, **Largest that fits**, or a larger size. *The Drawing ribbon shows nothing to edit*: the sheets are declared in another file of a design. Edit them there, or
ask STEVE. A setting shown as written in the code (a variable or an expression) isn't changed by the tools: change it in the
code, or ask STEVE. Related [Views](/docs/drawing/views/) [Print and export](/docs/drawing/export/)

pages.title: Views
pages.description: Add base, projected, section and detail views to a drawing sheet, move them and line them up.
pages.html:
Goal: show the model the way the drawing needs it.

Views are placed by the projection method: first angle on ISO sheets (the top view under the front view), third angle on ASME sheets (the top view above it). Section and detail views go beside the view they're taken from, and move and scale with it.

Prerequisites

  • A sheet: see Sheets.

Base view

  1. Click Base in the Views group.
  2. In the right-hand panel, choose the orientation: Front, Top, Right, Left, Bottom, Back or Isometric (only those not on the sheet yet are offered).
  3. Click where the view goes on the sheet.

What you should see: the view appears, then moves to where you clicked once the sheet is redrawn.

Flat pattern view

On a sheet of a sheet-metal part, Base also offers Flat pattern: the developed blank, the same one its flat pattern DXF cuts. It shows the blank's outline and holes, each bend as a thin chain line with its note (for example UP 90° R2), and the blank's overall size, labelled FLAT PATTERN. It follows the part as its flanges, cuts and bends change, so there's no blank to redraw by hand.

When the sheet draws more than one sheet-metal body (a design with several brackets), choose the Body in the right-hand panel; change it later in the view's properties. A sheet has one flat pattern view: draw other bodies' blanks on sheets of their own.

The flat pattern takes Dimension like the other views: pick the blank's edges, holes, and the bend lines themselves, so each bend's position from an edge of the blank (or from the bend before it) is a real dimension that follows the model. A bend line is the bend's centre line, the one the DXF draws and the one you mark and gauge to when bending by hand. GD&T on the blank's geometry, hole tables, welds, balloons, sections and details go on the folded views.

Projected view

  1. Click Projected in the Views group (or right-click a view and choose Projected view from here).
  2. Click the view to project from.
  3. Move the pointer to the side the new view goes. The label at the pointer names the view the projection method puts there (for example Top view), or says it's on the sheet already.
  4. Click.

A projected view stays lined up with the view it was projected from: it only moves along the way it was projected.

Section view

  1. Click Section in the Views group (or right-click a view and choose Section view).
  2. Draw the cutting line across a view: press and drag, or click its start and its end. The line snaps across or up, and through the nearest hole's axis or corner within a few millimetres of paper.
  3. Move the pointer to the side the section should look from, and click: the section goes on that side.

What you should see: SECTION A-A under the new view, the cut faces hatched, and the cutting line with arrows and letters on the parent view. Section letters go A, B, C… (ASME skips I, O and Q); change the letter in the right-hand panel before you finish.

Cutting lines are horizontal or vertical on their view.

Detail view

  1. Click Detail in the Views group (or right-click a view and choose Detail view).
  2. Click the centre of what the detail shows: it snaps to a hole's axis or a corner.
  3. Move out to size the circle, and click.
  4. Click where the detail goes.

What you should see: DETAIL B (2:1) (twice the parent's scale by default) and the circle with its letter on the parent view.

Where a section cuts and where a detail is centred are written as the model's persistent names when you snapped to a hole or corner, so they follow the model as it changes; elsewhere, as a model point.

Move and line up views

  • Drag a view to move it. Views projected from another move only along the way they're projected; hold Alt to move one freely. Dragging the front view takes the views lined up with it along.
  • A moved view's right-click menu has Align with its parent (or Back to its place), which puts it back where the projection method puts it.
  • A section's right-click menu has Flip direction: it looks the other way and goes on the other side.

Edit a view

Double-click a view (or right-click it and choose Edit view). In the Inspector: its Scale (the sheet's, or its own), Hidden lines (as the sheet, dashed, or none; the iso view has none unless you choose dashed), Shading (as the sheet, shaded, or lines only), and how far it's Moved right and Moved up (paper mm). A section also has its Cutting line (across or up) and which way it's Looking; a detail its Radius (model mm).

Delete a view

Select it and press Delete, or right-click it and choose Delete. Section and detail views taken from it, and the dimensions and other annotations on them, go too: you are asked first. Deleting the last view leaves a blank sheet, ready for a new Base view.

Common problems

  • Section or Detail is unavailable on a design's sheet: cut and detail each part on its own sheet (add a sheet that draws the component).
  • A section or detail view isn't drawn (marked in the drawing tree): the geometry it cut through is gone from the model, or the cutting plane misses the part. Delete it and make it again.
  • The flat pattern view isn't drawn (marked in the drawing tree): its body isn't sheet metal any more, or a sheet-metal feature failed so the blank can't be developed; the message says which. Fix the part, or pick another Body.

Related

  • Dimensions
  • Select and edit

pages.title: Dimensions
pages.description: Dimension the model's holes, edges and corners on a drawing view, with tolerances and ISO 286 fits.
pages.html:
Goal: add dimensions whose values come from the model, so they follow it as it changes.

Every sheet also shows each orthographic view's overall dimensions (turn them off in Format). The Dimension tool adds feature dimensions: a hole's diameter, an edge's length, the distance or angle between two.

Prerequisites

  • A part's sheet (or a sheet of one component of a design) with a front, top or side view.
  • A model built with STEVE's modelling tools (or steve.Model in code): its faces, edges and corners have persistent names. Plain CadQuery geometry has none, and the tool says so.

Add a dimension

  1. Click Dimension in the Annotate group.

  2. Point at the view: what the tool can pick lights up. Click:

    • a circle, for its diameter;
    • an edge, for its length;
    • or two edges, two corners, or a corner and an edge, for the distance between them. Two edges that aren't parallel give the angle between them.

    The dimension and its value show on the sheet as soon as you pick, and the right-hand panel names its kind and value. Pick a second edge and it changes to the distance (or angle) between the two. Once you place it, the sheet redraws and shows the value measured on the model itself.

  3. Move the pointer to where the dimension goes and click. A dimension above or below the view measures across it; beside it, up it. A diameter goes on a leader toward the pointer.

  4. Pick the next one, or press Esc to close the tool.

Instead of clicking a place, press Enter (or click OK) to let the sheet place it. With one circle picked, choose Radius in the right-hand panel (or Radius instead in the right-click menu) for its radius.

Esc drops the last pick first; pressing it again closes the tool.

Tolerances, fits and text

Double-click a dimension (or right-click it and choose Tolerance…). In the Inspector:

  • Tolerance or fit: ±0.1 (or 0.1) for a symmetric tolerance, +0.1 -0.05 for upper and lower, or an ISO 286 class: H7 for a hole, g6 for a shaft. A fit's limits come from ISO 286 for the nominal size, and the Inspector shows them; Fit shown as chooses the class, the class with its deviations, or the limits.
  • Shown as: Value, Basic (boxed), Reference ( ) or Limits (limits need a tolerance; basic and reference dimensions carry none).
  • Decimals: Auto or 0 to 4.
  • Text: shown in place of the measured value (the measured value is still reported).
  • Side, Text position (Centred, At start, At end) and Offset (paper mm), 1 to 200.

Place and move

  • Drag a dimension's line to move it out from the view or to the other side; drag its text to slide it along the line. Drags snap to the standard spacing and to other dimensions' lines; hold Alt to place freely.
  • Right-click a dimension for Flip side, Move text to start, Move text to end, Place text automatically and Reset placement.

Dimension to a virtual sharp

Formed sheet metal and wire are usually dimensioned to virtual sharps: the corner two straight faces or edges would make if the bend between them were sharp. Ask STEVE, for example "dimension the flare from the base to the virtual sharp, outside to outside". In the sheet's code a virtual sharp is sharp(<one>|<other>), like sharp(leg.bottom|flare.bottom):

{"view": "front", "refs": ["base.bottom", "sharp(leg.bottom|flare.bottom)"]}

The sheet draws thin lines running on from both straights, past where they meet, and the extension line starts at that corner. A virtual sharp is a point: it ends a distance, not a length, angle or radius. Two halves that are parallel in the view never meet, and the dimension says so. On formed wire, use the path's straight lines, like sharp(path.p.side0|path.p.side1), for centreline legs to the sharps.

Inside and outside of wire and tube

Wire benders and vendors usually dimension round wire and tube to its outside (or inside), not its centreline. Select a distance that ends on a wire's round face and choose Outside, Inside or Centre (axis) for each end under First end and Second end in the Inspector. Outside measures to the side of the wire away from the other end, inside to the side towards it. Or ask STEVE, for example "dimension the down-turn outside to outside" or "locate the wire from the bracket's top to the top of the wire". In the sheet's code that's ends, one per ref:

{"view": "front", "refs": ["wire.along(p.side0)", "wire.along(p.side2)"], "ends": "outside"}
{"view": "front", "refs": ["wire.along(p.side0)", "sharp(wire.along(p.side1)|wire.along(p.side2))"], "ends": "outside"}

An end can be a straight's face (measured across it), a bend's face (its outermost point that way, the top of the wire over a bend) or a circular edge. On a virtual sharp of two straights' faces, outside gives the outside sharp: where the outsides of the wire would meet. The path's own lines are the centreline, so they have no inside or outside: use the round face swept along them.

Common problems

  • "This geometry has no persistent name": the part is plain CadQuery. Ask STEVE to dimension it with a selector.
  • A dimension isn't drawn (marked in the drawing tree, and counted in the bar above the sheet): its geometry is gone from the model, or it can't be measured in that view (an edge seen end-on). Delete it and add it again.
  • Dimension is unavailable on a design's sheet: dimension each part's own features on its component's sheet. To locate parts against each other on the design's sheet (beside its parts list, balloons and welds), ask STEVE, for example "dimension the wire's top from the plate's top": it names one placed part's faces, like "plate_1:base.top".

Related

  • GD&T: datums and frames on a dimension's feature of size
  • Select and edit

pages.title: GD&T
pages.description: Add datum feature symbols and feature control frames to a drawing, on model features or on a dimension.
pages.html:
Goal: specify form, orientation, location and runout tolerances (ASME Y14.5-2018, ISO 1101).

Prerequisites

  • A part's sheet with a front, top or side view, of a model with persistent names (see Dimensions).

Add a datum

  1. Click Datum in the Annotate group. The right-hand panel shows the next free Letter (A, B, C…; ASME skips I, O and Q); change it if you like.
  2. Click a feature in a view: a face seen edge-on, an edge, or a hole or shaft. Or click a dimension, for its feature of size.
  3. Click where the symbol goes (its distance from the feature), or press Enter to let the sheet place it.

The tool stays open with the next letter; press Esc to close it.

Add a feature control frame

  1. Click GD&T in the Annotate group.
  2. In the right-hand panel, set the Characteristic (flatness, position, perpendicularity…; concentricity, coaxiality and symmetry on ISO sheets only), the Tolerance in the sheet's units, the Zone (width, or a ⌀ cylinder where it applies), the Material condition (RFS, MMC or LMC where it applies) and up to three datums: Primary, Secondary, Tertiary. Only datums on this sheet are offered, and form tolerances take none.
  3. Click a feature in a view, or a dimension.
  4. Click where the frame goes, or press Enter.

Edit and delete

Double-click a datum or frame to edit it in the Inspector. Rename a datum in the drawing tree (F2): the frames that refer to it follow. A datum a frame refers to can't be deleted until that frame no longer does; the Delete entry says which frame.

Projected tolerance zones and other modifiers are written in code, or ask STEVE.

Related

  • Dimensions
  • Select and edit

pages.title: Weld symbols
pages.description: Place weld symbols (AWS A2.4, ISO 2553) on a drawing by hand, with an arrow to each part of the joint.
pages.html:
Goal: call out welds on a weldment's sheet, drawn the sheet's way: AWS A2.4 on ANSI sheets, ISO 2553 on ISO sheets.

Prerequisites

  • A sheet with a view of a model with persistent names (see Dimensions).

Add a weld symbol

  1. Click Weld in the Annotate group.
  2. In the right-hand panel, set the weld's type (fillet, plug, slot, spot, or a groove), its side (arrow side, other side or both), and the size, length and pitch in the sheet's units. Leave a value empty when it isn't given; add the tail (the process or a note), all around and field weld if they apply.
  3. Click one or more edges, faces or corners of the joint in one view: each gets its own arrow.
  4. Click where the reference line starts, or press Enter to let the sheet place it.

The tool stays open with the same values for the next weld; press Esc to step back a pick, or to close it.

Edit, move and delete

Select a weld symbol on the sheet or in the drawing tree (it's listed under its view) to edit the same values in the Inspector; its place stays where it is. Drag it on the sheet to move it. Its right-click menu has Add arrow (then click the edge, face or corner it points at), Remove arrow (when it has more than one), Reset placement and Delete.

Everything is written into the sheet's code as welds=[...], the same rows STEVE writes. Welds written as an expression in the code, and groove angles, root openings, contours and finishes, are edited in the code, or ask STEVE.

Related

  • GD&T
  • Select and edit

pages.title: Notes and balloons
pages.description: Write notes on a drawing sheet, keep numbered general notes, and balloon a design's parts.
pages.html:
Goal: add text to a drawing, and number a design's parts to match its parts list.

Place a note

  1. Click Note in the Annotate group (or right-click empty paper and choose Note).
  2. Click where the note goes on the sheet.
  3. Type it, and press Enter. Esc goes back to choosing the place.

Double-click a placed note to change its text in place; drag it to move it. In the Inspector its position is given in paper mm from the sheet's lower-left corner.

Numbered notes

General notes ("Break all sharp edges") are listed and numbered above the title block. Select Notes in the drawing tree to edit or remove them, or type a new one in Add a numbered note. Templates keep numbered notes (see Sheets).

Balloon a design's parts

Balloons go on a sheet of a whole design: each balloon's number is its item in that sheet's parts list, so the two always agree.

  1. Click Balloon in the Annotate group.
  2. Click a part in a view: a base view, or a section or detail view for a part seen only there.
  3. Click where its balloon goes: past the side or corner of the view you click toward.

Drag a balloon to move it; right-click it for Reset placement. With a balloon on every part written in the code (balloons=True), drag one to give it its own place.

Common problems

  • Balloon is unavailable: the sheet draws a part, or one component; balloons go on a design's sheet.
  • A part has a balloon already: each part takes one balloon.

Related

  • Tables

pages.title: Tables
pages.description: Add a parts list, hole tables, a revision table and a cut list to a drawing sheet.
pages.html:
Goal: list what the drawing's reader needs alongside the views.

Tables stack above the title block (the revision table goes in the top-right corner) and share its width; rows that don't fit are summarised, and every row is in the drawing's CSV files (see Print and export).

Parts list

On a design's sheet, the parts list is on by default: item, quantity, name and description. Click Parts list in the Tables group to put it back if it was removed and select it; select it in the drawing tree to turn it off.

Hole table

  1. Click Hole table in the Tables group.
  2. Click the view that looks along the holes.
  3. Optionally click holes to list just those (click again to leave one out), and a corner to measure from. With no holes picked, every hole that shows round in the view is listed; with no corner, positions are from the view's lower-left corner.
  4. Click OK.

What you should see: each hole tagged in the view (A1, A2, B1…, one letter a size) and listed with its position, diameter, depth and its counterbore, countersink or thread, read from the model's hole features.

Revision table

  1. Click Revision in the Tables group.
  2. Check the Revision (the next letter or number), Date (today) and By, and type What changed.
  3. Click OK.

Select Revisions in the drawing tree to edit or remove rows. The title block's revision is the last row's unless you set one.

Cut list

Click Cut list in the Tables group: each body's stock size and material, per component.

Remove a table

Right-click it on the sheet or in the drawing tree and choose Delete.

Related

  • Notes and balloons

pages.title: Select and edit
pages.description: Select, edit, move, rename and delete what's on a drawing sheet, from the sheet, the drawing tree, menus and keys.
pages.html:
Goal: change what's already on a drawing.

Select

  • On the sheet, click a view, a dimension, a balloon, a datum, a frame, a note, a table or the title block. What's selected takes the workspace colour.
  • In the left-hand panel, the drawing tree lists every sheet; under it its views (section and detail views under the view they're taken from, and each view's dimensions, datums, frames and balloons under it), then its tables, notes and title block. Choosing a row selects it on the sheet, and the other way round; a row on another sheet shows that sheet.
  • A click on empty paper (or Esc) lets go.

What's selected shows its properties in the Inspector, where each change is written at once. A double click on the sheet or in the tree (or Edit in its right-click menu) opens the Inspector with the cursor in its first field.

Something the build couldn't draw (its geometry is gone from the model) is marked in the tree, with why.

The model's geometry

A click on a line of a view selects that face, edge or corner of the model, as a click in the 3D view does (Shift or Ctrl adds to the selection), and draws it in every view that shows it. Right-click it and choose Show in 3D view to see it on the model.

Move

Drag views, dimensions, balloons and placed notes. Hold Alt to move freely; press Esc during a drag to put it back. See Views and Dimensions for how each one moves.

Right-click menus

Right-click anything on the sheet or in the tree, or press the Menu key or Shift+F10 for what's selected. Each menu lists what that thing can do now:

On Menu
A sheet (in the tree) New view, Sheet format…, Title block…, Rename, Duplicate, Move up, Move down, Delete sheet
A sheet's tab (above the paper) the same, with Move left / Move right; drag a tab to move its sheet (a move that would change what the code does is refused, and the menu says why)
A view Edit view, Projected view from here, Section view, Detail view, Align with its parent (once moved), Flip direction (a section), Delete; Rename in the tree (section and detail views)
A dimension Edit, Tolerance…, Flip side, Move text to start / Move text to end or Place text automatically, Reset placement (once moved), Delete
A datum, frame, note or table Edit (Edit text for a note), Delete; Add revision on the revision table; Rename for a datum in the tree
The title block Edit
Empty paper Base view, Note, Dimension, Fit sheet
While a tool is open that tool's own: OK, Undo last pick, Radius instead, Cancel

Keys

Key Does
Delete Deletes what's selected (as its menu's Delete)
F2 Renames the sheet, section or detail view, or datum selected in the tree
Alt+↑ / Alt+↓ Moves the sheet selected in the tree up or down
Enter Finishes the open tool (its OK)
Esc Steps back the open tool's last pick, then closes it; with no tool open, lets go of the selection
Menu key, Shift+F10 Opens the right-click menu for what's selected

Scroll to zoom the sheet, drag empty paper to pan, and double-click empty paper to fit the sheet.

Delete

Deleting a view also deletes the views taken from it and what's on them; deleting a dimension also deletes the datums and frames on it; deleting a sheet deletes everything on it. You are asked first in each case.

Related

  • Drawings

pages.title: Print and export
pages.description: Print drawing sheets to PDF, download them as SVG and DXF with their tables as CSV, or package a whole product's drawings and STEP.
pages.html:
Goal: get the drawing out of STEVE.

Prerequisites

  • A sheet, and a model that builds.

Download a PDF

Export → Drawing (PDF) downloads every sheet as one PDF, a page per sheet at its own paper size. Text is real text (you can search and copy it), with its font embedded, so it looks the same on every computer, and the PDF has no scripts, links or forms.

View or print

  1. Click Drawing in the ribbon's Export group (or Export → Drawing (view · print)).
  2. The sheets open in a full-window preview inside Steve. Use the sheet arrows, zoom and Fit sheet.
  3. Choose Save PDF, then print that PDF at 100% in your PDF application. Close the preview to return to the model.

Download SVG and DXF

Click Drawings in the ribbon's Export group (or Export → Drawings (SVG · DXF)). You get every sheet as SVG and DXF, with the parts list, cut list and hole tables as CSV.

In the DXF, each dimension, balloon, datum, frame, placed note, hole table's tags, and section or detail view is a group of its own, so it moves as one in other CAD programs.

The DXF is in millimetres, with its text as real text, on these layers: VISIBLE (outlines), HIDDEN (dashed hidden lines), DIMENSION (dimensions' lines, arrows and values), TITLEBLOCK (the title block, revision table, parts list, cut list and hole tables), TEXT (notes and labels), THIN (other thin lines), FRAME (the sheet's border), IMAGE (title block logos), and CHAIN and HATCH where a section view has them.

A whole product: every linked document's sheets and STEP

When a product is several documents linked together (a design that links its parts and subassemblies), you can send the whole drawing package without opening each one.

  1. Open the top document: the design that links the others.
  2. Click Product in the Drawing ribbon's Export group (or Export → Product drawings (PDF · STEP)).
  3. STEVE builds each document in turn (a model already generated is reused, so it's quick the second time); the status bar shows which one.
  4. Choose a local destination for <name>-drawings.pdf: every sheet as one PDF, one page per sheet at its own paper size.
  5. It also downloads <name>-step.zip: one STEP file per document, named after it. Each STEP file is made then, so a large product can take a few minutes.

The order is the assembly's: the open document first, then each linked document at the revision it's pinned to, depth first, in the order the code names the links. A document linked twice appears once. The open document is used as it is in the editor, unsaved edits included.

A document with no sheet is left out of the PDF, and one that doesn't build is left out of both; the message at the end names them. Documents build locally when you request the package.

The item is greyed out when the open document links nothing. A link cycle, or links nested more than six levels deep, is refused with a message saying so.

Related

  • Sheets
  • Downloads
